title: Building AI Agents with Bedrock AgentCore, Strands Agents, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)
abstract: Throughout the book, I focused on the theory of data engineering, its practical implementation on AWS, and where to apply generative and agentic AI to add significant value. I focused on the theory and fundamentals of building AI agents for data engineering. I saved the mechanics of building agentic systems for the last chapter of the book for exactly the following reason. The pace of innovation is so severe that just during the time it took me to write this book—admittedly longer than anticipated—models were augmented with agentic systems capable of tool use and sophisticated deep reasoning. Model context protocol (MCP) was open sourced by Anthropic. AWS released the Strands Agents SDK and its groundbreaking toolkit of agentic primitives, Bedrock AgentCore. While this volatility will continue, we can see the formation of a long-term agentic AI technology strategy driven by the industry and wider developer community. In this chapter, I dive deep into the mechanics of implementing agentic AI for data engineering on AWS. I demonstrate how to enhance existing APIs and data sources with MCP to enable agentic AI integration. I’ll build agents trained for data engineering tasks using the Strands Agents SDK. I’ll show you how easy it is to deploy AI agents to production with Bedrock AgentCore.

title: Exploring Agentic AI with Model Context Protocol: A Case Study of Salesman in E-Commerce
abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents that perform multi-step, actionable tasks represent one of the most compelling frontiers in applied AI research, yet many existing systems interact with external services in ad hoc, unstructured ways that undermine predictability, safety, and long-term maintainability. This paper presents Salesman, a case study implementation of an e-commerce AI assistant built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a structured interface specification that governs how large language models (LLMs) invoke external tools. The system pairs a locally hosted LLM with a modular MCP server that exposes tools for product search, order creation and tracking, and promotional offer retrieval. A formal schema-validation layer enforces type safety and graceful error handling at every tool boundary. Evaluated against a 40- task suite spanning five representative e-commerce interaction categories, the system achieves an overall tool selection accuracy of 93.5% and a task completion rate of 94.1%, with a mean endto-end response latency of 2.08 seconds on commodity Apple Silicon hardware. These results demonstrate that MCP-based architectures offer measurable improvements in modularity, explainability, and safety over unstructured agentic pipelines, and suggest a practical template for deploying autonomous AI agents in real-world commercial settings.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: THEORETICAL BASIS AND ARCHITECTURAL MODEL OF THE MODEL CONTEXT PROTOCOL IN AUTOMATED MANAGEMENT OF NETWORK CONFIGURATIONS
abstract: This paper presents the theoretical foundations and architectural model of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as an enabling framework for automated management of network configurations. MCP formalizes the representation, persistence, and exchange of contextual knowledge between AI-driven agents, automation controllers, and programmable network infrastructures. By introducing a context-centric abstraction layer, MCP bridges human intent, machine reasoning, and devicelevel execution, while preserving compatibility with established network management paradigms. The proposed architecture supports intent-based orchestration, closed-loop automation, and multi-vendor interoperability across heterogeneous environments. Emphasis is placed on the separation of concerns between context modeling, decision logic, and execution mechanisms, ensuring scalability, resilience, and operational safety. The analysis demonstrates that MCP constitutes a viable theoretical and architectural basis for next-generation, intelligent, and autonomous network configuration management systems.

title: Enhancing Clinical Decision Support and EHR Insights through LLMs and the Model Context Protocol: An Open-Source MCP-FHIR Framework
abstract: Enhancing clinical decision support (CDS), reducing documentation burdens, and improving patient health literacy remain persistent challenges in digital health. This paper presents an open-source, agent-based framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with HL7 FHIR data via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for dynamic extraction and reasoning over electronic health records (EHRs). Built on the established MCP-FHIR implementation, the framework enables declarative access to diverse FHIR resources through JSON-based configurations, supporting real-time summarization, interpretation, and personalized communication across multiple user personas, including clinicians, caregivers, and patients. To ensure privacy and reproducibility, the framework is evaluated using synthetic EHR data from the SMART Health IT sandbox (https://r4.smarthealthit.org/), which conforms to the FHIR R4 standard. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on hardcoded retrieval and static workflows, the proposed method delivers scalable, explainable, and interoperable AI-powered EHR applications. The agentic architecture further supports multiple FHIR formats, laying a robust foundation for advancing personalized digital health solutions.

title: Understanding How Enterprises Adopt the Model Context Protocol for LLM-Driven Software Engineering
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in AI-based software engineering, but their limitations in complex task execution and multi-tool coordination have driven growing interest in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Existing research has mainly focused on MCP's technical design, with limited empirical evidence on how it is adopted and used in enterprise practice, particularly with regard to deployment challenges, operational risks, and practitioner expectations. To address this gap, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 practitioners from eight companies in the Internet and financial sectors. The findings show that MCP is valued for supporting cross-system collaboration, task decoupling, and knowledge reuse in LLM-based workflows, but its adoption remains constrained by ecosystem fragmentation, cross-component coordination difficulties, and unresolved problems in distributed state management and fault diagnosis. Participants also expressed strong demand for better standardization, lower adoption barriers through low-code or plugin-based approaches, and more systematic operational support. These results provide early empirical evidence on enterprise MCP practice and offer practical implications for improving MCP's standardization, usability, and deployment readiness in real-world software engineering environments.

title: Fail-Open by Default: Divergent requestState Integrity Across Model Context Protocol Reference SDKs
abstract: Version 2 (2026-10-07) — supersedes v1 (2026-10-06). v2 adds Section 9, "Ecosystem Response," documenting that the Python SDK reversed its plaintext requestState default (PR #3032, merged 2026-06-30), a verbatim-sourced validation of the original finding. All v1 sections are retained unchanged. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) 2026-07-28 revision introduced Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR, SEP-2322), in which a server defers a call by returning an InputRequiredResult carrying an opaque, server-minted requestState that the client echoes back on retry. Because this value leaves the server's trust boundary and returns through a party the server does not control, the specification requires servers to integrity-protect it and reject state that fails verification. This note reports a source-level audit of the three official reference SDKs (Python, Go, TypeScript), finding that they shipped divergent and mostly-unsafe defaults for this security-mandated field: the Python SDK protected requestState automatically (authenticated encryption plus principal, audience, and lifetime binding), while the Go and TypeScript SDKs applied no integrity protection by default — Go offering no built-in facility at all, and TypeScript providing one but leaving it disabled unless explicitly configured. Version 2 adds an ecosystem-response section: the Python SDK subsequently reversed its own plaintext default, sealing requestState by default under authenticated encryption (PR #3032, merged 2026-06-30), whose description confirms the prior plaintext behavior in the maintainers' own words. This validates the original finding and narrows the exposed surface to the explicitly-documented low-level / no-codec tier. A direct read of three active MCP servers that use MRTR for destructive or sensitive confirmation found all three converging on the safe pattern. The finding is a default-safety characterization and its ecosystem follow-through, not an exploit against any named deployed product. All evidence is drawn from the SDKs' public source, documentation, and merged pull requests, and is independently reproducible. The TypeScript current-state in Section 9 is labeled secondhand (as characterized by the Python maintainers in PR #3032); the Python-SDK and server observations are from direct reads.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: First Comprehensive Security Audit of the Model Context Protocol Ecosystem: 728 Servers Analyzed
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an emerging standard for LLM-tool integration seeing rapid adoption in production environments. Despite its importance to AI infrastructure security, no comprehensive security baseline exists for the ecosystem. We conducted the first systematic security audit of 728 publicly documented MCP servers, applying a 7-category exploitability-focused methodology across input validation, information disclosure, rate limiting, CORS configuration, tool output safety, resource isolation, and known vulnerabilities. Results indicate a 98% baseline security posture with 2 critical input validation vulnerabilities enabling arbitrary code execution, 6 high-severity issues in CORS and authorization, and 700 servers missing rate limiting protections. Findings are fully reproducible through open-source tooling and publicly available raw data. This baseline establishes the first authoritative security reference for the MCP ecosystem and provides actionable remediation guidance.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: shebanq-mcp: a Model Context Protocol server for querying the BHSA Hebrew Bible in plain language
abstract: shebanq-mcp is a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets biblical-studies scholars query the BHSA Hebrew Bible, the ETCBC linguistic database behind SHEBANQ, in plain language. A question is translated into an Emdros MQL query, validated against the BHSA feature catalogue, and run on a local Emdros engine; the server returns both the query and the real results. The design keeps the query visible and checkable rather than hidden. Every result carries the exact MQL that produced it, queries are validated before they run, and empty results are reported honestly. The goal is to lower the barrier to MQL for teaching and research without removing the scholarly act of reading and judging a query: AI as a way in, not a way around. The server exposes six read-only tools (search_bhsa, run_mql, run_tf, to_citable_mql, to_tf_template, lookup_feature) and can be used from any MCP client or through a hosted web app. It builds on the BHSA dataset (ETCBC), the Emdros text database engine, and SHEBANQ. Live demo: https://shebanq-web.onrender.com What's new in v0.6.0: The BHSA feature catalogue is now generated from the engine itself instead of hand-maintained. A build step joins a snapshot of the engine (object types, kinds, and the value codes that actually occur in the data) with a curated layer of glosses and caveats, and a round-trip test keeps the catalogue in sync on every push. The published ETCBC docs are used as an advisory cross-check. Building the catalogue this way found and corrected real inaccuracies in it: five features were listed on object types the engine does not carry them on, and several value sets did not match the engine (a phantom clause type, the phrase-relation set, and missing not-applicable and unknown values). Validation now accepts exactly what the engine accepts. What's new in v0.5.0: Stated assumptions: every answer now lists the BHSA encoding choices its query depends on (gender and number are word-level form; the gloss is the lexeme gloss; and so on), shown as a one-line note with a detail view in the web app and as an assumptions field in the MCP responses. A valid query that answers a slightly different question than intended is caught before it is cited. Faithful sibling-block conversion, settled empirically: MQL's [A] .. [B] (anywhere after) converts to Text-Fabric's << ordering with row-for-row identical results on both engines (40371 rows on the test shape). Bare sibling juxtaposition turns out to mean adjacent-within-the-parent (25827 rows; gaps skipped), which Text-Fabric templates cannot express, so it is refused with a message that teaches the distinction. What's new in v0.4.1: Documentation accuracy. The README now states plainly that results run on Emdros and the Text-Fabric template shown beside each answer is derived from the MQL by deterministic code, not executed on the live deploy. The Tests section separates the pure-Python suite that runs anywhere from the data-backed Emdros and Text-Fabric suites (including the cross-engine row-level equivalence check) that run in CI. No code or behaviour changed from v0.4.0. What's new in v0.4.0: Every answer now shows the query in two languages: the Emdros MQL that runs, and its Text-Fabric search template, derived from the MQL by deterministic code (no second model call). A test suite proves on every change that the derived template returns the identical result rows on Text-Fabric as the MQL does on Emdros. New tools and surfaces: to_tf_template (MQL to Text-Fabric, the mirror of to_citable_mql), a TF → MQL converter in the web app for turning notebook queries into citable SHEBANQ saved queries, an about page, and search-engine/social metadata. The examples gallery shows both languages for every example, with honest refusals where no Text-Fabric equivalent exists. What's new in v0.3.0: Word-level morphology layer: the translator can now query pronominal-suffix agreement (prs_ps, prs_gn, prs_nu), phrase-dependent part of speech (pdp), lexical set (ls), and name type (nametype). This answers questions like "words with a third person masculine singular suffix", "proper nouns that are place names", or "cardinal numbers" that earlier versions could not express. Every value set was confirmed against the live ETCBC2021 engine, and the new example queries are pinned as regression fixtures. Feature coverage rises to roughly a third of the queryable BHSA features, still weighted toward the features that appear in most scholarly queries. What's new in v0.2.2: The web demo's “include the reference” checkbox no longer re-translates the question. A question is translated once; the checkbox toggles between the flat query and the verse-wrapped query in place, so the same question can no longer yield a different query (or different results) just because the box was toggled. What's new in v0.2.1: Fixed a crash on multi-block queries: a query with two sibling sub-blocks that each request features (for example a predicate verb and its complement, as in “spoke with”) aborted the query worker. Each matched object is now read with exactly its own feature list. The web demo's “include the reference” option now strips a verse wrapper when unchecked, instead of only adding one when checked, so an unchecked box reliably yields a flat query.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Метод доверенной контекстуализации Model Context Protocol для интеллектуальных агентов маркетинговой аналитики
abstract: The paper proposes the MCP-Trust method for trust-calibrated contextualization of intelligent marketing analytics agents. The method extends the use of the Model Context Protocol by introducing a formal context package, MCP server ranking, source consistency checking, evidence graph construction and replay tracing. A mathematical apparatus is proposed for selecting MCP servers and estimating the trust of analytical outputs. A simulation experiment with 180 synthetic analytical requests and 12 virtual MCP servers showed that MCP-Trust reduced MAPE from 15.93 to 8.28%, increased evidence coverage from 0.233 to 0.971 and increased replay reproducibility from 0.46 to 0.99. The integral efficiency metric reached 0.270 compared with 0.228 for CAMIA and 0.190 for the static MCP scheme. The results confirm the applicability of trust-calibrated contextualization for reproducible market intelligence systems.

title: Model Context Protocol Threat Modeling and Analyzing Vulnerabilities to Prompt Injection with Tool Poisoning
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has rapidly emerged as a universal standard for connecting AI assistants to external tools and data sources. While MCP simplifies integration between AI applications and various services, it introduces significant security vulnerabilities, particularly on the client side. In this work we conduct threat modelings of MCP implementations using STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege) and DREAD (Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected Users, Discoverability) frameworks across five key components: (1) MCP Host and Client, (2) LLM, (3) MCP Server, (4) External Data Stores, and (5) Authorization Server. This comprehensive analysis reveals tool poisoning-where malicious instructions are embedded in tool metadata-as the most prevalent and impactful client-side vulnerability. We therefore focus our empirical evaluation on this critical attack vector, providing a systematic comparison of how seven major MCP clients validate and defend against tool poisoning attacks. Our analysis reveals significant security issues with most tested clients due to insufficient static validation and parameter visibility. We propose a multi-layered defense strategy encompassing static metadata analysis, model decision path tracking, behavioral anomaly detection, and user transparency mechanisms. This research addresses a critical gap in MCP security, which has primarily focused on server-side vulnerabilities, and provides actionable recommendations and mitigation strategies for securing AI agent ecosystems.

title: Design and Implementation of an Automated Trojan Reverse Analysis System Based on Model Context Protocol
venue: IEEE International Conference on Information Technology, Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (ICIBA)

title: A Reconnaissance Methodology for Mapping the Pre-Authentication Attack Surface of Model Context Protocol Servers
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is becoming standard infrastructure for connecting language models to external tools and data. Published MCP security work concentrates almost entirely on the agent layer — tool poisoning, prompt injection, and malicious tool descriptions — where the threat is semantic and the victim is the model. That focus leaves a gap. A remotely hosted MCP server is also an ordinary HTTP deployment with an OAuth 2.1 authorization stack in front of a JSON-RPC endpoint, and that stack is reachable by an unauthenticated attacker who never speaks to the model at all. This surface is structurally different from a typical REST API: the protocol mandates machinereadable discovery metadata, encourages open dynamic client registration, and hides the entire tool schema behind a bearer token, which concentrates pre-authentication attack surface into the authorization flow itself. I present a four-stage reconnaissance methodology for mapping that surface on any MCP deployment, with a checklist a tester can apply directly. I illustrate it with an anonymised worked example from authorized testing. No vulnerability was confirmed in that engagement, and none is claimed here; this is methodology, not disclosure.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: MCPToolBench++: A Large Scale AI Agent Model Context Protocol MCP Tool Use Benchmark
abstract: LLMs' capabilities are enhanced by using function calls to integrate various data sources or API results into the context window. Typical tools include search, web crawlers, maps, financial data, file systems, and browser usage, etc. Integrating these data sources or functions requires a standardized method. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized way to supply context to LLMs. However, the evaluation of LLMs and AI Agents' MCP tool use abilities suffer from several issues. First, there's a lack of comprehensive datasets or benchmarks to evaluate various MCP tools. Second, the diverse formats of response from MCP tool call execution further increase the difficulty of evaluation. Additionally, unlike existing tool-use benchmarks with high success rates in functions like programming and math functions, the success rate of real-world MCP tool is not guaranteed and varies across different MCP servers. Furthermore, the LLMs' context window also limits the number of available tools that can be called in a single run, because the textual descriptions of tool and the parameters have long token length for an LLM to process all at once. To help address the challenges of evaluating LLMs' performance on calling MCP tools, we propose MCPToolBench++, a large-scale, multi-domain AI Agent tool use benchmark. As of July 2025, this benchmark is build upon marketplace of over 4k MCP servers from more than 40 categories, collected from the MCP marketplaces and GitHub communities. The datasets consist of both single-step and multi-step tool calls across different categories. We evaluated SOTA LLMs with agentic abilities on this benchmark and reported the results.

title: An Advanced AI Chatbot with Tiered Memory, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Model Context Protocol Integration
abstract: Modern conversational AI systems face three fundamental limitations: inability to recall prior interactions, no access to privatedomain knowledge, and no deterministic connection to external services. This paper presents the design and implementation of an advanced AIchatbot that overcomes all three limitations simultaneously. The system introduces: (i) a six-tier hierarchical memory model with exponentialdecay scoring and dual-write persistence to PostgreSQL and a pgvector semantic index; (ii) a four-stage Retrieval-Augmented Generation(RAG) pipeline combining query rewriting, parent-child chunking, BM25-pgvector hybrid search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and crossencoderre-ranking; and (iii) a Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration layer enabling dynamic tool binding via stdio, SSE, and streamableHTTP transports. The system is orchestrated by a LangGraph directed state-graph agent supporting task complexity classification, LLMgeneratedmulti-step planning, Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) safety interruption, and automatic conversation summarisation. Deployed on aFastAPI, PostgreSQL, and React stack with Docker Compose, the system achieves sub-400 ms median response latency for simple queries anddemonstrates coherent, context-aware, multi-step task execution in production conditions. Comparative evaluation shows the tiered memoryrecall accuracy reaches 91.4% on a held-out biographical quiz benchmark, and the four-stage RAG pipeline outperforms naive single-queryvector search by 23 percentage points of mean reciprocal rank. The HITL safety layer blocks 100% of destructive tool invocations inadversarial testing without a single false negative.
venue: International Journal of Pharmacy with Medical Sciences

title: Domain-Oriented Tooling for Model Context Protocols: Replacing Generic Query Interfaces with Declarative Abstractions
abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly integrated with enterprise data stores via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a prevalent architectural anti-pattern has emerged: exposing generic database query interfaces (e.g., `execute_sql()` or `query_database()`). While versatile in experimental environments, this paradigm introduces operational friction, including high token consumption, non-deterministic query generation, business logic drift, and heightened security risks. This paper formalizes the Domain-Oriented Tooling Pattern, an architectural approach that abstracts relational databases behind a curated set of deterministic, domain-specific tools. We introduce MCP Blueprint, an open-source, configuration-driven framework that decouples tool metadata and SQL execution from application code. We discuss how domain-oriented tool abstractions lower the cognitive threshold required from the orchestrating model—enabling small, lightweight language models (SLMs) to serve the majority of enterprise data retrieval needs—while enforcing business logic determinism and reducing query execution risks.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Trust-as-a-Service: Intelligent Collaboration Orchestration via Model Context Protocol-Aided Agentic AI
abstract: As future networked systems increasingly rely on collaborative task execution among distributed devices, trust becomes essential for identifying reliable collaborators whose capabilities and resources match task-specific needs. However, diverse task needs, limited task-owner knowledge, and complex inter-device relationships make it challenging to evaluate the trustworthiness of potential collaborators and to select suitable collaborators for task completion. To address these challenges, this paper proposes Trust-as-a-Service (TaaS), an intelligent collaboration orchestration paradigm that enables trust evaluation and collaborator selection to be autonomously tailored to different task needs. To realize TaaS, we develop a Model Context Protocol (MCP)-aided agentic AI framework. The central server-side agent autonomously performs trust-related operations according to task-specific needs and delivers trust assessment services to task owners through a unified interface. Meanwhile, device-side agents expose their capabilities and resources via MCP servers, allowing devices to be dynamically discovered, evaluated, engaged, and released to form task-specific collaborative units. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed TaaS achieves 100\% collaborator selection accuracy, along with high reliability and resource-efficient task completion.
