The present research was conducted in collaboration with Superhood Oy to address this problem by investigating whether a rule-based geoparsing and ranking pipeline can automatically identify the primary geographic location from Finnish news articles, reducing reliance on manual effort. A hybrid pipeline was designed and evaluated combining Stanza-based named entity recognition (NER), a postal-first hierarchical ranking strategy, a dynamic Geoapify geocoding resolver, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) correction layer using the Llama 3.3 70B language model for document-level disambiguation. Four pipeline configurations were evaluated on a manually annotated dataset of 60 Finnish news articles. The pipeline configurations were tested in isolation so that the contribution of each component could be measured independently. The baseline configuration achieved an exact match accuracy of 66.67%. Introducing postal-first hierarchical ranking improved accuracy to 80.00%, a gain of 13.33 percentage points. Replacing the static resolver with a dynamic GeoAPI resolver reduced accuracy to 68.33% due to the introduction of noisy candidates. Adding the MCP correction layer recovered accuracy to 83.33%, exceeding both the baseline and the static resolver. The results show that LLM-based contextual reasoning via MCP can recover ranking errors introduced by dynamic geocoding, though at the cost of increased processing time and occasional regressions. The evaluation was conducted on 60 articles, and the results do not generalize beyond the evaluated dataset. The findings demonstrate that a hybrid rule-based and LLM-assisted approach is a viable direction for location extraction in morphologically complex, low-resource language settings.

title: MCP-SandboxScan: WASM-based Secure Execution and Runtime Analysis for MCP Tools
abstract: Tool-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) agents create a new supply-chain surface: Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools are installed like third-party packages, yet their outputs can enter the agent's reasoning context. This enables confused-deputy risks in which attacker-controlled inputs cause otherwise benign tools to exercise legitimate authority over files, environment variables, or network-facing operations and reflect sensitive or instruction-like content into LLM-visible fields. We present SandScope, an MCP-aware audit framework that combines runtime witness detection with semantic tool profiling. SandScope executes portable tools under WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) or drives unmodified MCP servers over standard input/output (stdio), extracts LLM-visible sinks from tool results and prompt/message fields, and reports auditable source-to-sink witnesses from environment, file, and tool-input sources while separately recording network-intent and egress evidence. Its semantic layer recovers declared capabilities from tools/list metadata and static registrations to characterize attack surface when execution is incomplete. We evaluate SandScope on controlled cross-language subjects, an evasion benchmark, and a 100-repository MCP corpus. SandScope completes shallow dynamic scans for 35 repositories and, through a broader semantic profiling pass, recovers metadata for 1,127 tools across 71 repositories, including 886 tools with security-sensitive declared capabilities. A schema-guided exploration pass over the 35 dynamically scanned repositories re-executes 33 and observes source-to-sink witnesses in 12. These results show that SandScope provides practical, auditable evidence for MCP tool risk through controlled execution, MCP-aware sink extraction, runtime witness reporting, and semantic capability profiling.

title: DADL: A Declarative Description Language for Enterprise Tool Libraries in LLM Agent Systems
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the standard interface between large language model (LLM) agents and external tools. At organizational scale, however, it exposes two structural problems. First, every API integration is shipped as a dedicated server process with its own deployment, dependency tree, and credential handling; recent empirical work shows the overwhelming majority of these servers are thin wrappers around REST APIs. Second, the per-tool registration model causes context window consumption to grow linearly with catalog size, forcing real deployments to expose only a small fraction of the APIs an organization actually uses. We present DADL (Dunkel API Description Language), a YAML format describing a REST API's endpoints, authentication, pagination, response shaping, and access classification in a single declarative file. A DADL file is interpreted by an execution layer at runtime; no per-API server process is deployed and no integration code is generated, though the runtime is itself a server. Because all tools share that runtime, credentials and authorization are managed centrally, and the catalog reaches the LLM through a fixed-size Code Mode interface independent of size. The result is an Enterprise Tool Library: a versioned, auditable collection of API integrations any team can extend, share, and consume through one authentication and authorization boundary. The DADL v0.1 specification is released under CC BY-SA 4.0, and a public registry contains 1,833 tool definitions across 20 services. On this catalog, Code Mode reduces the context cost of tool advertisement from approximately 142,000 tokens to approximately 1,000, a 142x reduction; the per-call cost of search and execute invocations is additional and depends on the task.

title: Construction methodology of large language models and intelligent agents for shale oil
abstract: To address the requirement for comprehensive analysis of multi-source geological information and intelligent decision-making in shale oil exploration and development, we propose a method for constructing a domain-specific large language model (LLM) for the shale oil, along with a framework for building and evaluating an LLM-based intelligent agent for shale oil seismic processing and interpretation. Using Qwen2.5-72B and Qwen3-32B as foundation models, we construct a specialized corpus of 21 billion tokens by integrating public shale oil literature and domain knowledge graphs. Leveraging expert annotation and model generation, we also construct 5.8×10 4 question-answer pairs in specific domain with high quality to serve as supervised fine-tuning dataset. We build a multi-stage efficient domain adaptation training framework for the shale oil large language model. First, domain knowledge is injected via task-aware continuous pre-training method, and supervised fine-tuning is executed using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) combined with context-parallel algorithms. Then, direct preference optimization (DPO) and group relative strategy optimization (GRPO) are employed to align domain-specific preferences and enhance reasoning capabilities. In addition, a reflective retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework is built to optimize the accuracy and interpretability of model output. To enhance the tool-use capabilities of LLM and effectively mitigate hallucinations during tool-use process, we construct a specialized toolset by selecting open-source geoscience tools and employ targeted fine-tuning focused on tool utilization. Building on the foundation, we develop an intelligent scheduling service leveraging the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to deeply integrate core functions, such as seismic data processing, seismic interpretation, visualization, and report generation, thereby creating an LLM-driven agent for seismic processing and interpretation of shale oil. Experimental results demonstrate that the shale-oil domain-specific LLM achieves significantly higher accuracy in specialized Q&A compared to general-purpose foundation models, exhibiting excellent domain adaptability. Furthermore, following supervised fine-tuning using geoscience tools, the tool-use capability of shale-oil domain-specific LLM has been improved significantly compared with open-source foundation models.

title: Ambient Cognitive Design (ACD): The Governance Framework for the Second Mind — Volume II: The 120‑Bit Human as Governor of the Teraflop Machine
abstract: The first volume of this series introduced Ambient Cognitive Design (ACD) as a framework for systems that participate implicitly in human cognition, formalizing concepts such as generative affordances, implicit cognitive delegation, and cognitive sovereignty. This second volume builds on that foundation with a quantitative, information‑theoretic reframing of the governance problem. Human conscious thought operates at a bandwidth of 10 to 120 bits per second — confirmed by independent research at Bell Labs, the University of Vienna, and Caltech. This is the channel capacity of conscious authorship, the bandwidth available for deliberate, identity‑constituting cognitive acts. It has remained fixed across human history. Personal Intelligence systems — the convergence of Generative AI, Agentic Workflows, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and Agent‑to‑Agent communication (A2A) — operate at hundreds of trillions of floating‑point operations per second. A single GPT‑4 forward pass requires approximately 560 trillion floating‑point operations. The cognitive gap between human and machine is measurable, quantified, and growing exponentially. This paper presents ACD as the step‑down transformer between the teraflop machine and the 120‑bit human. It introduces: The AAA Protocol (Agency‑Authorship‑Autonomy) — a compression algorithm that translates machine‑channel conclusions into plain‑language disclosures calibrated to the 120‑bit human channel. The Cognitive Transparency Score — a continuous readout showing users what was processed, what was concluded, and what their current Agency, Authorship, and Autonomy scores are. Kamble’s Cognitive Governance Law — a falsifiable law stating that any system participating in human cognition above Stage 4 must satisfy four conditions (human intent sovereign, non‑delegable domains protected, contestability guaranteed, governance context propagated). Production‑ready design artifacts, a 25‑item pre‑launch Governance Checklist, a four‑dimension ACD Certification Scorecard, and implementation roadmaps for both greenfield and brownfield deployments. Together, these volumes provide a complete governance framework for ambient AI, ensuring that the 120‑bit human remains always and irreversibly the Governor of the Teraflop machine.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: robo-cortex: Git-Anchored, Evidence-Based Memory for AI Coding Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly rely on persistent memory to carry lessons across sessions, yet most existing memory stores treat a stored memory as trustworthy indefinitely: a note recorded about a piece of code remains "active" long after the code it described has changed. We present robo-cortex, a local-first memory store for AI coding agents built around a single principle we call knowledge integrity: a memory is only as trustworthy as the code it points at. Every memory may be anchored to the Git blob hash of the source file(s) it describes; a lazy staleness check, triggered on every read, recomputes those hashes and flags any memory whose underlying code has changed for review, while healing memories whose code has reverted to its recorded state. Memories carry explicit, mechanically-derived evidence strength and author-stated confidence rather than opaque relevance scores. The system uses no embeddings, no vector database, and no cloud service; it is pure Python standard library over a single SQLite file per repository, exposed through a command-line interface, a Python SDK, and eight Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools. We describe the design in full and report an honest empirical evaluation: six of six pre-registered functional scenarios pass; a controlled token-economy benchmark on a small subject model (Claude Haiku 4.5, n=5 per arm across three real historical bugs, 30/30 correct fixes) shows a median 11.9% reduction in fresh tokens and 15.1% reduction in API-equivalent cost when the agent is supplied a retrieved context pack, with a recorded memory breaking even after roughly five reuses. We keep every limitation of these measurements in view: a single small model, a single self-documenting codebase, three tasks, and modest sample sizes. The git-blob-hash anchoring, the code-change-triggered invalidation-and-healing lifecycle, and the evidence model are, to our knowledge, novel in combination; the underlying content-addressable primitive is Git's.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Memory Operations in MCP Agent Ecosystems: an Operation Taxonomy, an Evaluation Protocol, and a Reference Implementation
abstract: Version 1.0. This deposit contains the taxonomy, the evaluation protocol, the verified reference base and the first two validated protocol runs of a paper on agent memory in the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem. Contents: (1) a taxonomy of six memory operations - WRITE, READ, CONSOLIDATE, REVISE, INTEND, ASSERT - defined by preconditions, postconditions and externally checkable evidence, plus two mandatory record axes, PROVENANCE and LIFECYCLE, and a mapping of seven existing systems onto them; (2) an evaluation protocol with ten task families, per-metric definitions that name the program that computes them, a run procedure with budgets and repetitions, and a JSON-Schema-validated report format with a mandatory reproducibility disclosure block; (3) a reference implementation of five of the six operations as public MCP servers, with commit-pinned facts and its gaps stated before any measurement; (4) two validated reports of two memory servers measured over MCP stdio in a store-only configuration - ten task families, three repetitions per family, per-family metrics with percentile bootstrap confidence intervals, per-operation profiles read side by side rather than ranked, and the raw request/response logs (33 JSONL files per run) beside which every number can be recomputed; (5) a table generator that produces every comparison table and every inline number of the paper from those two report files, with a check that fails when they drift; (6) a machine-generated verification table for all 135 cited sources (arXiv API, Crossref, direct HTTP probes), a report validator with negative tests, and the raw API responses. Every citation was resolved programmatically and the build refuses to emit a bibliography containing an unresolved source. Token and cost metrics are null by construction, because no model is in the loop; the sample is two servers from one author's reference set and the confidence intervals rest on three repetitions. What is not confirmed is stated explicitly in the paper and in the claim ledger (claims.md). AI assistance in preparing the manuscript is disclosed in the paper and in the repository README; the human author is solely responsible for all claims.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Advancing CERN's AccGPT: Agentic and Graph-Enhanced RAG for Scientific Knowledge Retrieval
abstract: CERN’s extensive documentation spans 71 years of particle physics research and presents significant knowledge retrieval challenges. While the baseline AccGPT system already provides basic RAG capabilities, it struggles with structural relationships, complex queries, and specialized terminology. This thesis presents four enhancements to address these limitations. First, we implement GraphRAG which constructs a knowledge graph of 400,000 entities and 650,000 relationships from CERN’s documentation. This graph enables local entity-based and global community-based retrieval. Second, we develop AccGPT-Agentic which combines GraphRAG with iterative AccGPT retrieval using the ReAct agent framework that adaptively gathers information in multiple steps. Third, we integrate external sources via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that provides real-time access to information sources like event schedules and publications. Fourth, we fine-tune an embedding model for CERN’s vocabulary using a knowledge-graph guided synthetic Q&A set. We evaluate these RAG pipelines using a comprehensive framework that combines individual metrics for each pipeline (DeepEval) with direct head-to-head LLM-judge comparisons. The results reveal a divergence where GraphRAG achieves the highest scores on individual metrics, yet AccGPT-Agentic decisively wins in direct comparison (52.6% preference rate on three-way comparison). This highlights that traditional RAG metrics may not predict actual answer quality with implications for how RAG pipelines should be evaluated. The pipelines demonstrate clear quality-latency trade-offs: AccGPT responds in 0.92s, GraphRAG in 4.34s, and Agentic in 11.81s on average. Domain-specific embedding fine-tuning yields strong improvements (Recall@10: +13.8%) with minimal training cost and hardware requirements. This work delivers two main contributions. For CERN, it provides domain-adapted advanced RAG architectures (GraphRAG and Agentic RAG) that improve answer and retrieval quality. For RAG research, it reveals a critical methodological insight where individual metrics and direct judge preferences can give contradictory results.
venue: CERN Document Server (European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Automated Remediation Guardrails: A Risk-Aware Framework for Validating AI-Generated Production Scripts in Regulated Financial Infrastructure
abstract: The integration of AI coding assistants into DevOps and site reliability engineering workflows has accelerated infrastructure automation, enabling engineers to generate Terraform configurations, shell scripts, and deployment parameter files at speeds previously requiring significantly more time. However, AI-generated infrastructure artifacts introduce a novel category of operational risk: code that is syntactically valid but semantically incorrect in the specific production context, hallucinated API calls, or configurations that create valid infrastructure with unintended security or reliability implications. Research has shown that approximately 40% of programs generated by AI assistants contain exploitable vulnerabilities, and that iterative AI code generation without human validation can increase critical vulnerabilities by as much as 37.6%. In regulated financial services environments where infrastructure changes require documented change control and SOC 2 audit evidence, deploying AI-generated production scripts without a structured validation framework creates compliance gaps that outweigh the productivity benefit. This paper presents a risk-aware remediation guardrail framework developed and deployed at NCR/Candescent for validating AI-generated infrastructure artifacts before their application to production banking environments. The framework implements a four-tier risk classification system based on blast radius analysis, reversibility assessment, and scope validation against existing Terraform state. It integrates with the Jira DCR change control workflow through Model Context Protocol tooling, ensuring every AI-generated artifact modifying production infrastructure is associated with an approved change record. Evaluated against a production corpus of 108 AI-generated artifacts, the automated tier classifier achieved 91% accuracy against expert human review as ground truth, with a 4.6% false negative rate in the safety-critical undertierring direction. The framework caught 7 artifacts containing production errors that visual plan review alone would not have detected.
venue: International Journal of AI BigData Computational and Management Studies

title: AI-Powered Malware Detection: Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Agentic Intelligence in Autonomous Threat Classification
abstract: The exponential growth of malware variants has rendered purely signature-based detection strategies insufficient for modern cybersecurity operations. Machine learning and deep learning have emerged as the primary scalable responses to this challenge – enabling automated classification of unknown samples, detection of behavioral anomalies, and generalization from analyzed specimens to novel variants sharing underlying characteristics. This chapter presents a comprehensive treatment of AI-powered malware detection, progressing from foundational feature engineering through classical gradient-boosted classifiers, raw-byte convolutional neural networks, recurrent sequence models, and graph neural networks, to the frontier integration of these detection capabilities within the agentic AI frameworks established in Chapters 3 and 4 . A central contribution is the demonstration of how a trained malware classifier can be exposed as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool, enabling the multi-agent orchestration patterns of Chapter 4 and the MCP infrastructure of Chapters 6 and 7 to incorporate autonomous threat classification within broader detection and response pipelines. The chapter addresses adversarial machine learning – the systematic evasion of trained classifiers – as a first-order operational concern and treats concept drift and model lifecycle management as practical engineering requirements rather than theoretical considerations. Explainability methods, including SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and large-language-model (LLM)-generated analyst narratives, are presented as bridges between automated detection scores and actionable human understanding. Hands-on exercises implement complete pipelines in Python integrating Splunk, LightGBM, and Claude-backed agent orchestration. Readers completing this chapter will understand how to design, deploy, and critically evaluate AI-powered malware detection systems and how to integrate those systems into the autonomous security operations architectures described throughout this book. As with all technically specific content in this volume, practitioners are advised that the rapidly evolving landscape of both malware and detection AI means that operational specifics described here should be continuously re-evaluated against current developments.

title: Priority-Driven Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems with Fine-Tuned LLMs
abstract: Ambient Assisted Living (AAL) environments aim to enable older people to remain active and lead an autonomous and independent life for as long as possible. Among the technologies that can be incorporated into these settings, socially assistive robots (SAR) seek to establish a more natural and intuitive means of interaction with people, whilst helping them to carry out everyday tasks. One of the main challenges facing the design of these robots is how to enable them to undertake more complex tasks. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have opened new avenues for flexible robot deliberation, yet their integration into real-time robotic systems remains challenging due to latency constraints, reasoning reliability, and the complexity of coordinating multi-step tasks. This paper proposes a hierarchical multi-agent architecture for robot deliberation that addresses these challenges by combining LLM-based planning with structured execution mechanisms within the ROS 2 ecosystem. The proposed architecture employs a supervisor agent that decomposes high-level natural language instructions into prioritised subtasks, enabling a priority-driven execution model that dynamically adapts to task relevance, temporal constraints, and environmental feedback. Subtasks are delegated to a set of Single-Purpose Agents (SPAs), orchestrated via LangGraph state machines and coordinated through a priority-aware scheduling mechanism. A key design principle is the use of Behaviour Trees (BTs) as high-level callable tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), encapsulating closed-loop control strategies while enabling preemptive and priority-consistent execution. This reduces the number of LLM inference steps required per task and improves robustness under dynamic conditions. A further contribution concerns the deployment of fine-tuned, lightweight LLMs—on the order of 0.6 billion parameters—specifically adapted for both the supervisor and the individual SPA roles through parameter-efficient low-rank adaptation (LoRA). These models are trained on role-specific tool-calling datasets to specialise in constrained reasoning patterns and task-specific decision-making, enabling efficient, low-latency inference directly on edge hardware. The combination of fine-tuning and hierarchical priority control enhances both the determinism and responsiveness of the system while mitigating error propagation across agent interactions. The paper presents the full software architecture, a formal characterisation of the system as a priority-aware hierarchical policy over a graph of agent workflows, and an experimental evaluation in an Ambient Assisted Living scenario assessing task success rate, inference efficiency, responsiveness under competing priorities, and overall user experience. Because SPA execution is decoupled from the supervisor’s own reasoning loop, the architecture is designed to keep accepting, processing, and queuing new user queries while previously dispatched SPAs are still executing their tasks.

title: A practical LLM-based agentic framework for strategic cost savings in operations management
abstract: This study presents a practical large-language-model-based agentic framework for strategic cost-savings analysis in enterprise operations management. The work addresses a common gap in enterprise AI: static dashboards lack analytical flexibility, while unconstrained conversational models often lack grounding, governance, and auditability. To bridge this gap, the study designs and implements a proposed hierarchical multi-agent framework centered on a primary analyst agent that orchestrates deterministic tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The system combines governed SQL-based access to structured operational data, documentation retrieval, graph-enhanced reranking, and a bounded custom-analysis path for ad hoc analytical tasks and visualization. The proposed framework is implemented as a Flask-based analytical assistant over a governed relational data environment. At the conceptual enterprise-architecture level, this data layer is represented as Azure SQL Database, while the current prototype instantiates it with a multi-table SQLite environment derived from operational datasets. Its design emphasizes controlled orchestration, read-only computation, scoped table access, and surfaced evidence such as tool traces, retrieval metadata, and executed analysis outputs. For confidentiality, however, the concrete examples reproduced in this report are presented using synthetic or redacted values rather than raw enterprise records. The current evaluation is bounded to implementation-level verification, a retrieval-oriented evaluation framework, representative case-based analytical prompts, and an illustrative backend-comparison benchmark across Azure OpenAI deployments. The current results show that the proposed framework provides a credible basis for grounded enterprise analysis by integrating structured computation, retrieval grounding, and explainability within a single workflow. The backend benchmark further provides bounded operational evidence of trade-offs between latency and token consumption across model deployments. Although the system remains a prototype rather than a production deployment, it demonstrates a reproducible and practically useful foundation for governed enterprise analytical AI and future multi-agent decision-support research.

title: LLM-Assisted Forensic and Compliance Auditing for Public Sector Organizations
abstract: From an IT perspective, modern organizations often exhibit a dichotomy between day-to-day operational practice and formal policy enforcement for security, quality, and regulatory compliance. Reconciling these dimensions remains challenging, particularly in large-scale infrastructures that generate high-volume, heterogeneous, and unstructured data, while relevant policies and standards are typically expressed in natural language and therefore difficult to translate into actionable rules and automated compliance checks. This paper presents FOCUS-PA, a project that develops methods and tools to strengthen digital forensics and continuous auditing for compliance management in the Public Administration (PA) sector. FOCUS-PA delivers a Forensic and Compliance Auditing (FCA) platform tailored to public-sector environments, explicitly accounting for the specific characteristics of administrative information systems, their data sources, workflows, and domain-driven legal and privacy constraints. The platform is designed for the continuous ingestion and analysis of operational data, enabling both ongoing compliance monitoring and the forensic investigation of security incidents. To address these requirements, FOCUS-PA introduces an agentic framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) via a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach. By adopting the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the platform provides a unified mechanism to connect natural-language policy documents with structured operational logs, supporting consistent interpretation, correlation, and evidence-driven auditing. A central contribution of FOCUS-PA is reducing the cost of security policy engineering in compliance-auditing solutions. Today, experts must translate regulatory texts and internal procedures into machine-readable specifications - a process that is slow, expensive, and quickly becomes outdated as policies and regulations evolve. We investigate how large language models (LLMs) can help extract and structure policy specifications from unstructured documents (e.g., procedure manuals) and observed operational data, facilitating their conversion into machine-verifiable rules (“Policy as Code”). This approach aims to accelerate policy onboarding and maintenance and to enable the timely adoption of emerging regulations and standards (e.g., NIS2) by streamlining the translation of high-level requirements into actionable compliance checks. We detail requirements for PA deployments and LLM-assisted policy engineering, describe the platform architecture and implementation, and discuss integration aspects, demonstrating how FOCUS-PA can improve compliance governance and accelerate incident investigation through scalable analytics and expert-supervised automation.
venue: European Conference on Cyber Warfare and Security

title: ПРОЄКТУВАННЯ АРХІТЕКТУРИ БЕЗПЕЧНОЇ АВТОНОМНОЇ МУЛЬТИАГЕНТНОЇ СИСТЕМИ ТЕСТУВАННЯ НА ПРОНИКНЕННЯ НА БАЗІ ВЕЛИКИХ МОВНИХ МОДЕЛЕЙ
abstract: The article provides a comprehensive analysis of methods and approaches for designing the architecture of a secure multi-agent system for autonomous penetration testing based on large language models. The relevance of the study is driven by the need to bridge the gap between resource-intensive, slow manual information security audits and the dangerous full automation of classic scanners, the uncontrolled use of which in production environments poses critical risks of Denial of Service (DoS) or exceeding the authorized scope. An analysis of recent publications revealed that existing AI-based solutions (e.g., PentAGI or Penligent) suffer from specific threats such as cascading failures, identity spoofing, and group hallucinations of language models. The theoretical foundation of the work is the concept concept of integrating a neural network approach and cryptographic protection of operations, according to which large language models exclusively perform the functions of semantic context management, strategic planning, and task routing. The direct execution of commands and the generation of evidence are delegated to real specialized tools, eliminating the risk of artificial artifact fabrication. The research methodology involves designing the backend infrastructure as a modular monolith using TypeScript and the Nest.js framework based on CQRS and Saga architectural patterns. To manage the attack deployment process, the LangGraph framework is utilized, formalizing the audit as state graphs with a clear distribution of tasks (reconnaissance, vulnerability search, verification) among independent agents. The main result of the research is the developed mechanism for strict tool isolation: all destructive utilities, including Metasploit, nmap, and OWASP ZAP, are launched in disposable Kali Linux-based Docker containers. Communication between the orchestrator and the isolated environment occurs solely through standard input/output streams according to the Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification, without exposing external network ports. To ensure control over the process, a dynamic interruption system (Approval Gating) has been implemented, supporting three levels of autonomy (Manual, Semi-auto, Full-auto) and allowing the specialist to approve high-risk actions. To guarantee the immutability of the evidence base, cryptographic signing of the obtained artifacts using the Ed25519 algorithm is implemented. The conclusions prove that the proposed architecture eliminates the problem of excessive artificial intelligence agency, creating a reliable intermediary layer between the target system and the expert. Future research will focus on scaling the infrastructure to enable parallel testing of a significant number of hosts.

title: Evolution of Systems Design in AI Era
abstract: The rise of artificial intelligence, particularly generative models and autonomous agents, is reshaping how modern software systems are conceived, built, and operated. For decades, system design has been grounded in deterministic principles: predefined workflows, stateless services, and predictable execution paths. However, the emergence of large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic frameworks has introduced a new design philosophy in which adaptive intelligence is treated as a first-class architectural primitive rather than a bolt-on feature. This paper presents a practitioner-informed study of how system design has evolved in the AI era, moving from monolithic and microservices paradigms toward AI-native architectures centered on reasoning, tool orchestration, and continuous learning. We identify four fundamental architectural shifts: from static workflows to dynamic orchestration, from batch and streaming pipelines to continuous context, from stateless services to contextual memory, and from monolithic intelligence to specialized agents. We examine agentic design patterns (ReAct, Planning, Tool Use, Reflection, Multi-Agent Collaboration, Human-in-the-Loop, and Human-on-the-Loop), emerging interoperability protocols (Model Context Protocol and Agent-to-Agent communication), and the role of skills as a complement to tools in the capabilities layer. We also examine when traditional architectures remain preferable to AI-native designs, discuss token-cost and context-window economics, and analyze the CapEx-to-OpEx maturation curve that enterprises should expect. Four case studies drawn from financial services, marketing technology, e-commerce, and healthcare illustrate measurable outcomes. A challenge-impact matrix is proposed to help enterprises prioritize mitigation strategies, a five-level AI-native maturity model is offered to guide transformation, guidance is provided for keeping pace with a rapidly evolving model and vendor landscape, and ethical, governance, and societal considerations are discussed alongside the architectural framework. The study concludes that AI-native architecture is not a discrete technology choice but a discipline that redefines the role of the system architect in an era of adaptive, reasoning-capable software.
venue: International Journal on Science and Technology

title: A Unified Model Predicting Opsin Spectral Properties Across Protein Folds
abstract: Type I (microbial) and type II (animal) opsins are two independent solutions to the same problem in Nature: photoreception. These membrane proteins bind the chromophore retinal—a vitamin A derivative—in structurally analogous pockets whose residue composition determines spectral properties through the same physics. LAMBDA (Light Absorption Modeling through Binding Domain Analysis), the central contribution of this thesis, exploits this convergence: it is a graph neural network that predicts lambda max (the wavelength in the absorption spectrum where the absorbance is maximum) of opsins from binding pocket composition. By representing binding pockets as graphs aligned on retinal, LAMBDA treats spectral tuning as a property of the chromophore environment rather than the surrounding fold. Trained on 2,120 sequences, it achieves 7 nm mean absolute error on type I opsins and 5 nm on type II. Application of LAMBDA to 47,700 sequences allowed to produce the Opsin Atlas, a dataset of predicted spectral properties spanning the known diversity of both families. Cross-family learning of properties requires a shared structural vocabulary. While type II opsins have the Ballesteros–Weinstein numbering system, type I opsins lacked an equivalent. MOGRN (Microbial Opsin Generic Residue Numbering) has been developed to fill this gap. MOGRN is a structure-based numbering system anchored to the conserved retinal-binding site, validated against 129 structures spanning the functional diversity of microbial rhodopsins. LAMBDA uses MOGRN positions for type I opsins and Ballesteros–Weinstein positions for type II to construct binding pocket graphs from sequence alone. ProtOS, a Python framework that integrates protein data management with access to machine learning models, provides the infrastructure that makes this feasible at scale: it handles sequences, structures, embeddings, and annotations through a consistent processor architecture, routing 47,700 sequences through the full analysis pipeline without manual intervention. ProtOS-MCP extends this infrastructure through a natural language interface via the Model Context Protocol, making spectral prediction, annotation, and protein engineering workflows accessible to structural biologists through conversation rather than code. As an example of a workflow that integrates these tools, ProtOS is used to combine models for structure prediction, backbone design, and sequence design into a single pipeline to design a light-gated enzyme, rhodozyme, a rhodopsin scaffold carrying a transplanted catalytic triad.
venue: Repository for Publications and Research Data (ETH Zurich)

title: Chakravyuh: A Graph-Grounded, Policy-Bound Agent for Card-Fraud Investigation under Uncertainty
abstract: Fraud analysts spend most of an investigation assembling evidence rather than judging it, and automated alerting systems flag far more legitimate customers than fraudsters. We present Chakravyuh, an agent that investigates card-fraud alerts end to end on a property graph: it gathers evidence through installed graph queries exposed over the Model Context Protocol, recalls prior cases, estimates a fraud probability from typed evidence, recommends actions under a written fraud policy with explicit approval routes, requests additional evidence through controlled channels when the case is under-determined, and writes the finished case back into the graph as memory. Verdicts are produced by a deterministic log-odds evidence model; a language model is confined to follow-up tool selection and to drafting summaries and suspicious activity reports, and every identifier it writes is verified against the evidence. Working on the IEEE-CIS card transaction data (590,742 transactions), we show that: (i) identity granularity determines whether case memory is informative — at the customer or card level, 22% of fraud-linked entities also appear in cleared cases, whereas at the level of a reconstructed card fingerprint the overlap is 1 in 7,635; (ii) running a connected-components algorithm on the card-in-use rather than the card number separates genuine multi-device rings from a single 5,103-card artefact; (iii) the institution's own closed cases are so strongly selected that its risk model has an AUC of 0.058 on them, and calibrating evidence weights on that history, with no look-ahead, raises the AUC of the agent's pre-evidence probability on held-out cases from 0.45 to 0.66. An ablation study attributes most of the accuracy gain to device and network evidence, and most fraud recall to fingerprint memory. The central finding is an explaining-away effect: conditional on the bank's model having already fired, a new device lowers rather than raises the probability of fraud. On a 20-case benchmark, the agent reached a decision in 19 cases, requested evidence in 12, revised its recommendation in all 12, and surfaced two fraud schemes absent from the documented typologies. Built for the TigerGraph Agentic Fraud Investigation and Next-Best Action challenge at Hacker House Goa 2026. Code and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/Tanmay2006-Tech/chakravyuh-fraud-agent
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Failures: Deterministic Failure-Mode Guardrails Make Coding Agents Build Resilient Systems
abstract: This paper investigates whether deterministic failure-mode analysis can improve the resilience of software produced by AI coding agents. We present Failures, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that encodes eleven software reliability dimensions, including atomicity, idempotency, timeout and ambiguous-outcome handling, concurrency, ordering, consistency, availability, resource exhaustion, recovery, observability, and retry safety. Failures provides deterministic checks with line-level evidence and guides coding agents to reason about failure modes before implementation and verify completed code afterward. We evaluate the approach across six realistic software scenarios using controlled comparisons and blind agent studies involving Claude, Cursor, and Codex. Across 17 matched agent comparisons, 16 improved on at least one resilience criterion. We additionally evaluate six adversarial cases to identify limitations and false positives in the deterministic analyzer. The work examines how AI-assisted software development can move beyond functional correctness toward software that remains reliable under failures, ambiguity, retries, and concurrency. FILES- Failures_MCP_Paper.pdf — the paper (15 pp., 2 figures, 10 tables, 16 references).- failures-artifact.zip — evaluation/ + examples/ + mcp_server/, the complete artifact needed to reproduce Tables 7, 8 and 9 of the paper. REPRODUCING THE RESULTS pip install -e . (or: pipx install failures-mcp) python evaluation/run_evaluation.py --mode proxy python evaluation/run_evaluation.py --mode manual Both commands run offline with no external services. The proxy run reproducesthe 6-scenario study (Table 7); the manual run scores the frozen agent outputsin evaluation/runs/{claude,cursor,codex}/ and reproduces Table 8 (17 matchedbaseline/failures-enabled pairs; 16 improve on at least one resiliencecriterion). evaluation/results.json and evaluation/adversarial_results.json arethe machine-readable sources for every table. Scenario prompts are hashed andthe hash plus repository commit are recorded in each run manifest. CODE https://github.com/mayowa-kalejaiye/Failures CITATION Kalejaiye, Oluwamayowa (2026). Failures: Deterministic Failure-Mode Guardrails Make Coding Agents Build Resilient Systems. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22966362 LICENSE CC BY 4.0. The software artifact is also released under the MIT License.
