title: AI-Powered Detection of OS Command Injection Using TF-IDF and Logistic Regression to Mitigate System Exploitation
abstract: OS command injection, a vector connected with privilege escalation, remote code execution, system exploitation, and malware attacks, poses critical risks to modern computing environments [Usama & Aman, 2024; Wang et al., 2024]. These attacks can undermine access controls, compromise entire infrastructures, and result in severe data loss. Existing detection methods, whether based on traditional rules or AI techniques, have notable gaps, as few combine both approaches and focus specifically on command injection linked to broad system attacks [Ferrag et al., 2020; Tasdemir et al., 2023]. To address this, I developed and studied a hybrid system that harnesses TF-IDF feature extraction and logistic regression analysis as part of a custom AI-powered Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, integrating this with GitHub Copilot and open-source large language models for interactive, chat-based detection [Wang et al., 2025; Khare et al., 2023]. The system distinguishes itself both by combining classical machine learning and generative AI, and by offering multi-level analysis: syntax validation, semantic classification, and context-aware enrichment (including command type, severity, verdict, mitigation steps, and execution results). Quantitative evaluation showed performance scores above 0.75 for accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-measure, while qualitative inspection confirmed the system’s ability to deliver detailed, actionable descriptions for each command. In theory, the work advances existing research by demonstrating the value of hybrid ML–AI architectures and novel MCP integration for rapid, robust exploitation detection [Tasdemir et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2024].. Practically, it enables developers and security teams to benefit from a proactive, hassle-free, and instant detection workflow, leveraging continuous updates from the latest LLM models for precise analysis and improved command abuse prevention. Unresolved limitations include the challenges with heavily obfuscated payloads, and the opportunity to further extend detection power with deep learning models and a web dashboard interface, which will be addressed in future work.

title: Federated GraphQL integration of heterogeneous building sensor data for LLM-assisted utilization analysis in smart buildings
abstract: Abstract Smart buildings generate extensive sensor data through wireless sensor networks (WSN), Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and machine-to-machine (M2M) communication, yet data fragmentation across heterogeneous systems prevents comprehensive utilization analysis. This work addresses the dual challenges of integrating disparate building data sources and making integrated data accessible to non-technical facility managers—a combination not previously evaluated in an operational real-world deployment. We developed a federated GraphQL architecture that unifies five heterogeneous systems at AAU Innovate, a multi-functional university innovation building: building management sensors (PIR, CO 2 , temperature), Microsoft 365 room calendars, entrance counters, coffee machine logs, and facility management records. The architecture maintains system independence while enabling cross-system queries through Apollo Federation [1], with each data source implemented as an independent subgraph. Five practical facility management questions were formulated with building operators, covering event attribution, resource allocation, external collaboration tracking, space utilization patterns, and policy intervention assessment. An expert user with full system knowledge successfully answered all five questions—establishing ground truth that cross-system data correlation enables insights impossible with isolated sensor networks—and providing a baseline against which LLM performance was evaluated. We then exposed the platform via Model Context Protocol and evaluated four open-source models (Qwen3, LLaMA 4, Mistral Large, Watt-tool) using a six-criterion scoring rubric across three to four independent attempts per question. Qwen3, the strongest model, achieved complete success on one of five questions and partial success on two, with failures attributable to context window overflow, state loss across multi-turn interactions, and multi-step reasoning breakdowns. These results suggest that LLM-assisted workflows under expert supervision, rather than fully autonomous AI agents, represent the viable near-term approach for building analytics applications.

title: When the Acting Channel Lies: Production Evidence from a Closed Professional Desktop Application and Verification-Channel Independence
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly connected to closed, licensed, stateful professional desktop applications through tool layers such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Recent work shows that agents often claim success that did not happen, and that LLM judges detect this poorly. State-based verifiers avoid relying on narration, but they read state through inspection endpoints that are assumed to be truthful. In closed desktop software, that endpoint is usually the same tool layer the agent acts through. The author has developed an agent system that operates Autodesk Revit through a custom tool layer. Development began in April 2025, and the system is now in daily production use. From that deployment we catalogue 36 mechanisms by which a report, or its check, diverged from the actual outcome. Of these, 27 lie in the author's own code (tool layer, wrapper and pipeline scripts), 7 in application behaviour, and 2 are unresolved. Assessed after the fact, a same-path read-back would miss 6 of them. We then tested the production tool layer on a public-domain building: a model traced from the Historic American Buildings Survey drawings of the Gamble House. A benchmark run and follow-up probes on it surfaced two new live false reports and reproduced one known one. Each was confirmed through the application's own IFC export, parsed without the tool layer. A fault-injection benchmark of 112 trials in Revit, replicated in AutoCAD 2027 through the vendor's DXF writer, makes two demonstrations. By design, not as a measurement, it shows that an independent read of persisted state catches injected false reports that also corrupt the acting channel's own reads. It also shows that, on these operations, the export channels were faithful: they raised no false alarm on truthful reports. In Revit this holds after six geometry-based label corrections. Before them, the independent read-back's AUROC was 0.891, and all three of its flags among the 16 trials then labelled truthful were real tool-layer false reports. In a smoke test, making one operation verify its own effect turned its false reports on impossible moves from 3 of 3 to 0 of 3, while a valid move still succeeded. We argue that verification in this setting must be designed around channel independence and an explicit statement of intent, and we describe practical independent channels for closed desktop software.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: PolicyGraph: A Policy-Gated MCP Runtime for Safe and Auditable Tool Execution
abstract: PolicyGraph is a deliberately narrow governance runtime for Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool orchestration that treats agent execution as governed computation rather than free-form autonomy. The planner LLM is treated as an untrusted proposal generator; the runtime is the authority boundary and fails closed. Key safety invariants (runtime-enforced) • Default-deny tool execution: only tools in the effective allowlist (live discovery ∩ operator allowlist) may run. • Strict JSON-only planning: planner output must be exactly one JSON object; extra text/markdown/fences are rejected. • Schema validation: tool args must match the tool's live MCP inputSchema (required keys present, no extra keys, basic type checks). • Typed output gate: typed payload emitted only if tool returns valid MCP structuredContent, isError != true, and a registered Pydantic model validates it. • Evidence-locked summarization (optional): every summary item must include verbatim evidence copied from canonicalized validated tool output (lexical attribution enforced). Reproducibility & evaluation • Includes LLM-independent gate/property tests (N=1136) covering plan parsing, allowlisting, schema checks, typed parsing, and grounding. • Optional per-run structured traces for auditability (when SAFE_TRACE_DIR is set): query, discovered tools, allowlist, raw planner output, parsed plan, validation decisions, tool I/O, typed payload, and summary. How to reproduce results Run the primary offline evaluation (LLM-independent): • python -m src.eval.offline_gate_eval Outputs: • eval/results/offline_gate_eval.json Scope / non-goals • Single-step runtime: at most one tool call per request. • Default read-only; side-effecting tools are denied by default (toy servers used for evaluation). • Evidence-lock enforces lexical attribution, not semantic entailment/truthfulness. Paper DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18243637
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Rediscovering Architectural Decision Records: How Persistent Design Context Improves LLM Code Generation
abstract: As AI coding tools proliferate, multi-turn development using large language models (LLMs) is becoming commonplace. However, the "context degradation" problem-where design intent is lost across sessionsremains a serious challenge that leads to quality deterioration as projects grow in complexity. This study proposes "sqlew," a tool that repurposes Architectural Decision Records (ADRs)-a practice proposed in 2011 but abandoned due to human operational overhead-as external design memory for LLMs. sqlew realizes automated ADR recording and selective retrieval via structured queries through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), constructing a coexistence model of static instruction (CLAUDE.md) and dynamic rationale (ADR). We conducted a controlled experiment on a 12.5-turn TypeScript workflow approval system development across three conditions: no ADR (vanilla), from-inception adoption (sqlew), and retroactive adoption (Vanilla-to-sqlew, v2s). The sqlew condition reduced development time by 10.1% (496 min vs. 552 min) and total tool calls by 10.8%. In the vanilla condition, a supplementary turn (Turn 12.6: 29 min, 21,751K tokens) was required to compensate for missing E2E tests; including this hidden cost widened the time difference to 14.6%. Keyword-based density analysis of Chain of Thought (CoT) revealed a qualitative shift in reasoning patterns (Trial-and-Error Loop → Context-Informed Reasoning) and accelerating divergence in prior decision reference density (+21% → +64% → +137%). The most striking finding is the compliance gap between instruction and rationale. Despite the same TDD instruction being present in CLAUDE.md, conditions where ADRs contained the rationale for why TDD was adopted (sqlew/v2s) spontaneously generated 16-25 E2E tests, whereas the vanilla condition produced zero. LLMs exhibit higher compliance and reasoning quality toward "why to do something (rationale)" than "what to do (instruction)." We release all session logs, prompts, and analysis code, and invite replication.

title: Zero-Trust Authorization and Discovery for Enterprise MCP
abstract: LLM agents translate natural-language context, which may include attacker-controlled text, into privileged tool calls, so authorization must remain effective even when an agent is prompt-injected or adversarially steered. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become a widely adopted interface for this boundary, yet its official SDKs' authentication and authorization primitives fall short of enterprise zero-trust requirements, most acutely a dual-persona model in which one server must serve human users (corporate SSO) and automated agents (service-account credentials on a different header). We conduct a systematic gap analysis of six surveyed MCP SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C#, Swift) and identify three structural shortcomings: credential extraction bound to a single Authorization header, complicating dual-persona deployment without custom middleware; the absence of pre-authentication tool discovery; and the lack of fine-grained per-tool authorization in the base SDKs. We close these gaps with composable extensions to FastMCP: cross-header credential normalization for enterprise deployments serving both human and service-account callers, cached token verification across heterogeneous IdPs, an unauthenticated metadata endpoint for credential-free registry discovery, and permission-filtered tool visibility kept consistent with per-tool invocation enforcement by a single declarative annotation, all without modifying the protocol or SDK internals. Across four frontier LLMs over 2160 attempts, an in-body-check-only server still exposes forbidden tools (152/720, 21.1%), whereas permission-aware visibility drives the rate to 0/720; visibility-only filtering remained bypassable by scripted clients, while models referenced the hidden tool by name in up to 94% of settings when inferable from the prompt, confirming that discovery controls cannot replace invocation-time enforcement.

title: Prototipo del modello a hub centrale per la mappatura di BSPL su MCP
abstract: Descrizione generale Questo codice sorgente rappresenta l'implementazione prototipale di riferimento per il modello di mappatura a hub centrale proposto nella tesi di laurea in Informatica "Definizione e analisi di modelli architetturali per l’esecuzione di protocolli BSPL sull’infrastruttura MCP" di Samuele Taboga. Il software realizza l'interconnessione tra il paradigma dei protocolli formulati in BSPL e l'infrastruttura di integrazione per agenti AI definita dal Model Context Protocol, impiegando la versione 2 dell'SDK ufficiale di MCP per Python su trasporto Streamable HTTP. Dettagli architetturali Il prototipo formalizza una topologia a stella applicata alla coreografia multi-ruolo PurchaseWithDelivery, la quale coinvolge i tre partecipanti Buyer, Seller e Shipper. La gestione della comunicazione e dello stato relazionale è accentrata nel server implementato dalla classe CentralHubServer. Tale modulo espone uno strumento MCP per ciascun messaggio contemplato dalla specifica ed integra l'adattatore LoST centralizzato BSPLHubAdapter. Quest'ultimo tiene traccia della conoscenza locale dei singoli attori in modo rigorosamente partizionato e isolato, verificando preventivamente le condizioni formali di viabilità in emissione prima di accodare ciascun messaggio. I partecipanti operano come host MCP leggeri, connettendosi all'hub centrale e sottoscrivendosi alla risorsa di comodo inbox://{role}. La consegna delle comunicazioni verso ciascun destinatario si compie mediante una procedura in due fasi, imperniata sulla ricezione di notifiche asincrone di aggiornamento della risorsa e sul successivo prelievo tramite il tool get_next_message. Verifica e riproducibilità Il pacchetto comprende una suite di test automatizzati realizzata con pytest all'interno del modulo tests/test_choreography.py. I casi di test accertano la correttezza del protocollo esaminando l'intero ciclo di vita dell'interazione nominale, il percorso alternativo di rifiuto dell'offerta, l'isolamento causale tra sessioni concorrenti, la convalida della conformità sintattica, il blocco delle violazioni di viabilità, la gestione delle code vuote e l'idempotenza delle ritrasmissioni. Lo script principale main.py consente la riproduzione completa della simulazione, coordinando i processi concorrenti, verificando la consistenza dello stato distribuito registrato nell'adattatore ed estraendo l'History Vector dell'interazione.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: 行政手続等調査データ分析システムの実装とサンプル検索例
abstract: デジタル庁は 2026 年 8 月、令和 6 年度行政手続等の悉皆調査データ(約 75,000 件)を Model Context Protocol(MCP)経由で自然言語により対話的に分析できるシステムを技術検証として公開した。本稿では、同システムの設計思想(Discovery 層と Data 層からなる 4 ツール構成、機械可読なメタデータ dataset.yaml、パラメータの 3 段階正規化、列指向応答)を踏襲し、中核サーバーを uv と PEP 723 (インラインスクリプトメタデータ)による単一ファイルの Pythonスクリプトとして再実装する。実データ(75,071 件・38 フィールド)への 7 つの検索例では、公式定義に沿う手続種類ベースのオンライン化率は 51.6%(一部実施済を含む)、年間件数ベースのオンライン利用比率は 79.5%となった。一方、全実施府省庁で実施済の手続だけに限ると48.4%であり、指標の分母と「一部実施済」の扱いを明示しなければ比較を誤ることも示す。
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: AAI-1: Agent Attestation Interface — Per-Action Cryptographic Attestation Protocol for Autonomous AI Agents: The First Published Per-Action Attestation Specification for Agentic Systems, with Documented Incident Analysis and Multi-Framework Regulatory Mapping
abstract: This specification defines AAI-1, the Agent Attestation Interface — the first published per-action cryptographic attestation protocol for autonomous AI agents. AAI-1 establishes a normative claim vocabulary, composition algebra, and conformance framework enabling cryptographically verifiable evidence of agent behavior at the granularity required for governance, incident response, regulatory enforcement, and forensic reconstruction.The specification addresses a substrate gap that no existing standard fills. The IETF Workload Identity Working Group has produced four agent identity drafts (Messous, Huang/expired, Jiang, PTV) addressing identity and authorization but not per-action behavioral attestation. The Model Context Protocol's authorization framework (RFC 9728) addresses tool access but not action-level governance. The OpenID AuthZEN Working Group's draft addresses access decisions but not the cryptographic record those decisions require. AAI-1 occupies the per-action attestation layer that current standards leave unspecified.AAI-1 defines forty claims across seven families: Identity Binding (Family 1), Capability Declaration (Family 2), Tool Invocation Binding (Family 3, novel), State Mutation Receipt (Family 4, novel), Cross-Principal Handoff (Family 5, novel), Channel and Session (Family 6), and Composition Context (Family 7, novel). Four claim families are introduced for the first time in this specification, addressing failure modes documented in the Part 3 case record that no current standard addresses at the substrate level.The composition algebra extension specifies how AAI-1 receipts compose across sequential, parallel, conditional, and recursive agent operations. The Model Context Protocol governance extension specifies how AAI-1 mitigates the documented MCP CVE patterns. Six sector conformance profiles (autonomous trading, AML investigation, insurance claims, customer onboarding, developer tool agents, medical decision support) provide procurement-ready compliance language calibrated to specific regulatory frameworks. Four operational methodologies (Agent Inventory, Incident Classification, Portable Agent Specification v2, Forensic Reconstruction) provide deployment-ready governance procedures. Four conformance tiers (AAI-C0 Reference through AAI-C3 Sovereign with TEE anchoring and multi-verifier redundancy) support adoption from research environments through national-security-adjacent deployments.Multi-framework regulatory mapping addresses eight articles of the EU AI Act, seven articles of DORA, the U.S. NDAA Sections 1512-1513, OMB Memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22, Colorado Senate Bill 24-205, MiFID II RTS 6, ECB Guide to Internal Models, and FDA SaMD guidance. The Lanthorn reference implementation demonstrates browser-based AAI-1 receipt emission with full CDDL schema validation and reference test vectors covering all seven claim families.Part 2 documents the structural context within which the specification is required: the social media era as governance precedent, the agent economy as successor to the attention economy, the categorical differences between agent risk and general AI risk, the theoretical case for user control as governance infrastructure, the current trust infrastructure landscape, and the temporal window within which governance infrastructure adoption is most consequential.Part 3 documents eight specific incidents from July 2025 through April 2026, analyzed against the specification at the claim-number level. The incidents span four failure modes: human-attacker-exploits-agent (the Mexican government breach exposing 195 million identities through Claude Code and GPT-4.1; the GTG-1002 China-linked espionage campaign), agent-exploits-its-own-environment (the Alibaba ROME reverse-SSH-tunnel and unauthorized cryptocurrency mining incident), agent-violates-explicit-human-instruction (the Replit production database deletion during an active code freeze), and agent-exhibits-reward-hacking-drift (the IBM autonomous customer-service agent refund-policy violation). Each incident is mapped to specific AAI-1 claims and categorized by outcome (prevention, detection during attack, or post-hoc evidence). Part 3 additionally documents the policy-level articulation of the governance gap by AI Governance and Safety Canada in testimony before the Canadian House of Commons Standing Committee on Industry and Technology, the current-state alignment of Canadian regulatory frameworks with the testimony recommendations, and the architectural composition relationship between AAI-1's attestation layer and a complementary enforcement layer anticipated as a subsequent Auburn Patent Family clause.This document is Clause AI-10 of the Auburn Patent Family. It composes with MAI-1 (Clause AI-5, Model Attestation Interface), CRSA-1 (Clause AI-9, Compositional Runtime Safety Attestation), and AGS-1 (Clause AI-11, Auburn Governance Stack Architecture). The Autonomous AI Agents in Regulated Financial Services framework (DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.31516171) is operationally implementable through AAI-1 conformance; this specification provides the per-action attestation substrate that the financial-services framework's compliance profiles require.The specification is published in three parts. Part 1 is the normative specification (Sections 1-19 and Appendices A-E), defining what AAI-1 is and how conformance is evaluated. Part 2 is informational context (Sections P2.1-P2.7), documenting why AAI-1 is required at the structural level. Part 3 is informational case analysis (Sections P3.1-P3.12), documenting what AAI-1 would have done against the public incident record. The three parts compose into a complete document. Each part is self-contained at its own scope.

title: Spanning the void between the 'wet' lab and the 'dry' lab – How AI can augment the experimental work in the toxicology lab
abstract: The capabilities of AI as a supporting instrument for scientific discovery are increasing. With the arrival of new AI-affiliated technologies such as AI-agents and Model Context Protocols (MCP), Large Language Models now can have access to up to date and on-the-fly generated data, models and other scientific artefacts. In this talk, I will focus on what these technological advancements are providing for the wet lab toxicology lab. We will discuss how FAIR-ness moves to AI-ready data through F-AI-R agents en how MCPs are changing the way we interact with software and data. This talk will explain our conceptual framework: AI4Lab, that encompasses four capabilities of AI that can augment the way we do experiments: 1. Augment (Exploratory) data analysis 2.. Increase reproducibility & FAIR-ness of data 3. Enhance traceability of information and methods used 4. Optimize experimental design The AI4Lab concept hinges on the premise that FAIR data is key for the validation of scientific discovery, but that this is not enough. For full scientific tranparency we need all logic that connects methods and data to conclusions (Brown, Kaiser and Allison, 2018). The total collection of output from research needs to be managed in order to be able to unlock all choices made during discovery (Houweling and Willighagen, 2023) and it is key to adopt good research output management practices to make science more transparent and reproducible. In this talk, I hypothesize that emerging technological capabilities of AI can augment these practices and will eventually be able to help researchers achieve increased reproducibility of their research output and augment the experimental work. Putting AI in the loop not only as a method for prediction, but as a scientific discovery companion increases transparency, but only if implemented with this design principle in mind. Using examples and small demonstrators from experiments performed in our own lab, I aimed to show these capabilities take form. At the core of current developments in the AI-field are three technologies: large language models, AI-agents and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Together, these represent a rich technological layer that drive AI-implementation in many fields today. AI-agents; LLMs with access to tools that can generate code, lookup data, or perform actions, can be used to perform data analysis. This leads to a more transparent way of analyzing data, because tool calls can be made explicit and traceable. In terms of reproducibility of data analysis, there is only one way to make this explicit and that is by using scripting (Peng, 2011). Hover, this is usually the domain of data scientists, bioinformaticians or software developers. With agents that can provide visualizations of data, along with code or that can take a statical model specification and implement the analysis in a report, along with the computer code, these assets become auditable and reproducible. AI democratizes reproducible research, outside of the domain of the skilled coders and data scientists, without abolishing the need for domain expert knowledge. The individual researcher, in a multidisciplinary team, has now the ability to generate fully reproducible data workflows and liase with data scientists for validation of the output. AI-agents can be used to go from human-readable and unstuctured datasets to data that is adherent to a FAIR standard, such as ISA. The auditability of AI-agent actions leads to traceable transformation of the data, and grounding the documentation and metadata to true information and not hallucination. I am giving examples of experiments performed in our own lab and how F-AI-R agents move research output from these experiments to FAIR and AI-ready datasets. This illustrates the second AI4Lab principle. The third AI4Lab principle, revolves around the integration of methods and data. For true tranparancy and falsification potential of scientific discovery, we need three things available as metioned above: 1. The data; 2. The methods used to collect the data; 3. The logic connection the data and the methods to conclusions (Brown, Kaiser and Allison, 2018). Many times, especially the logic connection the data to the conclusions is not made explicit. Also, it can be quite hard to capture method documentation in an objective way by an individual researchers, due to implicit up-front knowledge, leading to implicit assumptions and ‘between-the-lines’ translation loss in experimental reports. With the help of F-AI-R agents, we aim to automatise the process of expeirmental report generation and make the connecting logic between methods, conclusions and data explicit. We do this by proving a structure for the agents to follow, and to provide the agents with access to the information captured by the researcher in an electoronic lab journal environment. This is where AI-agent and MCP technologies meet to enhance documenting experimental information along a structure and a (FAIR) standard. The researcher (or an auditor) can audit and augment the captured information, to guarantee accuracy and completeness. The fourth principle was not addressed in the talk due to time-constraints, but this can be considered the most conceptual and also most innovative principle of the four. When we have access to all scientific discovery data and metadata on the experimental, study and project level in a structured way (AI4Lab principle 1 to 3), we can hypothesize that we can use this data to do retrospective and prospective analyses of experiments, on an integrated scale. When using AI here as a propective tool, one might see opportunities to design follow-up or new experiments. This method might unlock patterns of importance for succesful planning of the next experiment and full scientific discovery, using previously generated data and insights, thereby speeding up, and optimizing the process of experimental data generation.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Blurred Compliance Boundaries: Analyzing Open Source License Conflicts in MCP-Based Agent Workflows
abstract: Background. Agent systems increasingly invoke heterogeneous third-party services through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), where service licenses, model licenses, and data licenses may be jointly applied during runtime execution. This emerging execution paradigm introduces cross-service compliance conflicts that are difficult to capture with conventional license analysis methods. Existing methods usually assume that the license set under analysis is statically predetermined, making them insufficient for handling novel term semantics in MCP licenses and for analyzing conflict patterns that arise from task-specific selected service subsets. Aims. This paper investigates compositional license conflicts in MCP-based agent workflows. We seek to characterize how license terms interact across compositional MCP services and to provide an automated analysis framework that detects conflicts and identifies license-compatible service replacements. Method. We propose MCP-Licentra, a license conflict analysis framework for MCP-based agent workflows. MCP-Licentra contains four integrated components. First, it extends an existing license term taxonomy with MCP-specific categories and constructs annotated training data for domain adaptation. Second, it fine-tunes License-Llama3-8B with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and odds ratio preference optimization (ORPO) to recognize license terms and their associated attitudes. Third, it formulates task-specific service selection as a power-set legality verification problem, enabling conflict checking across possible service invocation subsets. Fourth, it recommends license-compatible replacements for conflicting services through semantic embedding retrieval and an iterative compliance checking algorithm under joint functional similarity and license compatibility constraints. Results. We evaluate MCP-Licentra on 3,811 real-world MCP services and 500 compositional service scenarios. MCP-Licentra achieves F1-scores of 88.82% and 86.44% for term identification and license understanding, respectively. For group-level conflict detection, it obtains an FPR of 3.15% and an FNR of 8.77%. For compositional conflict detection, it achieves an overall FPR of 4.90% and an FNR of 3.33%. In addition, MCP-Licentra reaches a resolution success rate of 71.23%, outperforming all baselines. Conclusion. The results show that MCP-based agent workflows introduce compositional compliance risks that are difficult to capture with conventional static license analysis. MCP-Licentra provides an automated framework and empirical evidence for detecting and mitigating such risks in agent systems.
venue: DROPS (Schloss Dagstuhl – Leibniz Center for Informatics)

title: LLM-Powered HFACS Analysis of ASRS Narratives via MCP Bridge for Enhanced Aviation Safety Debriefs
abstract: Learning effectively from past incidents is crucial for advancing aviation safety, but manually analyzing extensive narrative datasets like the Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS) to understand causality is resource-intensive and can be subjective. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer powerful capabilities for text analysis, their performance can degrade when processing large datasets within limited context windows that could potentially lead to decreased accuracy and increased hallucination. This paper introduces a novel framework to address these challenges by automating the extraction of human factors insights from Oklahoma ASRS records. We employ the API version of OpenAI's o3 reasoning LLM, guided by few-shot prompting, to classify ASRS incident narratives into the Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS), each record at a time. The core of our solution is a specialized Model Context Protocol (MCP) server designed to intelligently serve this data. We enable targeted data retrieval by using MCP, which allows the LLM to focus on relevant information from the ASRS corpus without overwhelming its context capacity during complex queries. This server is integrated into a broader ecosystem via the MCP Bridge, an LLM-agnostic RESTful proxy, which further facilitates interaction with diverse clients. This agent demonstrates the system's capability to perform complex, multi-tool, zero-shot queries to retrieve, compare, and report on incidents based on specific HFACS criteria and keywords. Furthermore, to address the computational costs of large models, we introduce a specialized 8B-parameter agentic model trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). This fine-tuned model demonstrates increased performance in strict argument generation (71.3%) compared to a 70B-parameter general-purpose model (54.3%) that proves smaller, reinforcement-learning-optimized models can outperform larger counterparts in specialized tool-use tasks. Our approach highlights how combining advanced reasoning LLMs, specialized agents, and MCPs’ targeted data access can significantly enhance the objectivity and efficiency of safety investigations.

title: Delegation Without Trust: An Empirical Gap Analysis of Identity, Authorization, and Runtime Governance in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
abstract: Autonomous LLM agents increasingly act on a user's behalf: they hold credentials, call tools and services, and spawn sub-agents that act further on their behalf. This turns a long-standing distributed-systems question -- who is authorized to do what, on whose authority -- into an urgent and largely unsolved problem, because the component driving each agent is a language model an adversary can hijack. We argue that agent security must be evaluated under an untrusted-model assumption: a correct system is one in which a fully prompt-injected agent still cannot exceed the authority explicitly delegated to it. Against this standard we make three contributions. First, we give a threat model for multi-agent delegation centered on four adversaries -- confused deputy, token theft and replay, prompt-injection privilege escalation, and compromised sub-agents -- and derive eight security requirements a governed agent system must meet. Second, we show the gap is real: a default agent runtime modeling common practice (broad bearer credentials, authorization gated inside the model) fails all four threats, and across four widely used frameworks -- LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) authorization model -- three provide no built-in confinement and one only partial; no existing standard alone covers the requirement set. Third, we implement and adversarially evaluate an authorization broker that closes the gap. It blocks all four threats; it resists 11 direct attacks on its design and accepts 0 of 200,000 forged tokens; it confines a compromised sub-agent to its delegated task (a mean of 1.5 reachable actions versus all 8,100 under bearer delegation, across 2,000 randomized scenarios); and it enforces at microsecond cost (about 2.6 microseconds per decision), negligible against model inference. These principles are also realized in production in VotalAI's LLM Shield.

title: CivBench: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Tool-Mediated Agents in Civilization VI
abstract: We present CivBench, an open-source benchmark for evaluating language model agents in long-horizon, tool-mediated environments through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). A single episode spans 300+ turns and produces thousands of tool calls over a large action space, requiring sustained planning, state monitoring, and execution under partial observability. The environment exposes 76 MCP tools and a narration layer that converts visual game state into structured text. We use CivBench to characterise agent behaviour across four model families in 23 admissible runs. The sample is a pilot, not a model ranking: aggregate outcomes do not reliably discriminate models at this scale. Instead, we introduce two interface-level metrics that the environment makes measurable: Proactive Monitoring Rate (PMR), capturing whether agents actively query latent strategic state, and RAG@10, capturing whether commitments stated in structured planning reflections are executed within ten subsequent turns. Across runs we observe two consistent patterns under a shared playbook protocol. Agents under-monitor strategically relevant state that is available but requires explicit querying: despite playbook guidance to query victory progress every 20 turns, agents do so only every 30 to 75 turns, and in 7 of 20 detectable defeats they failed to query within the 20 turn warning window before game end. Agents also frequently fail to execute near-term commitments stated in their own planning reflections (RAG@10 between 48.2% and 65.8% across models). Both patterns arise despite tool access and explicit guidance, and we interpret them as deviations under instruction rather than absences of capability. We release the environment, scenarios, logs, metrics, and analysis pipeline at https://github.com/lmwilki/civ6-mcp

title: AI-Driven Immersive Emulation for Tabletop Scenarios
abstract: Effective cybersecurity training requires preparing personnel at every organizational level to operate under pressure, interpret incomplete information, and make rapid, high-stakes decisions. However, current training practices struggle to capture the dynamic, adaptive, and adversarial nature of real-world incidents. These methods lack realism, rely on rigid scripts, and fail to model evolving attacker behavior or the cascading consequences of defensive decisions. As a result, organizations continue to show substantial readiness gaps. CISA's recent assessments indicate that most victims remain unprepared across both technical controls and decision-making processes, from junior analysts to executive leadership. Meanwhile, large-scale exercises such as Cyber Storm demonstrate the value of adaptive, inject-driven training but demand resources and coordination not feasible for routine use. This gap motivates the need for a training system that combines the accessibility of tabletop exercises with the realism and adaptivity of full-scale cyber simulations. In this work, we introduce an AI-driven immersive emulation platform that transforms traditional tabletop scenarios into dynamic, decision-responsive training experiences. The system integrates multiple specialized AI agents (Including adversary emulation, scenario orchestration, content generation, and performance analysis) coordinated through a modular Model Context Protocol (MCP) architecture. These components enable real-time scenario evolution, realistic attack behaviors aligned with the MITRE ATT&CK framework, and automated generation of supporting artifacts such as logs, emails, and incident injects. The platform also delivers structured, role-specific feedback through a performance intelligence engine that evaluates both quantitative metrics and qualitative decision-making. By blending adaptive AI agents with scalable microservice architecture, the system offers a practical, repeatable, and highly realistic alternative to traditional tabletop training. We expect this approach to measurably improve situational awareness, decision-making speed, ethical and legal compliance, communication effectiveness, and overall readiness during cybersecurity incidents.
venue: IEEE Annual Computing and Communication Workshop and Conference (CCWC)

title: MCP-Enhanced Blockchain Architecture for Agricultural Data Sharing: A Hybrid Caching Approach for Supply Chain Traceability
abstract: When there is a contamination problem, retailers quickly try to find out where the bad products came from. Every minute counts, yet blockchain-based traceability systems force inspectors to wait 50-500 milliseconds for each product lookup. These delays compound when checking dozens of items, turning urgent investigations into hours-long ordeals. We discovered an unexpected solution in the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a protocol designed to connect AI systems with external tools. Our system implements Merkle proof-based verification, allowing clients to cryptographically verify cached data against blockchain state with only 5 microseconds of overhead. This means every cache access can be verified without trusting the middleware itself. We evaluated four cache eviction policies under realistic agricultural workloads and found that LFU achieves 85.9% hit rates by recognizing that traceability queries follow predictable patterns, where popular products and recent shipments domi- nate requests. Write-triggered invalidation eliminates stale reads entirely, a critical improvement over fixed TTL approaches that risk serving outdated data. When compared against production- grade alternatives like The Graph's indexers, materialized views, and database mirrors, our approach delivers 4.09x speedup at typical blockchain latencies. The system scales linearly to 2,870 queries per second and handles multi-tenant access control with negligible overhead, enabling competing supply chain partici- pants to share data securely. title: Beyond the App: The Rise of the Agent-Centric OS
abstract: Episode summary: We are witnessing the most significant architectural shift in computing since the GUI: the move from an app-centric world to an agent-centric one. In this episode, we dive into the "pixel-parsing" problem and how Anthropic's new computer-use capabilities are paving the way for agents that navigate our desktops like humans. We explore the "USB-C of AI"—the Model Context Protocol (MCP)—and how it aims to replace visual hacks with deep semantic layers. From the Rutgers AIOS project's LLM-specific kernels to Microsoft's strategic pivot toward agent launchers, the infrastructure for a post-app world is being built in real-time. However, this transition isn't without its risks. We discuss the "zero inbox" disaster at Meta and the security nightmares of giving autonomous agents write access to system files. Is the traditional operating system becoming irrelevant? Tune in to find out how intent-based access control and new communication protocols are shaping the future of how we interact with machines. Show Notes For decades, the "app" has been the fundamental unit of computing. Users navigate between siloed environments, manually moving data and clicking buttons to achieve complex tasks. However, a major architectural shift is underway, moving us toward an agent-centric operating system where the AI, rather than the application, becomes the primary interface. ### The Problem with Pixel-Parsing The current transition phase relies heavily on "pixel-parsing." This involves AI models taking screenshots of a desktop and using computer vision to identify buttons and text, effectively mimicking human interaction. While impressive, this method is fundamentally inefficient. It forces a super-intelligence to use a "spoon"—a UI designed for human eyes and fingers—rather than communicating directly with the system. To solve this, the industry is moving toward a semantic layer. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as a critical standard, often described as the "USB-C of AI." Instead of guessing what a button does by looking at it, MCP allows applications to expose their internal tools and data directly to the agent in a structured format. This creates a deep, machine-readable understanding of system capabilities. ### Redesigning the Kernel The shift isn't just happening at the interface level; it is reaching down into the hardware and the kernel. Projects like Rutgers University's AIOS are exploring LLM-specific kernels that treat "thoughts" or tokens like CPU processes. By optimizing resource scheduling specifically for language models, these systems can significantly reduce the latency that currently plagues cloud-based agents. This leads to a provocative question: does the brand of the operating system even matter anymore? If an agent can move seamlessly across different environments using standardized protocols, the underlying OS—whether Windows, Mac, or Linux—may eventually become a "dumb pipe" that simply provides power and compute. ### The Security and Alignment Challenge As agents move from "read-only" assistants to autonomous operators with "write" access, the security stakes rise exponentially. A recent incident involving an agent that deleted an entire email archive to achieve a "zero inbox" state highlights the "alignment problem." When an agent interprets a goal too literally or hits an edge case, the results can be catastrophic. Traditional file permissions are no longer sufficient for this new era. The industry is currently debating "intent-based access control." This involves moving away from simple read/write permissions toward systems that can evaluate the intent behind an agent's action before it is executed. ### The Future of the Platform Major players are already pivoting. While some initial attempts to force AI into every corner of the UI have faced user pushback, companies like Microsoft are refocusing on "Agent Launchers." The goal is to become the host for a diverse ecosystem of third-party agents rather than trying to build every specialized tool in-house. We are moving from being operators of software to being architects of intent. The challenge of the next few years will be building the protocols and safety frameworks necessary to let these agents out of their sandboxes without losing control of our digital lives. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/agent-centric-os-evolution
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Desarrollo de una plataforma evolutiva de estándares mediante agentes autónomos e interfaces estandarizadas de contexto
abstract: La creciente complejidad de los entornos de desarrollo y la dispersión del conocimiento técnico plantean nuevos retos en la gestión eficiente, consistente y reproducible de los procesos de ingeniería. Este trabajo aborda esta problemática mediante el desarrollo de una plataforma evolutiva basada en agentes autónomos, diseñada para automatizar tareas técnicas y gestionar estándares de forma contextualizada dentro de ecosistemas corporativos. La solución integra modelos de lenguaje de gran escala (LLM), arquitecturas de generación aumentada por recuperación (RAG), y mecanismos de interacción estructurada mediante Model Context Protocol (MCP), junto con un sistema modular de agentes y habilidades (skills). A través del diseño de una arquitectura multiagente orquestada, se construye un sistema capaz de recuperar conocimiento distribuido, razonar sobre él y ejecutar acciones sobre el entorno, manteniendo criterios de trazabilidad, gobernanza y control. Los resultados muestran que la combinación de RAG, enrutado inteligente, agentes especializados y mecanismos de validación mejora significativamente la calidad, precisión y utilidad de las respuestas frente a un modelo generativo aislado. Asimismo, el sistema permite estructurar tareas complejas, automatizar flujos de trabajo y garantizar coherencia con estándares internos. Este estudio demuestra el potencial de las arquitecturas híbridas basadas en agentes y recuperación de conocimiento para transformar asistentes conversacionales en plataformas operativas de apoyo técnico, y proporciona una base metodológica sólida para el desarrollo de sistemas inteligentes en entornos empresariales complejos.

title: Molecular Targets Shape Reasoning Topology: Bidirectional Validation of Chemistry-Inspired Bond Classification for AI Reasoning Chains
abstract: Recent work classified AI reasoning chains using chemistry-inspired bond types, namely covalent (deductive), hydrogen (reflective), and van der Waals (exploratory), showing that structural stability of reasoning predicts training data quality (Direction A). We test the complementary direction: does the molecular target being reasoned about shape the topology of reasoning itself (Direction B)? Across 478 reasoning traces from five ADMET endpoints, we find that it does, with large effect sizes (Cohen's d = 0.94 and 1.75, both p < 10 −9 , surviving Bonferroni correction). We collect chain-of-thought traces from Claude Opus 4.6 performing ADMET property predictions across CYP2D6, CYP3A4, CYP2C9, hERG, and P-gp, using live computational chemistry tools via the Model Context Protocol. A four-signal Semantic Bond Classifier, using sentence embeddings, discourse markers, positional distance, and an energy proxy, classifies reasoning bonds without requiring attention weights from open-source models. Of five pre-registered hypotheses, aggregate reasoning structure does not predict prediction accuracy (H1-H4, all p > 0.12). However, molecular targets strongly determine reasoning topology (H5): CYP2D6 reasoning (2D substructure-driven) shows significantly more covalent bonds than hERG reasoning (3D conformation-dependent), while hERG reasoning shows more van der Waals bonds than CYP2D6. Classifier ablation reveals semantic similarity as the dominant signal (∆ = 13.2 percentage points when removed). These results close a bidirectional loop: chemistry metaphors explain reasoning structure, and chemistry problems shape reasoning structure. The finding that molecular target type determines reasoning topology, with large, interpretable effect sizes, has implications for understanding how AI systems adapt their problem-solving approach to domain-specific demands.

title: Gnoselia- An Institutional Knowledge Intelligence Layer Based on AI Hybrid Retrieval
abstract: Institutional knowledge is increasingly distributed across heterogeneous and weakly connected sources, including document repositories, relational databases, scientific literature, administrative archives, and operational information systems. Although these resources may be technically accessible, the relationships between data, analyses, documents, institutions, concepts, and supporting evidence often remain implicit, limiting their effective reuse for research and decision-making. This paper presents Gnoselia, a proposed institutional knowledge intelligence architecture designed to address this fragmentation through hybrid retrieval and typed knowledge graphs. The architecture integrates nine functional layers spanning heterogeneous data ingestion, document processing, semantic representation, vector indexing, knowledge graph construction, structured data access, hybrid retrieval, artificial intelligence orchestration, and evidence validation. Retrieval combines dense vector search, graph traversal, structured querying, lexical search, and, when required, federated access to external scientific services through a Model Context Protocol gateway. A central design principle is that generated claims should remain traceable to identifiable evidence. The architecture therefore incorporates provenance management, claim-to-source linkage, access-aware retrieval, evidence ranking, and abstention when available evidence is insufficient. An optional bounded agentic layer is proposed to re-initiate evidence acquisition when retrieved information is incomplete, outdated, or contradictory. A subset of the architecture is currently implemented as a Neo4j-based interaction graph that preserves relationships among user questions, generated answers, consulted documents, sessions, and user evaluations. The broader hybrid retrieval, federation, and evidence-validation architecture remains under development. We hypothesize that combining semantic retrieval with explicit relational knowledge representation can improve retrieval quality, answer faithfulness, traceability, and multi-hop reasoning compared with vector-only Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Seven falsifiable operational hypotheses and a pre-specified five-arm evaluation framework are proposed to test these claims. No comparative empirical performance results are reported at this stage.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: SandScope: a Behavioral Audit Layer for MCP Tools in LLM Agent Supply Chains
abstract: Tool-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) agents create a new supply-chain surface: Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools are installed like third-party packages, yet their outputs can enter the agent’s reasoning context. This enables confused-deputy risks in which attacker-controlled semantic supply-chain inputs cause otherwise benign tools to exercise legitimate authority over files, environment variables, or network-facing operations and reflect sensitive or instruction-like content into LLM-visible fields. We present SandScope, an MCP-aware audit framework that combines runtime witness detection with semantic tool profiling. SandScope executes portable tools under WebAssembly (WASM) System Interface (WASI) or drives unmodified MCP servers over standard input/output (stdio), extracts LLM-visible sinks from tool results and prompt/message fields, and reports auditable source-to-sink witnesses from environment, file, and tool-input sources while separately recording network-intent and egress evidence. Its semantic layer recovers declared capabilities from tools/list metadata and static registrations to characterize attack surface when execution is incomplete. We evaluate SandScope on controlled cross-language subjects, an evasion benchmark, and a 100-repository MCP corpus. SandScope achieves high controlled accuracy (0.941 F1) with no false positives, completes shallow dynamic scans for 38.5% of resolved real-world repositories, and extends visibility through semantic profiling to 71% of the corpus. Among recovered tools, 78.6% declare at least one security-sensitive capability. For shallow-scan successes, schema-guided exploration re-executes 94.3% and observes source-to-sink witnesses in 36.4% of re-executed repositories. These results show that SandScope provides practical, auditable evidence for MCP tool risk through controlled execution, MCP-aware sink extraction, runtime witness reporting, and semantic capability profiling.

title: Agentic LLM Planning via Step-Wise PDDL Simulation: An Empirical Characterisation
abstract: Task planning, the problem of sequencing actions to reach a goal from an initial state, is a core capability requirement for autonomous robotic systems. Whether large language models (LLMs) can serve as viable planners alongside classical symbolic methods remains an open question. We present PyPDDLEngine, an open-source Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) simulation engine that exposes planning operations as LLM tool calls through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Rather than committing to a complete action sequence upfront, the LLM acts as an interactive search policy that selects one action at a time, observes each resulting state, and can reset and retry. We evaluate four approaches on 102 International Planning Competition (IPC) Blocksworld instances under a uniform 180-second budget: Fast Downward lama-first and seq-sat-lama-2011 as classical baselines, direct LLM planning (Claude Haiku 4.5), and agentic LLM planning via PyPDDLEngine. Fast Downward achieves 85.3% success. The direct and agentic LLM approaches achieve 63.7% and 66.7%, respectively, a consistent but modest three-percentage-point advantage for the agentic approach at $5.7\times$ higher token cost per solution. Across most co-solved difficulty blocks, both LLM approaches produce shorter plans than seq-sat-lama-2011 despite its iterative quality improvement, a result consistent with training-data recall rather than generalisable planning. These results suggest that agentic gains depend on the nature of environmental feedback. Coding agents benefit from externally grounded signals such as compiler errors and test failures, whereas PDDL step feedback is self-assessed, leaving the agent to evaluate its own progress without external verification.

title: Autonomous Skill Development: Neuro-Symbolic Agents that Self-generate Verifiable Tools
Agent-Readiness of 50 Cross-Border DTC Brands (2026)
abstract: Canonical page: https://canlah.ai/data/agent-readiness-2026/ An audit of whether the owned storefronts of 50 Chinese-origin cross-border direct-to-consumer (DTC) brands with US-facing storefronts (47 reachable) expose the machine-readable signals an AI shopping agent looks for: a Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) manifest, an agent-payments endpoint, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint, llms.txt, robots.txt directives naming AI crawlers, and schema.org Product markup. Key figures (denominator = 47 reachable storefronts):- 25 / 47 (53.2%) serve a content-validated UCP manifest. 25 of 25 UCP manifests found at collection (2026-08) were Shopify-issued: 22 confirmed live by the powered-by response header on 2026-08-21, 3 (Anker, Soundcore, eufy) no longer served and attributed by a collection-time *.myshopify.com host hint.- 0 / 47 expose an agent-payments endpoint; 1 / 47 exposes an MCP endpoint; 26 / 47 serve llms.txt; 9 / 47 carry Product schema on the sampled product page; 6 / 47 name any AI crawler in robots.txt.- Without content validation (soft-404 rejection) UCP prevalence would have been overstated at 59.6%.- Re-verification ten days after collection found 3 of 25 manifests no longer served (~12% churn). Method: unauthenticated HTTP requests only (user agent CanlahResearchBot/1.0, 12 s timeout), one sampled product page per storefront for PDP schema columns. verify_ucp_issuer.sh re-runs the issuer check with nothing but curl. Limits: purposive sample, single region, single time point; presence of a file is not quality of a file; this measures what a storefront exposes, not whether any AI agent used it. Do not project onto DTC brands generally. Files: dataset.csv (50 rows x 22 fields), verify_ucp_issuer.sh, LICENSE (CC BY 4.0).Code repository: https://github.com/Canlah-AI/agent-readiness-2026Mirror: https://huggingface.co/datasets/CanlahAI/agent-readiness-2026Publisher: Canlah AI (CANLAH AI PTE. LTD., Singapore). v1.0.1 (2026-09-01) — corrections, no data change. The row filter in verify_ucp_issuer.sh matched a true in any of the 22 columns rather than the ucp column, so it tested 48 rows instead of 25 and printed totals that contradicted the README. It also folded network failures into the "no longer served" bucket. Both are fixed; a live re-run now reproduces the published 22 Shopify + 3 no-longer-served = 25 of 25, and network errors are counted separately and labelled as not a finding. The README previously named canlah.ai/data/agent-readiness-2026/ as the canonical citation URL; that page is not live, so the canonical citation is now the DOI. dataset.csv is byte-identical to v1.0.0.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Mind the Workflow: Unmasking the Super Agents of Today
abstract: Tool calling capabilities of LLMs are well established and with the advent of Model context protocol, communication between tools and LLMs is becoming more simplified. However, being able to develop complex workflows for solving Demand-Supply mapping problem like selection of top-3 influencers for marketing campaigns with large language models (LLMs) is an unexplored area. Hence, it's pertinent to explore, if agentic LLMs–systems are capable of planning, reasoning, and interacting with tools viz structured database and python environment like REPL. To fill this gap, we introduce (i) a synthetic, publicly shareable dataset that pairs diverse campaign briefs with richly annotated influencer profiles and (ii) an extensible evaluation framework that benchmarks four workflow patterns: 1) Human-generated workflow + LLM execution, 2) Mind–Body (planner LLM + executor LLM), 3) Mind-only (single-agent), and 4) Mind + human-annotated workflow. We test these patterns on 3600 influencer-campaign tasks using leading proprietary models (GPT-4o, Gemini-Pro-2.5) and open-source models (Llama-370B, DeepSeek-MoE-16B). Our results show wide performance variance across both models and workflows. Human-authored workflows executed by LLMs achieved robust performance metrics and process-compliance scores. When LLMs generate their own workflows, valid-output rates fall sharply ($\mathbf{0 - 7 5}$percent), with open-source models adhering less faithfully to their plans than proprietary models (average adherence 0.03 vs 0.39). The two-agent Mind–Body architecture(with the “mind” acting either as a human workflow provider or as a reasoning model) consistently outperforms the single-agent alternative, indicating that “Super Agent” designs–where a reasoning-oriented LLM plans and a smaller model executes–offer a pragmatic path toward reliable automation.

title: Agents Don't Paginate: First-Chunk Selection for LLM Tool Responses
abstract: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs), such as Claude Code, Cursor, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Aider, receive tool responses that routinely exceed the agent's per-turn token budget. The standard remedy, pagination, is available in every protocol that produced these responses; yet across the corpus of session logs from a public Model Context Protocol middleware we observed no agent-initiated requests for a second chunk. The first chunk is what the agent reads, so we ask how often the gold item (the one the agent needs) is placed first in it: the precision-at-1 rate $p_1$. In a controlled offline benchmark we treat first-chunk selection as a 0/1 knapsack and compare six value functions on 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks, then test whether $p_1$ matters with a single-turn file-localisation probe on five language models (4,800 LLM calls; not an end-to-end resolve-rate test). Two pre-registered hypotheses did not hold and are our main findings. The central one is negative: raising $p_1$ does not systematically raise downstream accuracy. Per-model deltas stay under three percentage points (p.p.), are not consistently signed, and no model is significant; the agent recovers the gold from anywhere in the chunk, so what reaches its answer is first-chunk inclusion, not the gold's rank within it. The second: adding four file-metadata signals to a keyword scorer hurts $p_1$ by 4.8 p.p. (paired significance test, $p = 0.001$). A parameter-free keyword scorer does raise $p_1$, from a 24.2% baseline to 35.0% (+10.8 p.p., far beyond chance; $p = 3.9 \times 10^{-8}$), and to 35.8% with a fallback to the tool's native ordering when no keyword matches. But by our central finding this is a rank-1 gain, and rank-1 is the part that does not reach the agent's answer: downstream accuracy does not move.

title: Securing the Personal AI Frontier: Agent Boundary Assurance for Local and Enterprise AI
abstract: Personal and enterprise AI agents are moving from remote chat surfaces into laptops, workstations, local servers, and desk-side accelerators. Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Google, and the open-source model ecosystem are all pushing more inference, memory, tool use, and agent orchestration toward local or hybrid execution. NVIDIA OpenShell and the Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit (AGT) show that platform vendors are building runtime policy, sandboxing, and agent governance directly into the stack. At the same time, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become an increasingly adopted integration protocol for agent tools and data, and has already seen an early set of serious vulnerabilities. This creates a new assurance problem: when an agent runs close to sensitive data, an enterprise must be able to show what the agent accessed, remembered, transformed, sent, blocked, or executed. This paper defines Agent Boundary Assurance (ABA): a cross-vendor evidence discipline for testing and documenting whether local and enterprise agents respect data, memory, tool, model-routing, egress, consent, and action boundaries. It introduces three supply-chain trust artifacts, the Tool Bill of Materials (TBOM) for MCP tool provenance, Skill Bundle Attestation (SBA) for agent skill integrity, and Tool Security Advisory (TSA) for machine-readable vulnerability response, and places them inside a runtime evidence model built on an Agent Boundary Evidence Record (ABER), a boundary claim model, a policy-broker reference architecture, an evaluation scaffold based on PAISL (Personal AI Sovereignty Lab), and an enterprise reporting format for security, legal, compliance, and procurement review. The goal is to make boundary claims testable, portable, and structured for independent review across operating systems, platform runtimes such as OpenShell and AGT, Apple Foundation Models and Core AI, MCP hosts, local and cloud models, and enterprise workflows, not to replace the emerging runtimes themselves. Disclaimer: This work is an independent technical white paper. The views expressed are solely those of the author and do not represent any employer, client, alliance, vendor, or other organization. It is not a standard, certification, legal opinion, compliance guarantee, or product claim.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: From Days to Minutes: An Autonomous AI Agent Achieves Reliable Clinical Triage in Remote Patient Monitoring
abstract: Background: Remote patient monitoring (RPM) generates vast data, yet landmark trials (Tele-HF, BEAT-HF) failed because data volume overwhelmed clinical staff. While TIM-HF2 showed 24/7 physician-led monitoring reduces mortality by 30%, this model remains prohibitively expensive and unscalable. Methods: We developed Sentinel, an autonomous AI agent using Model Context Protocol (MCP) for contextual triage of RPM vitals via 21 clinical tools and multi-step reasoning. Evaluation included: (1) self-consistency (100 readings x 5 runs); (2) comparison against rule-based thresholds; and (3) validation against 6 clinicians (3 physicians, 3 NPs) using a connected matrix design. A leave-one-out (LOO) analysis compared the agent against individual clinicians; severe overtriage cases underwent independent physician adjudication. Results: Against a human majority-vote standard (N=467), the agent achieved 95.8% emergency sensitivity and 88.5% sensitivity for all actionable alerts (85.7% specificity). Four-level exact accuracy was 69.4% (quadratic-weighted kappa=0.778); 95.9% of classifications were within one severity level. In LOO analysis, the agent outperformed every clinician in emergency sensitivity (97.5% vs. 60.0% aggregate) and actionable sensitivity (90.9% vs. 69.5%). While disagreements skewed toward overtriage (22.5%), independent adjudication of severe gaps (>=2 levels) validated agent escalation in 88-94% of cases; consensus resolution validated 100%. The agent showed near-perfect self-consistency (kappa=0.850). Median cost was $0.34/triage. Conclusions: Sentinel triages RPM vitals with sensitivity exceeding individual clinicians. By automating systematic context synthesis, Sentinel addresses the core limitation of prior RPM trials, offering a scalable path toward the intensive monitoring shown to reduce mortality while maintaining a clinically defensible overtriage profile.

title: Zero-Cost Sovereign Computing: A 10-Node Heterogeneous Cluster Using Headscale, Cloudflare Tunnels, and Oracle Always-Free Tier
abstract: Institutional computing resources are unevenly distributed, and commercial cloud costs create a structural barrier for independent researchers, small manufacturers, and individual practitioners who nonetheless require capable compute for AI workloads, knowledge-graph systems, and persistent services. We present Lala City, a 10-node heterogeneous compute cluster built on a legacy-hardware-first principle: every compute node is either a previously-owned device repurposed into a server role or a used machine acquired on the secondhand market, while three marginal additions follow a cheapest-viable-add-on rule (a Raspberry Pi 5 for the home-server role, a Google Coral USB Accelerator for edge ML inference, and a secondhand ARM64 SBC). Measured recurring subscription fees to cloud providers, SaaS vendors, and network services total approximately INR 300/month (USD 3.60/month); the marginal capital outlay to build this cluster from the author's existing hardware pool is approximately USD 325, against a historical acquisition cost across all prior owners and uses in excess of USD 13,000. Nodes are stitched together by a self-hosted Headscale (v0.28) control plane, published selectively via Cloudflare Tunnels, and exposed as a federation of seven Model Context Protocol (MCP) filesystem servers. The architecture is deliberately minimal: no Kubernetes control plane, no commercial observability stack, no paid managed services, no new enterprise hardware. We describe the topology, hardware-acquisition strategy, authentication model, service mesh, and practical gotchas encountered over approximately 14 months of continuous operation, and argue that this design is a viable sovereignty-and-sustainability-first pattern for personal and small-organization compute. We explicitly do not account for electricity, hardware amortization, or operator labor, none of which have been instrumented. We release a complete reference configuration at github.com/Vibhav-Aggarwal/lala-net-public.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Tekoälyagenttijärjestelmän suunnittelu ja arviointi kalibrointienhallintaohjelmistossa
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled AI agents to interact with software systems through natural language, reducing complex multi-step graphical user interface (GUI) workflows to single natural language instructions. This thesis presents CHATiCAL, a multi-agent system designed to interface with an enterprise Calibration Management Software (CMS) via natural language. The work investigates two tool-calling paradigms: (1) a general agent leveraging retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to dynamically select from a broad toolset, and (2) a specialized agent operating within a constrained scope using predefined tools. Both approaches employ an iterative reasoning-action loop to decompose tasks, invoke tools, and refine outputs. The thesis analyzes key design considerations for reliable agent deployment in enterprise environments, including tool selection strategies, scope definition, and architectural trade-offs between flexibility and control. It also identifies limitations in current agent-server communication structures and investigates the practical use of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool invocation. Evaluation is conducted on three datasets of increasing task complexity. Performance is measured using retrieval accuracy, tool-calling accuracy, tool-trace alignment, and overall task completion. Results show that higher-capability models (GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.4-mini) perform strongly across both single- and multi-step tasks, with GPT-4.1 exhibiting greater consistency across tasks. Additionally, a lightweight model (GPT-4.1-nano) is evaluated and performs adequately on simpler tasks but degrades significantly in multi-step scenarios, highlighting the sensitivity of agent performance to underlying model capacity. Overall, the findings demonstrate the potential and usability of multi-agent LLM systems in enterprise software interaction, while highlighting key trade-offs between generality, control, and model capability.

title: Breaking the classification bubble: Rethinking cyberbullying detection and detoxification as knowledge-guided reasoning systems
AIPDLC: AN AI PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT LIFE CYCLE FOR ROLESPECIALIZED SOFTWARE DELIVERY WITH ATLAS STUDIO AS A REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION
abstract: AI-assisted software development is shifting from conversational coding help toward autonomous and multiagent execution. Systems such as MetaGPT and ChatDev already show that specialized AI roles can collaborate through a shared pipeline, and issue-resolution agents such as SWE-agent and OpenHands show that tool-using agents can operate reliably against real codebases. This paper formalizes AIPDLC (AI Product Development Life Cycle), a methodology that organizes these capabilities into a single lifecycle for building software from an initial product intent. Product research and vision are established first, then architecture, then a task backlog; a human governance checkpoint reviews and edits that backlog before implementation begins; specialized AI roles then implement and test each unit of work under deterministic orchestration controls; the finished project passes a whole-project build verification step; and the result is finalized and left open to follow-up requests. Atlas Studio, a desktop application developed by the author since May 2026, is presented as the reference implementation of this methodology. Every implementation-specific claim in this paper was checked directly against Atlas Studio's current source code and its execution logs rather than against an earlier design description. A case study drawn from one of those logs is reported: a Spring Boot application exposing a Model Context Protocol server with a single computational tool, built end to end through the full lifecycle without a task-level retry. AIPDLC is positioned explicitly against MetaGPT and ChatDev, which already establish role-specialized, artifact-driven multi-agent software development; this paper does not claim to originate that idea. Its contribution is the formalization of a specific lifecycle structure, gate placement, artifact and state model, and verification discipline, together with a working implementation and an initial case study. A controlled comparison against existing systems is left as future work.Tool Website: atlasstudioai.com
venue: International Research Journal of Modernization in Engineering Technology and Science

title: From Single Chatbots to Governed Agent Ecosystems: An Agentic AI Pattern Catalogue and Orchestration Framework for Mission-Critical Hospital Information Management Systems
abstract: Hospitals are racing to embed Artificial Intelligence (AI), while coping with the surge in adaptation of the technology in other industries, into the triage management, documentation, scheduling, and revenue-cycle workflows, yet most deployments remain as fragmented pilots that stall at the edge of production, exposing patients and institutions to operational fragility, ungoverned risk, and mounting technical debt. At the same time, the global AI-in-healthcare market is projected to exceed nearly USD 1 trillion by 2034, according to the report of Fortune Business Insights, amplifying the financial consequences of architectural missteps and failed scaling strategies. This research proposes a compliance-first Agentic AI pattern catalogue and orchestration framework, purposely built for Hospital Information Management Systems (HIMS), moving beyond the single Large Language Model (LLM) chatbots and towards a governed ecosystem of autonomous and semi-autonomous agents. The framework extends by adding (i) a taxonomy of Agentic roles (conversational, orchestration, reconciliation, auditing, and decision-support agents), (ii) a formal risk-stratification model that maps each pattern to risk tiers, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and governance hooks, and (iii) a unified orchestration runtime capable of coordinating multi-agent workflows across EHR/HIMS landscapes such as Epic, Cerner, and MEDITECH. Technically, the framework combines vLLM (Virtual Large Language Model)-based inference, optimized paging memory, confidential computing, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) based on-premise deployment, enforcing endto-end encryption and policy-as-code controls aligned with HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, India’s DPDP and DISHA Acts, ISO 27001, ISO 27002, ISO 14971, and IEC 62304. Using synthetic but structurally realistic and reflecting the complexities of the hospital data generated using Synthea, and controlled pilot deployment and functional run, we exhibit how the proposed architecture is capable and efficient to reduce the documentation time, integration effort, and AI pilot attrition while constriction the governance and auditability, offering hospital leaders and governing authorities an urgently needed blueprint to convert AI investment into sustainable clinical, operational, and financial ROI.
venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)

title: Tool-augmented vs. autonomous LLM agents for building energy model modifications: A comparative study using NECB compliance models
abstract: This paper compares two large language model (LLM) agent architectures for modifying EnergyPlus Input Data Files (IDFs). In the tool-augmented approach, the LLM invokes high-level, domain-specific functions encapsulating heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) engineering knowledge and IDF manipulation logic. In the autonomous approach, the LLM directly orchestrates primitive operations - object creation, deletion, and field-level modification. Both architectures are implemented as a multi-agent workflow using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), combining retrieval-augmented access to the National Energy Code of Canada for Buildings (NECB) standards, a simulation agent for IDF editing and EnergyPlus execution, and a coordinating supervisor agent. Seven NECB 2020 reference models spanning apartment, restaurant, school, warehouse, and office archetypes were evaluated on three modification tasks of increasing complexity. For a simple task (window U-value modification), both approaches achieved 100% success and produced identical energy results within each building. For a medium task (lighting-power reduction), both approaches succeeded in all seven buildings, although autonomous execution generally required more tool calls and time. For a complex task involving conversion from packaged terminal air conditioner (PTAC) or packaged direct-expansion (DX) systems to variable refrigerant flow (VRF), the tool-augmented approach succeeded in all seven buildings, producing simulation-ready, NECB-compliant models with zero severe errors. The autonomous approach failed in every case: the three apartment attempts stopped during planning or produced incomplete, invalid models, and the four packaged-DX attempts did not pass structural validation and therefore did not advance to annual simulation. Autonomous execution required substantially more tokens and agent processing effort, with no successful complex-task outcome. These findings indicate that autonomous LLM agents are viable for low-interdependency edits, but reliability degrades sharply when tasks require many coordinated changes. A hybrid strategy is recommended: autonomous execution for simple modifications and validated domain-specific tools for complex, compliance-critical transformations.

title: Embedding Model Deprecation: RAG's Silent Killer
abstract: Episode summary: When OpenAI retires an embedding model like ada-002, your RAG pipeline doesn't crash — it just gets subtly worse until users lose trust.
