title: Pratyakṣa: A Context-Engineering System for Long-Context, Hallucination-Resistant Agentic AI
abstract: We present Pratyakṣa, a context-engineering system for long-context, hallucination-resistant agentic AI, packaged as a Claude-Code- and Cursor-compatible plugin (15 Model Context Protocol [MCP] tools, 3 skills, 3 agents, 4 commands, 3 lifecycle hooks). The system operationalises seven constructs drawn from classical In- dian epistemology — specifically from Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika, Advaita Vedānta, Pūrva Mīmāṃsā, and Sāṃkhya — into runtime mechanisms for an LLM agent’s working context: pratyakṣa (direct perception), avacchedaka (typed limitor conditions), bādha (sublation), buddhi/manas (judging vs. attending faculties), sākṣī (witness invariants), khyātivāda (a six-class taxonomy of cognitive error), and adaptive forgetting. We validate across three orthogonal evidence layers: (L1) seven preregistered hypotheses (H1–H7) on six public long-context and hallucination bench- marks (RULER, HELMET, NoCha, HaluEval, TruthfulQA, FACTS-Grounding) with multi-seed multi-model paired permutation tests; (L2) a deterministic, reproducible live case study (P6-B) on three real GitHub issues spanning Django, Requests, and pandas; and (L3) a head-to-head A/B test on 120 SWE-bench Verified instances (P6-C, 720 paired runs across 2 models × 3 seeds × 120 issues) under a fixed 512-token research-block budget. SWE-bench Verified instantiates the harness on one challenging coding domain; the mechanisms themselves are agent- and domain-agnostic and the L1 evidence is the general claim. Across 10 quantitative studies, the system produces a Stouffer-combined 𝑍= 9.114 (two-sided 𝑝 = 7.94 × 10−20), with mean per-study delta +0.476 in the harness’s favour and a 100% target-path-hit rate on SWE-bench Verified versus 50.3% for the budgeted baseline. The khyātivāda 6-class hallucination annotator achieves Cohen’s 𝜅 = 0.736 (“substantial”) on 𝑛 = 3,000 jointly annotated examples. The contribution is not a new model architecture but a typed, witness-tracked, sublation- aware context discipline that any LLM-based agent — research assistants, document QA, multi-tool orchestrators, code-review agents — can adopt today via a drop-in plugin. The system, the plugin, and the full reproducibility manifest are open-sourced.

title: Using agentic AI to assign gene function across multiple genomes
abstract: The Gene Ontology (GO) provides a foundational framework for representing gene function across species, encompassing a structured vocabulary, gene function assertions, and causal activity models (GO-CAMs). Maintaining and extending this knowledge base requires expert biocurators to distill findings from the scientific literature—a process that cannot scale to match the pace of modern genomics. While machine learning approaches to GO function prediction have attracted significant interest (e.g., the CAFA challenge series), rigorous evaluation reveals persistent limitations, particularly for uncharacterized proteins. Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from earlier "LLM-as-oracle" approaches that relied on narrow context windows and were prone to hallucination. Modern agentic systems combine a simple but powerful architecture—loop, tools, and state—enabled by large context windows, reasoning-capable models, and universal coding agents (e.g., Claude Code, Codex). Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent skills, these systems achieve a decoupled architecture that can autonomously plan, research, and execute complex curation tasks while maintaining a collaboration dial between full autonomy and human oversight. We describe our deployment of multiple agentic AI systems for GO curation: an Ontology Agent for vocabulary maintenance, a Gene Annotation Review Agent that can re-review hundreds of annotations and flag biologically incorrect automated predictions, a GO-CAM Pathway Agent for constructing causal models, and OpenScientist, a co-scientist agent for interpreting molecular data. To combat hallucinations—particularly of ontology term IDs, citations, and clinical codes—we employ LinkML-based agentic harnesses with expressive but tightly constrained schemas, anti-hallucination checksums, and dedicated term and reference validators. We frame human-agent collaboration as a pyramid: deterministic processes (automated QA/QC, schema validation) at the base, defined high-level agent processes (research, report generation, ontology maintenance) in the middle, and human management and governance at the top—shifting the role of humans from being "in the loop" to "regulating the loop." Evaluation remains challenging given the jagged frontier of AI capabilities, but validation experiments with OpenScientist demonstrate that the platform can distinguish true biological signals from technical noise. By automating lower-level curation tasks, agentic AI frees biocurators to focus on high-level modeling, consensus building, and direct engagement with the research community.

title: Toward Composition-Aware Operational Assurance for MCP: Observable Control Gaps, Outcome-Evidence Classes, and a Status-Bounded Design-Science Case
abstract: Composable Model Context Protocol (MCP) workflows require assurance beyond endpoint reachability. This position and design-science preprint defines observable objects and bounded closure conditions for three related problems: the Registry-Runtime Gap, pre-execution and runtime Composition-Control Gaps, and the Execution-Outcome Gap between provider-reported success and evidence of the intended target state. The framework separates controls required by a plan, controls evidenced as configured before execution, and controls observed during or after an execution trace. It replaces an ordinal verification-tier model with non-ordered Outcome Evidence Source Classes evaluated across source authority, organizational independence, technical failure independence, cryptographic integrity, temporal proximity, identity binding, and observation completeness. A fully synthetic support-notice workflow demonstrates how missing task cancellation, provider substitution, and contradictory delivery evidence leave different gaps open. The accompanying public design supplement provides a generic Operational Assurance Profile JSON Schema, a synthetic example, bounded structural validation, and tests. SaSame is included only as an author-reported, status-bounded design case frozen at an exact internal branch snapshot. Observation and evidence components existed on main, while plan contracts, provider observation, dynamic resolution, composition planning, deterministic adapters, and a read-only execution lab existed only in an unmerged, non-production prototype. The paper does not claim that SaSame reduces risk, safely composes tools in production, or has established external-customer validity. Research status: Preprint v0.3.0. This work has not been peer reviewed. The proposed profile has not been validated for policy utility or inter-rater reliability, and no controlled comparative experiment currently establishes production effectiveness. Data and code availability: The accompanying supplement contains only a generic schema, a fully synthetic example, standard-library validation code, tests, citation metadata, and publication-boundary notices. It excludes private SaSame implementation, endpoint or observation data, provider-selection and composition logic, production security controls, credentials, customer information, internal infrastructure, pricing, entitlements, and commercial fulfillment systems. Conflict of interest: The author is affiliated with SaSame S.R.L., which designs and operates the case-study systems and offers commercial MCP services. The SaSame case is not an independent evaluation. Funding: This work received no external research funding.

The Demiurge Framework: Emergent Multicellular Predation and Morphogenesis from Mesoscale Prebiotic Thermodynamics
abstract: A persistent bottleneck in origin-of-life computational biology is the "Mesoscale Explanatory Gap": ab initio quantum chemistry and all-atom molecular dynamics are computationally confined to femtosecond scales ($\sim 10^{-12}$ s) and tens of angstroms, while traditional artificial life models rely on non-physical heuristics (e.g., boids, kinematic automata) devoid of mass conservation and thermodynamic dissipation. Here, we present **The Demiurge Framework**, a mesoscale, first-principles computational platform demonstrating the spontaneous, unscripted transition from an open, non-equilibrium CHONPS (Carbon, Hydrogen, Oxygen, Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Sulfur, with Fe, Si, and Ti catalysts) thermal-gradient environment to predatory, multicellular proto-bilaterians. Beyond terrestrial biochemistry, the platform provides an **Extensible Universal Stoichiometric Engine**, enabling arbitrary user-defined chemical elements (hypothetical, synthetic, and non-terrestrial) and planetary-scale geochemical regimes (Titan cryo-hydrocarbons, Europa subglacial brine, Venusian supercritical fluid, and Chondritic baths). The framework integrates:1. An analytical kinematic hydrothermal convection field governed by Speer-Rona plume dynamics and Rayleigh-Bénard downwelling;2. An open chemical registry supporting arbitrary elemental valences $V$, electronegativities $\chi$, and Pauling-Arrhenius bond kinetics;3. Vesicular compartmentalization driven by Tanford-Israelachvili critical micelle concentration (CMC) and evaluated via Tibor Gánti’s Chemoton closure criterion;4. Spontaneous gastrulation governed by René Thom’s cusp catastrophe ($4u^3 + 27v^2 \le 0$);5. Neuromotor coordination driven by Piezo-type mechanotransduction, electrotonic gap junctions, and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP);6. Phagotrophic predation governed by Michaelis-Menten vacuolar lysis and Lindeman trophic efficiency. To establish a reproducible metric for open-ended evolution, we introduce the **Prebiotic Complexity Benchmark (PCB-18: Phase I Reference Trajectory)** — an 18-milestone verification suite tracking macroscopic phase transitions from inorganic dimers to cognitive bilaterian predation, serving as the benchmark foundation for Phase II macro-ecological diversification. Operating as a data-oriented, zero-garbage-collection Go engine at 60 FPS on standard consumer hardware, the architecture decouples immutable thermodynamic substrate physics from an exploratory, agentic "Demiurge" layer operating via the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

title: Autonomous Refinery Intelligence Architecture
abstract: Abstract Refinery decisions often require evidence that is distributed across plant historians, maintenance systems, work permits, incident records, management-of-change registers, audit actions, shift logs, engineering documents, and workforce-compliance records. Conventional search or dashboard solutions generally address one source type at a time and leave engineers to assemble the complete operational story manually. This paper presents the Autonomous Refinery Intelligence Architecture (ARIA), an on-premise, evidence-grounded architecture developed in-house at a public-sector refinery to unify structured plant records and unstructured operational knowledge while maintaining data sovereignty. The architecture is designed to connect 15 enterprise systems through governed tools and a Model Context Protocol integration layer. A refinery-wide source inventory contained 423,614 structured records and 6,898 shift-log records across 12 operational domains. The detailed case study evaluates eight operational source classes using controlled subsets from crude and vacuum distillation and hydroprocessing units. The method combines canonical equipment identity, deterministic source-quality checks, structured and chronological candidate generation, retrieval-augmented language-model synthesis, a refinery-specific qualification gate, and human review. Three domain patterns are supported: safety investigation, reliability investigation, and contractor-workforce compliance. The language model acts as a controlled reasoning and summarization layer; it is not permitted to authorize plant or workforce decisions. The evaluated crude-distillation pipeline assembled 52,664 evidence rows and reduced 124 candidate packs to 15 final cards, of which only three met the strongest machine qualification. The hydroprocessing pipeline assembled 81,313 rows and reduced 132 candidate packs to 15 cards, again with three receiving the strongest qualification. The deliberate rejection and review rates show that conservative evidence gating is more important than maximizing the number of generated insights. The evaluation also exposed material source-data limitations, including missing work-permit tags, invalid notification dates, and incomplete closure fields. These limitations were carried forward as confidence constraints rather than silently repaired by the model. An initial internal workflow benchmark for a representative incident investigation indicated approximately 80% less evidence-assembly time than the prior manual approach. This is a preliminary operational benchmark, not a controlled statistical trial. A 15-20% reduction in unplanned downtime remains a projected benefit to be tested through longer-term asset performance monitoring. The principal conclusion is that agentic artificial intelligence can support refinery operations only when identity, provenance, qualification rules, human accountability, and on-premise governance are designed as first-class system components.
venue: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)

title: Metcore-suite: Unified software suite for quantum, rheological, and neural memory diagnostics
abstract: Initial Release of Metcore Suite We are pleased to announce the first official release of Metcore Suite. Metcore is designed to answer a critical and expensive question in scientific computing: does the memory of your system actually matter, and is heavy non-Markovian computation worth the overhead? Instead of guessing or committing to weeks of heavy simulations like HEOM, pseudomodes, or TEDOPA, or blindly accepting the Markovian short-cut via Lindblad, Metcore allows you to measure the answer mathematically in seconds. Based on the Markov Embedding Theorem (MET), this suite provides a unified mathematical engine usable across quantum, classical, rheological, and neural problems. Key Features This initial release delivers the core engine through three pathways: 1. Cross-Platform Desktop App (metcore-gui) No Python environment is required. A production-ready desktop interface featuring five specialty tabs: Quantum: Spectral density to bath correlation and non-Markovian diagnosis. Classical and Rheology: Maxwell-Wiechert and Prony relaxation spectrum analysis. Neural: Retarded synaptic and dendritic kernel diagnostics. Diagnostics: Geometric non-Markovianity of qubit channels. Shortcuts: Closed-form, instantaneous answers for asymptotic Lindblad rates, Kuramoto synchronization thresholds, and reaction-time scaling. The app also features academic-grade figure exporting in seven formats (including PDF, SVG, EPS, PNG, and TIFF) with custom lab branding and value tables. 2. Model Context Protocol Server (metcore-mcp) This integrates the suite into any compatible LLM client like Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, or Continue. It includes 17 custom tools allowing an LLM to run full memory diagnostics, choose Prony orders via Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt), and chart non-Markovianity directly from standard prompts. 3. Developer Python Library (metcore) A robust Python API to integrate the MET pipeline into your own research scripts and automated workflows. Python from memkern import zoo, full_diagnosis import numpy as np k = zoo.get_kernel("underdamped") tau = np.linspace(0, 25, 800) print(full_diagnosis(tau, k.C(tau), t_max=25)["summary"]) Installation and Getting Started For the Desktop App: Scroll down to the Assets section below and download the installer or binary for your operating system (.exe for Windows, .dmg for macOS, or .AppImage for Linux). For Python Developers and MCP users: Bash pip install metcore metcore-mcp metcore-mcp configure

title: TaxAgent: An Orchestration Framework for Tax-Optimized Investing
Sistema agentic per avaluació de pràctiques i exercicis
abstract: Problema Avui dia, l'avaluació d'activitats en plataformes d'aprenentatge com Moodle requereix una intervenció manual intensiva per part del professorat, i això limita la rapidesa de correcció i la personalització de la retroalimentació als estudiants. Tot i l'emergència de la intel·ligència artificial generativa com a eina àmpliament usada en la nostra societat, la seva integració amb sistemes de gestió de l'aprenentatge per a automatitzar processos educatius encara presenta reptes tècnics, tant en l'àmbit d'interoperabilitat com de seguretat de dades i sobretot de mantenibilitat i escalabilitat. Solució proposada Aquest projecte pretén desenvolupar un servidor que empri el Model Context Protocol (MCP) per a actuar com a pont entre agents d'intel·ligència artificial i l'API externa de la plataforma Moodle. El servidor implementa un conjunt extensiu de funcionalitats de l'API REST de webservices de Moodle com a eines MCP, que permet que agents d'IA puguin accedir a informació de cursos, estudiants, activitats i qualificació, i també publicar retroalimentació automatitzada i resultats d'avaluació. Metodologia S'implementa el servidor amb una arquitectura per capes que separa les responsabilitats del servidor MCP (exposició d'eines a l'agent IA), els models de validació de dades i el client de comunicació amb Moodle. S'ha escollit un enfocament de stateless proxy que garanteix seguretat, simplicitats i mantenibilitat. El projecte s'ha desenvolupat usant Python 3.11+, el framework FastMCP d'Anthropic, i Docker per a l'entorn de proves amb Moodle 5.1+ Resultats El servidor implementa 24 funcionalitats de Moodle organitzades en categories de gestió de cursos, usuaris, matriculacions i qualificacions. S'han validat mitjançant un conjunt de tests unitaris amb cobertura superior al 80% i proves d'integració tan semimanuals amb MCP Inspector com end-to-end amb l'agent IA Claude Desktop. El projecte aporta una solució reutilitzable i de codi obert que facilita l'ús d'IA en el camp de l'educació, reduint el temps i esforç necessari per a activitats educatives i fomentant l'ús d'eines d'intel·ligència artificial generativa per part d'institucions educatives.

title: Design and evaluation of MCP-server for agentic reservoir simulation workflows
abstract: Summary Computational workflows in subsurface exploration and production combine multiple simulation stages, including seismic interpretation, geological modelling, petrophysical characterization, multiphase flow simulation, and history matching. Building and maintaining these workflows is labour-intensive because each stage requires fit-for-purpose configurations, curated data, and custom pre- and post-processing. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs), agentic systems, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) offer new opportunities for automating such tasks. However, the stochastic and fallible nature of LLMs conflicts with the deterministic assumptions of conventional scientific software, requiring interface designs that explicitly manage uncertainty. We present open-darts-mcp, an MCP integration for the open-darts reservoir simulator that exposes simulation capabilities through standardized interfaces for LLM-driven clients. We investigate four complementary server designs spanning the declarative-imperative spectrum: (D1) explicit API exposure, in which a curated subset of the Python API is provided as strictly typed deterministic tools; (D2) schema-guided generation, in which the LLM produces constrained structured input; (D3) retrieval-augmented generation, in which documentation, examples, and API references support simulation-script generation; and (D4) a developer-orchestrated finite-state workflow, in which deterministic code controls routing, validation, retries, and rollback, while the LLM is invoked only at predefined stages. We evaluate these designs across representative reservoir models, prompts, implementation variants, and LLM backends, measuring success rate, failure modes, retries, rollback behaviour, and token cost. Designs that constrain LLM outputs through local, typed, and immediately validated contracts are the most reliable. Explicit API exposure (D1) and the finite-state workflow (D4) consistently outperform one-shot configuration generation and retrieval-based script synthesis. In particular, transferring orchestration, validation, and recovery to deterministic program logic enables smaller, locally hosted LLMs to complete structured simulation subtasks reliably. Schema-guided generation (D2) is compact but fragile when a complete globally consistent configuration must be generated in one step. Retrieval-augmented generation (D3) provides the greatest flexibility but depends strongly on representative documentation, API references, and examples. D4 achieves the lowest token consumption, while D3 is similarly economical when successful; D1 and D2 require larger contexts, partly offset by prompt caching. Overall, the results support hybrid architectures in which deterministic program logic governs routine simulation operations and LLM autonomy is reserved for tasks requiring interpretation, diagnosis, or open-ended reasoning.

title: AI-Native Platform Engineering for Physical AI
abstract: This presentation provides a comprehensive architecture specification for an AI-native internal platform designed to support Physical AI applications — autonomous unmanned aerial systems (UAS), ground robots, and heterogeneous sensor networks — in defense technology, law enforcement, border patrol, and search-and-rescue domains. The deck synthesizes industry and academic sources into a unified platform design organized around five horizontal capabilities: simulation and digital twin (Isaac Sim, Gazebo, Pegasus), multimodal data management and replay (Rerun Cloud, MCAP, ROS2), intelligence fusion (OSINT and CLOSINT aggregation into a common operating picture), browser-based 3D/4D visualization (React, Rust/WASM, CesiumJS, MapLibre GL, 3D Gaussian Splatting), and agentic developer experience (Claude Code, Model Context Protocol, curated skills). Orchestration follows a proven two-tier pattern: Prefect 3.x for deterministic macro-orchestration of pipeline DAGs and Pydantic AI for optional LLM-assisted micro-orchestration within flows. The presentation makes three novel contributions. First, it demonstrates that Physical AI platform engineering — the intersection of platform engineering, robotics/autonomous systems, and defense — is a research gap with essentially no academic literature, despite significant industry investment. Second, it proposes a concrete OpenSpec methodology for specification-driven development (SDD) of such platforms, enabling parallel team execution without merge conflicts. Third, it introduces a three-layer governance architecture (Governance-as-Code via WASM policy modules, Governance-as-a-Service with Trust Factor scoring, and Content-Based Access Control for contextual information flow) that addresses the unique compliance requirements of classified defense environments. The slides are organized in six acts: Act 0 (Opening, slides 1-2) provides the executive summary and graphical abstract. Act I (Motivation & Landscape, slides 3-16) establishes why Physical AI needs dedicated platform engineering, surveys the competitive landscape, and identifies the gap. Act II (The Architecture, slides 17-32) details the five-layer platform architecture, from orchestration through intelligence fusion. Act III (Platform Tasks, slides 33-44) covers recording, annotation, sensor QA, calibration, and 3DGS sim-to-real. Act IV (Advanced Topics, slides 45-52) addresses edge compute continua, heterogeneous swarms, and RL infrastructure. Act V (Security & Governance, slides 53-57) presents MLSecOps, zero-trust, and the three-layer governance architecture. Act VI (Roadmap & Closing, slides 58-64) delivers the phased implementation plan, team structure, technology stack, TCO analysis, risk register, and the research opportunity.

title: GranumFL: an agentic, GPU-accelerated coupled DEM–SPH program for debris flows on real terrain
abstract: Debris flows on real hillsides involve grains, water and terrain together, yet the programsthat couple discrete elements with smoothed particle hydrodynamics on a GPU are eithercommercial and resolved at the grain scale or research codes that an engineer cannot setup without programming. This paper presents GranumFL, which couples a weakly com-pressible SPH water phase with a DEM grain phase through the unresolved formulation ofRobinson, Ramaioli and Luding (2014), runs both phases on one CUDA GPU, lays out acase on a digital elevation model, and exposes every step to a large-language-model agentthrough 20 Model Context Protocol tools. Each phase was calibrated against publishedbenchmark results. The DEM phase reproduces the Chung and Ooi impact benchmarkswithin 0.09 % of Hertz’s solutions and 0.19◦ of Kratos, and the DEM8 penetration testwithin the spread of eight open-source codes, in 1.1 min on an RTX 5090, as fast as thededicated GPU codes. For a sedimenting porous block, the coupled phase is closer totheory than the reference implementation of Robinson et al. at every resolution compared(−2.7, +9.3 and +14.4 % against +5, +15 and +22 % at h/d = 2, 5 and 6), whereas for asingle grain it is accurate only for 2.5 ≤ h/d ≤ 4, because of the grain’s own volume in theporosity at small h/d and a truncated buoyancy at large h/d, in a dense fixed bed it gives1.5 to 3.3 times Ergun’s pressure drop, and a loose submerged column collapses too farwith a base pore pressure of the wrong sign, so dense granular assemblies with their porepressure remain the open problem. The SPH phase follows the Martin and Moyce dambreak within 3.0–3.1 % RMS and hydrostatics within 0.68 %, and in SPHERIC Test 2 itfollows the water heights within about 8 % and times the impact on the box within 3 msbut over-predicts the peak pressure near the floor, at about the speed of DualSPHysicson a V100 at the coarser spacing. The CPU and GPU agree to three digits, and the waterphase sustains 1.6–1.9×108 particle updates per second up to 12 million particles, 55 to 66times a 30-thread CPU. In four independent trials an LLM agent, driving only the MCPtools, set up and edited the 2026 Patong (Phuket) debris-flow site from plain-languagerequests and passed all 33 objective checks, and two trials found on their own that thesteepest-descent path on the Copernicus surface model does not follow the reported route.

title: Execution Governance for AI Orchestration and Agentic Systems
abstract: Execution Governance for AI Orchestration and Agentic Systems v1.1.4 presents a cumulative execution-governance architecture for consequential actions produced by AI orchestration, autonomous agents, sub-agents, tools, protocols, memories, workflows, and effect-producing systems. The central proposition is simple: ability is not authority. Model capability, identity, authentication, credentials, tool access, protocol validity, model confidence, or successful execution do not, by themselves, establish that a particular consequential effect is authorized now. This edition extends the original pre-effect authorization foundation into a cumulative EG3–EG6 architecture specialized for agentic systems. The Six Conditions remain the normative authorization core, while later layers address distinct execution-integrity problems: EG3 — Agentic Commitment Integrity, preserving current authority through the exact action, tool, target, parameters, and release path; EG4 — Agentic Effect Fabric Integrity, preserving rooted, non-expanding, revocable authority across agents, protocols, tools, workloads, services, and effect surfaces; EG5 — Agentic Regime Integrity, governing material changes to policies, delegation roots, models, skills, memories, tools, composition rules, and enforcement mechanisms; and EG6 — Agentic Grounding Integrity, binding effect-dispositive claims to the correct referents, sources or procedures, semantics, time conditions, and uncertainty treatment. The paper introduces the Agentic Execution Event (AxE) as the effect-specific unit of governance and develops cumulative decision rules, delegation and monotonic authority attenuation, effect gates, authorization records and permits, effect receipts, runtime-change controls, grounding requirements, agentic-domain invariants, falsification vectors, and machine-readable candidate JSON profiles. The revision also positions Execution Governance relative to NIST AI RMF and agent-identity work, NIST AI 800-4, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act, OWASP agentic-security and runtime-control work, Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent2Agent (A2A), IAM/OAuth, policy engines, and reference-monitor traditions. These are treated as complementary governance, security, interoperability, identity, evidence, or enforcement mechanisms rather than independent sources of substantive authority for a specific governed effect. Version 1.1.4, dated 14 September 2026, is a publication-ready, profile-bounded, pre-standardization research architecture. It does not claim production deployment, certification, regulatory approval, formal standard status, complete mediation in open-world agent ecosystems, or independent validation of the full cumulative EG3–EG6 agentic stack. Historical baseline: Version 1.0, Execution Governance for AI Orchestration and Agentic Systems: From Model Capability to Governed Effect (July 2026). Canonical programme: ExecutionGovernance.org

title: Αυτόματος συντονισμός πολλαπλών εξειδικευμένων πρακτόρων για την εκτέλεση πολύπλοκων έργων με χρήση ισορροπημένης συνεργασίας, δυναμικών εικονικών μηχανών και επεκτάσιμων συνόλων εργαλείων
abstract: Η ραγδαία εξέλιξη των Μεγάλων Γλωσσικών Μοντέλων (Large Language Models - LLMs) πυροδότησε ταυτόχρονα τη μετάβαση από απλές διεπαφές συνομιλίας σε αυτόνομα Πολυπρακτορικά Συστήματα (Multi-Agent Systems - MAS), ικανά να εκτελούν πολύπλοκες τεχνικές ροές εργασίας. Ωστόσο, τα υφιστάμενα frameworks ενορχήστρωσης (orchestration frameworks) αντιμετωπίζουν τρία κρίσιμα εμπόδια: το «τείχος μνήμης» (memory wall), όπου η υποβάθμιση του context (context degradation) οδηγεί σε ψευδαισθήσεις (hallucinations) σε μακροσκελείς εργασίες, τον εγκλωβισμό σε συγκεκριμένους παρόχους (vendor lock-in) λόγω στενής δέσμευσης με συγκεκριμένα API, και τους σημαντικούς κινδύνους ασφαλείας που σχετίζονται με την εκτέλεση κώδικα παραγόμενου από πράκτορες χωρίς απομόνωση σε επίπεδο υλικού (hardware-level isolation). Η παρούσα διατριβή παρουσιάζει το SandBot (ένα Πλαίσιο Απομόνωσης & Ενορχήστρωσης Πρακτόρων - Agent Sandboxing & Orchestration Framework), μια αρχιτεκτονική MAS επαγγελματικού επιπέδου, σχεδιασμένη να γεφυρώσει το χάσμα μεταξύ της πειραματικής έρευνας και της ασφαλούς ανάπτυξης σε περιβάλλον παραγωγής. Το SandBot αντιμετωπίζει την εξάντληση του context μέσω μιας «Αρχιτεκτονικής Προτροπών Έξι Σημείων» (Six-Section Prompt Architecture) και μιας αλγοριθμικής τεχνικής Συμπίκνωσης Περιγραφής Εργαλείων» (Tool Description Deduplication), η οποία μειώνει τον επιπλέον φόρτο (overhead) του Πρωτοκόλλου Πλαισίου Μοντέλου (Model Context Protocol - MCP) κατά περίπου 47%. Για τη διασφάλιση της λειτουργικής ασφάλειας, το πλαίσιο ενσωματώνεται προγραμματιστικά με το OpenNebula για την παροχή προσωρινών, δικτυακά απομονωμένων Μικρο-Εικονικών Μηχανών (MicroVMs) για τις εργασίες των πρακτόρων, επιβάλλοντας αυστηρή απομόνωση που μετριάζει τον κινδύνο Αυθαίρετης Εκτέλεσης Κώδικα (Arbitrary Code Execution - ACE). Κεντρικό στοιχείο του framework αποτελεί ένα μοτίβο Ενορχηστρωτή-Αντιπροσώπου (Orchestrator-Delegate pattern), το οποίο χαρακτηρίζεται από ισορροπημένη ομότιμη συνεργασία (peer-to-peer cooperation). Αυτή η τοπολογία αντικαθιστά τις στατικές ιεραρχίες με ένα επίπεδο δίκτυο εξειδικευμένων ομότιμων κόμβων - τυποποιημένων ως «Ατομικοί Πράκτορες» (Atomic Agents) - που αλληλεπιδρούν μέσω απομονωμένων χώρων ονομάτων (isolated namespaces). Αποσυνδέοντας τη λογική ενορχήστρωσης από τα υποκείμενα γνωστικά μοντέλα (προσέγγιση Bring-Your-Own-Model), το σύστημα SandBot παρέχει μια ανεξάρτητη (sovereign), διαχρονική και ασφαλή κατεύθυνση για την αυτόνομη εκτέλεση πολύπλοκων τεχνικών έργων.

title: sdAbs-LLM: Generative Large Language Models For de novo Antibody Design and Agentic Evaluation
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite major advances in computational antibody engineering, no systematic comparison of modern open-source LLM backbone families for antibody sequence generation exists, nor is it known whether architectural differences matter at compact model scales. In this study, five compact transformer variants inspired by prominent open-source LLM families (Llama-4, Gemma-3, DeepSeek-V3, Mistral 7B, and NVIDIA Nemotron-3) were customized and trained from scratch for de novo VH single-domain antibody (sdAb) design. All five models were pretrained from scratch on 15 million sequences from the Observed Antibody Space (OAS) database. Pretraining yielded uniformly high generative fidelity across architectures: sequence diversity 0.507–0.516 (CV=0.8%), uniqueness approaching 1.0, and novelty 0.925–0.977 (CV=2.2%). The models were subsequently fine-tuned on disease-stratified repertoires spanning SARS-CoV-2 (n=4,688), HIV (n=430), HER2 (n=22,778), and Ebola virus (n=2,868). Structural assessment of top-ranked candidates of those case studies via AlphaFold-2, Boltz-2, RoseTTAFold-2, and ESMFold produced mean pLDDT scores of 92.88±1.54 to 93.77±2.16, with no statistically significant inter-model differences (Kruskal–Wallis H=2.06, p>0.05; N=100), indicating no statistically detectable difference was observed across architectures at this compressed scale in a single-seed experiment, suggesting that generative capacity at this parameter regime is primarily determined by training data and model scale rather than family-specific design elements at this scale. Computational docking yielded predicted binding free energies of −36.34 to −65.60 kcal/mol; independent biological rigor validation through IMGT-defined CDR-H3 extraction, BLASTp novelty assessment, and NetMHCIIpan 4.3 MHC-II immunogenicity profiling collectively confirmed antigen-binding loop novelty (CDR-H3 identity 0–29% to closest database hits), germline-consistent humanness (77–90% VH germline content), and immunogenically silent antigen-binding surfaces with no strong MHC-II binders detected across CDR regions in any candidate. We further introduce a proof-of-concept agentic evaluation pipeline leveraging the Model Context Protocol (MCP) with Claude Sonnet 4.6, enabling automated structural profiling and candidate prioritization across disease targets.

title: Vom Lesesaal zum Datenzentrum
abstract: Der Vortrag "Vom Lesesaal zum Datenzentrum" von Gerrit Gragert (Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin – Preußischer Kulturbesitz, Abteilung Informations- und Datenmanagement) zeichnet den Wandel bibliothekarischer Lizenzierungs- und Bereitstellungsmodelle von klassischen Textsammlungen hin zu datenzentrierten Diensten nach. Ausgangspunkt sind etablierte Formen der Lizenzierung digitaler Inhalte: die seit 2004 von der DFG geförderten Nationallizenzen, über die Bibliotheken abgeschlossene Textsammlungen verschiedener Wissenschaften mit unbegrenztem deutschlandweitem Zugriffsrecht erwerben, sowie die seit 2014 bestehenden Fachinformationsdienste (FID) für die Wissenschaft, die community-spezifisch Spitzenforschung mit Fachinformationen versorgen. Am Beispiel des FID Asien (CrossAsia) wird gezeigt, wie die Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin Digitalisate selbst hostet, Metadaten indexiert und Volltextsuchen aufbaut. CrossAsia stellt dabei mit 86 Millionen Volltextseiten und 540.000 Titeln (Bücher, wissenschaftliche Zeitschriftenartikel, zeitgenössische Zeitungen) in einem on-premise betriebenen Fedora-Repository ein umfangreiches, wenn auch aufgrund von Lizenzbeschränkungen closed-access geführtes Textkorpus dar, das für Text- und Data-Mining freigegeben ist. Den Schwerpunkt des Vortrags bildet die Vorstellung von Pontus-X, einem Gaia-X-konformen Digital Service Ecosystem für Daten, KI und Infrastrukturanbieter, das über das Prinzip Compute-to-Data eine Prozessierung von Daten ermöglicht, ohne dass diese die Institution verlassen oder heruntergeladen werden müssen – dies wahrt Datensouveränität und Datenschutz, verhindert durch Open-Source-Komponenten und offene Schnittstellen einen Vendor-Lock-In und eröffnet über dezentrale föderierte Analyse- und Lernverfahren sowie mögliche Monetarisierung neue Formen der institutionsübergreifenden Kooperation. Anhand eines Proof-of-Concept auf Basis von CrossAsia-Daten (Berlin State Library Portal Demonstrator) wird demonstriert, wie Service Offerings für Daten und Algorithmen im Pontus-X-Netzwerk angeboten und über gesicherte Compute-Jobs genutzt werden können. Als nächste Schritte werden die Überführung des Portals von Proof-of-Concept und Pilotbetrieb in die Produktion, die Anbindung weiterer Inhalte, der Einsatz von Model-Context-Protocol-(MCP-)Servern für agentische KI-Anwendungen sowie die Einbindung weiterer Kooperationspartner genannt.
venue: Publication Server (Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities)

title: Strategic Analysis of Anthropic Public Benefit Corporation (PBC): An Exploratory Case Study of AI Safety, Innovation, and Business Evolution
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this paper is to conduct an exploratory case study of Anthropic PBC by examining its business evolution, technological innovation, ethical AI practices, financial growth, and strategic positioning within the global artificial intelligence industry. The study applies established strategic management frameworks, including SWOC, ABCD, financial analysis, and technological strategy analysis, to evaluate the company's competitive capabilities and long-term sustainability. It further seeks to provide strategic recommendations for enhancing customer satisfaction, stakeholder engagement, and responsible AI development. Methodology: This study adopts an exploratory qualitative case study approach. Relevant information was collected from peer-reviewed journal articles, Google Scholar, official company publications, technical white papers, industry reports, financial reports, authenticated online sources, and AI-assisted research tools. The collected data were critically analysed and interpreted using strategic business analysis frameworks, including SWOC, ABCD, financial analysis, and technological strategy analysis, in accordance with the objectives of the study. Analysis & Suggestions: The analysis indicates that Anthropic has established a distinctive competitive position through its safety-first philosophy, Constitutional AI methodology, Responsible Scaling Policy, Model Context Protocol (MCP), and strong enterprise-focused business model. Despite rapid commercial growth and increasing enterprise adoption, the company continues to face challenges related to intense market competition, infrastructure costs, consumer brand recognition, and the need to maintain its responsible AI culture while scaling globally. The study recommends strengthening consumer brand awareness, expanding multimodal and agentic AI capabilities, diversifying revenue streams, enhancing international expansion, deepening regulatory collaboration, and preserving its safety-oriented organizational culture to achieve long-term sustainable growth. Originality / Value: This paper presents a comprehensive company analysis of Anthropic PBC by integrating technological, financial, strategic, ethical, governance, and competitive perspectives within a single exploratory case study framework. Unlike previous studies that primarily examine individual aspects of Anthropic's AI safety research or language models, this study provides a holistic evaluation using established business analysis frameworks to assess organizational performance and long-term sustainability. The findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on frontier artificial intelligence companies and provide practical insights for researchers, managers, policymakers, investors, and organizations seeking to understand responsible AI innovation and strategic business development. Type of Paper: Case Study based on Exploratory Research.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: ToxMCP: study data, source code and figures for auditable agentic workflows in computational toxicology
abstract: Supporting research materials for the revised manuscript “ToxMCP: Auditable Agentic Workflows for Computational Toxicology via the Model Context Protocol (MCP)” by Ivo Djidrovski. This deposit contains retained evidence for two live multi-server demonstrations (bisphenol F and triclosan), a 72-assignment comparison of a deterministic script and three LLM clients, frozen protocols and configurations, indexed tool outputs, numerical reference data, source code, an offline verifier and final figure sources. The supplementary guide explains the evidence bundles, exposure equations, execution controls and limitations. Start with REVIEWER_VERIFICATION_GUIDE.md and CLAIM_CHECKS.csv. The portable Python verifier checks retained-file integrity, reconciles recorded acceptance decisions, compares stored PBK trajectories with stored references, and recalculates selected exposure and pharmacokinetic summaries. It does not rerun scientific engines, query live services or perform scientific adjudication. Fresh execution requires the documented external services, scientific runtimes and client/provider access. LLM-assisted inspection is optional; uploading files alone is not verification. The comparisons evaluate workflow execution and reporting. They do not establish scientific validity, regulatory suitability, universal model compatibility or superiority in human report comprehension. The live BPF demonstration used R 4.2.3/rxode2 5.1.2; the comparison used the separately qualified Linux environment documented in the package. Historical records retain their original context and are accompanied by subsequent corrections. The live-case author review is conditional and not independent validation; comparison scientific adjudication remains uncompleted. Prepared for the Journal of Cheminformatics revision. Supported by the Dutch Research Council (NWO), VHP4Safety, NWA.1292.19.272. The journal manuscript and response to reviewers are submitted separately. Superseded editorial drafts are excluded from the cleaned archive; frozen scientific records are retained unchanged. Licensing is file-specific: CC BY 4.0 covers original study documentation, figures and original data; Apache-2.0 covers original study code. The Mian and Loer publication supplements retain CC BY-NC 4.0. Other upstream sources retain their own terms. No blanket relicensing or endorsement by source authors, OECD or other resource providers is intended. See RIGHTS_AND_ATTRIBUTION.md. Visual-production disclosure: the author confirms that the separate graphical abstract was created with OpenAI image generation as a conceptual illustration of the author-developed architecture. Claude Opus 5.5 assisted with the code-based redesign of the five numbered main figures; their source code is retained. Claude Opus 5 was the separate model evaluated in the comparison experiment.

title: FileVault: A Multi-Tenant Storage and Persistent Memory Infrastructure for LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents are stateless by default: les live in one system, vector memories in another, and neither survives between sessions without custom glue code. We present FileVault, a production storage system that unies le storage, semantic search, and persistent agent memory behind a single REST API and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. FileVault indexes uploaded files automatically (fixed-window chunking, text-embedding-3-small embeddings) and stores both file chunks and key/value agent memories in PostgreSQL with pgvector HNSW indexes for approximate nearest-neighbor search. We evaluate FileVault's production retrieval path against three self-contained baselines exact (brute-force) cosine search, lexical (BM25) search, and no retrieval across three research questions: whether persistent memory survives across sessions as unrelated memories accumulate, whether semantic search outperforms lexical matching once queries are paraphrased away from a document's exact wording, and how retrieval latency and approximation quality scale as an agent's corpus grows toward FileVault's 50,000-chunk free-tier ceiling. We nd that memory recall stays at 100% up to 1,000 distractor memories and degrades to 93.3% at 5,000; that lexical search fails completely (0% recall) on paraphrased queries while semantic search stays at 100%, at roughly half the latency of exact search; and that HNSW's agreement with exact search on the true top-10 nearest neighbors declines from 100% to 6.4% as the corpus grows from 100 to 50,000 chunks, even as HNSW's own query latency stays two orders of magnitude below exact search's. We report this evaluation's methodology in full, including two confounds we caught and xed during the study, and conclude with concrete tuning recommendations for FileVault's HNSW conguration at scale. As a nal check before publication, we veried the live deployment directly and found it was, in fact, unreachable: fiveve independent, compounding bugs a database column-naming mismatch, an authentication middleware gate that blocked the entire agent API, two corrupted environment variables, and a recursive middleware request loop left core functionality broken in production despite a passing unit test suite throughout. We x all ve, add integration testing and a live smoke test to catch regressions of this kind going forward, and report the diagnostic process in full since none of it was visible to the retrieval-path evaluation above.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: SOMAS CVE/CWE RADAR: Context-Aware Multi-Agent Security Intelligence Platform for Cloud-Native Infrastructure
abstract: Overview SOMAS (Security Overlay Multi-Agent System) CVE/CWE RADAR is a research project exploring context-aware vulnerability management for cloud-native infrastructure. The system addresses critical challenges in modern security operations: zero-day response delays, alert fatigue, and lack of deployment context awareness. Key Innovation Unlike traditional security scanners that generate context-free alerts, SOMAS implements a proactive intelligence approach. The system maintains a clean production inventory in a vector database and uses AI agents powered by local LLM (Ollama llama3.1) to continuously monitor global threat feeds, automatically cross-referencing new vulnerabilities against actual production deployments. Architecture Components 5-Level Security Radar: Level 1: Code logic analysis (CWE patterns) using Semgrep Level 2: Package dependency scanning (CVE) using Syft SBOM Level 3: Container image scanning using Syft CBOM Level 4: Kubernetes cluster configuration analysis Level 5: Infrastructure and host OS scanning AI Agent Framework: Scout Agent: Monitors threat intelligence feeds (NVD, GHSA, MITRE, Twitter/X) Analyst Agent: Performs contextual risk assessment using vector database inventory Dispatcher Agent: Intelligent incident routing to appropriate teams Technical Stack: Vector Database: Qdrant for semantic inventory storage AI Engine: Ollama llama3.1 (local LLM deployment) Agent Interface: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool access Automation: GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline Visualization: Next.js dashboard with real-time monitoring Research Contribution This project demonstrates how multi-agent systems powered by local LLMs can transform vulnerability management from reactive scanning to proactive intelligence. By separating clean inventory storage from vulnerability data and leveraging semantic search capabilities, the system enables instant zero-day impact analysis without requiring manual cross-referencing across repositories and clusters. Use Cases Automated security monitoring for cloud-native applications Context-aware vulnerability prioritization Reduced alert fatigue through intelligent filtering Rapid zero-day response (MTTD reduction) Multi-layer security coverage (code to infrastructure) Privacy & Security All operations run locally within infrastructure boundaries. Production inventory never leaves the environment, ensuring compliance with data residency requirements. The use of local LLM (Ollama) eliminates cloud API dependencies and associated costs.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: A Statistical and Practical Study of Deploying Fair, Safe, and Productive AI
abstract: This thesis presents a series of results that study the deployment of fair, safe, and productive AI. We begin in Chapter 1 by both motivating and introducing the three topics of study: algorithmic fairness in performative prediction, weak-to-strong generalization, and benchmarking AI adoption and capability across the economy. Additionally, a brief synopsis of the results we will present in subsequent chapters is included. In Chapter 2, we study the problem of enforcing fairness under distribution shift caused by human behavior. This distribution shift is known as performativity and is often caused by the reactions of individuals with vested interests in the outcome of the predictive model. While performativity is generally problematic, as it leads to changes in the data at test time, we develop algorithmic fairness practices that leverage performativity to achieve stronger group fairness guaranties in social classification problems (compared to what is achievable in non-performative settings). In particular, we show that it is possible to enforce traditionally conflicting group fairness definitions if performativity is present. In chapter 3, we study the problem of superalignment through the analogy of weak-to-strong generalization; or using weaker (less capable) feedback to train a stronger (more capable) model. We prove that weak-to-strong generalization is possible by eliciting latent knowledge from pre-trained LLMs. In particular, we cast the weak-to-strong generalization problem as a transfer learning problem in which we wish to transfer a latent concept from a weak model to a strong pre-trained model. We prove that a naive fine-tuning approach suffers from fundamental limitations, but an alternative refinement-based approach suggested by the problem structure provably overcomes the limitations of fine-tuning. Finally, we demonstrate the practical applicability of the refinement approach on multiple LLM alignment tasks. Finally, in Chapter 4, we work towards measuring both AI adoption and the capability of AI to perform discrete labor tasks across various occupations. To measure adoption, we develop an open-source economic index that uses publicly available user-LLM chat data and O*NET tasks to replicate studies produced by leading AI labs. To measure capabilities, we build a system that generates benchmark scenarios grounded in O*NET occupations, tasks, and model-context-protocol (MCP) servers. We test Kimi-k2.5 with an OpenAI agents SDK harness on scenarios across 9 occupations that appear frequently in our index, finding that there is ample room for improvement in tool calling, workflow completion, and grounding.

title: Case Study: An Agentic AI Framework for Large-Scale Well Modeling of Offshore Field Developments
abstract: _ Well modeling is a foundational activity in production engineering for artificial lift systems. Engineers routinely construct physics-based models to match flowing gradient survey (FGS) data, generate inflow performance relationship (IPR) and vertical lift performance (VLP) relationships, analyze pressure-temperature (PT) profiles, and evaluate tubing-size and gas-lift sensitivities. These workflows directly support decisions related to production optimization, stimulation planning, and liquid-loading diagnostics. In practice, however, such modeling remains highly manual and time intensive. For a single well, constructing and calibrating a physics-based model in a commercial simulator often requires several hours of focused engineering effort. When the number of wells increases to hundreds, as is common in large offshore developments, the task becomes prohibitively slow. As a result, many studies are either deferred, restricted to limited subsets of wells, or simplified to meet time constraints. Each of these approaches may compromise decision quality. To address this scalability challenge, agentic artificial intelligence (AI) was deployed for India’s Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC). The agentic AI enabled an automation framework that could complete large-scale well modeling in a rapid and repeatable manner while under the supervision of engineering teams (Fig. 1). The framework integrates a domain-specific Python library with an AI-driven command-line agent operating on SLB’s Pipesim engine. The central objective is not to replace engineering judgment, but to remove repetitive manual steps so that engineers can focus on interpretation and decision-making rather than model construction. Agentic-AI Architecture The automation framework consists of three tightly integrated components. Well-Analysis Python Library A custom Python library, named well-analysis, was developed to encapsulate the most common well-modeling operations in Pipesim. The library provides compact and reusable functions to define tubular geometry and completion configuration, black-oil PVT (pressure-volume-temperature) properties, reservoir inputs and productivity models, artificial-lift settings, IPR generation, VLP correlation selection, PT profiling, nodal analysis, and FGS-based model calibration. Conventional Pipesim scripting for these tasks often exceeds 100 lines of code per modeling scenario. Using the library, the same operations can typically be expressed in fewer than five lines, which dramatically simplifies automation, maintenance, and reuse. Small Language Model Agent A lightweight AI agent powered by a small language model (SLM) orchestrates the modeling workflow. The agent communicates with the simulator through a model context protocol server that exposes the functions of the well-analysis library as actionable tools. Engineers provide high-level natural-language instructions such as building and calibrating models from a data file, generating IPR-VLP and PT plots, or executing tubing sensitivity studies. The agent translates these instructions into structured execution steps while preserving full traceability of inputs, actions, and outputs.

title: DECENTRALIZED DATA ORGANIZATION AND MANAGEMENT SYSTEM FOR SMART CITY INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY PLATFORMS
abstract: Context. Smart City functions as a multidomain social and technical system in which engineering and infrastructure domains, as well as social and service domains, are connected through shared data, operational dependencies, and distributed project processes carried out by distributed domain teams. Under crisis conditions, degradation of a critical infrastructure domain may propagate to adjacent domains and trigger cascading effects. At the same time, contemporary approaches to urban data management still insufficiently integrate decentralized domain responsibility, formal modeling of interdomain dependencies, and practical mechanisms for governed data interaction within distributed teams.Objective. The aim of this study is to develop and validate a decentralized data organization system for Smart City that integrates Data Mesh principles, fuzzy cognitive modeling of interdomain influences, and a metadata-oriented governance layer to support coordinated work with data products in distributed domain teams.Method. The proposed approach combines a domain-oriented data organization system, fuzzy cognitive maps for representing cause-and-effect interdomain dependencies, and a governance layer implemented using DataHub and Google BigQuery. Practical validation was carried out using the Electric Power Industry domain as a critical infrastructure domain with a high potential for cascading impact. Four open datasets were integrated into the domain layer, describing attacks on energy infrastructure, electricity supply restrictions, the statuses of electricity market participants, and indicators of the day-ahead market. On this basis, domain data products and an integral indicator of cascading-effect risk were implemented.Results. The study proposes a decentralized data organization model for Smart City and demonstrates its practical implementation for the electricity domain. A domain portfolio of critical data products was established; owners and semantic descriptions were defined; data lineage relationships and data contracts were formalized; and an analytical representation was implemented to calculate the integral indicator cascade_risk_score. The obtained results show that the proposed architecture supports transparent interaction with domain data products, improves the reproducibility of interdomain integrations, and enables the identification of periods of elevated cascading risk. The practical implementation also confirmed that the model is not limited to a single analytical repository and can be extended to heterogeneous data sources used by different Smart City domains.Conclusions. The results demonstrate that the integration of Data Mesh principles, fuzzy cognitive modeling, and metadataoriented governance provides a viable foundation for data organization in Smart City under conditions of distributed team interaction. The proposed model supports decentralized responsibility for data products, improves the coordination of distributed project processes, and strengthens the capacity for the proactive detection of cascading risks in critical urban infrastructure. Further research should focus on interdomain empirical validation, scaling to Smart Region scenarios, and the integration of large language modelbased agents through the Model Context Protocol for the automated analysis of data contracts, metadata, and operational anomalies

ASQ-PHI: An Adversarial Synthetic Benchmark for Clinical De-Identification and Search Utility
abstract: Hospitals are beginning to deploy HIPAA-compliant Business Associate Agreement (BAA) large language models (LLMs). In the public setting, LLMs with fixed training cutoffs are routinely augmented with tools such as web search, deep research, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers so they can reach up-to-date knowledge. BAA LLMs, by contrast, almost never expose live web search or external tools, even though clinicians expect LLMs to surface current guidelines, drug safety updates, and literature. The constraint is that any query leaving a BAA-protected LLM for an external service must be free of Protected Health Information (PHI). We refer to this boundary as the safe handoff: the moment when a clinician’s PHI-containing query, generated inside a HIPAA-compliant BAA LLM, must be transformed into a HIPAA Safe Harbor–compliant version before being sent to non-BAA tools such as web search APIs, external evidence services, or MCP servers. Existing de-identification datasets are built from long electronic health record narratives rather than the short, compressed search queries clinicians type into LLM chat interfaces, so they do not allow de-identification performance to be tested at this safe handoff. ASQ-PHI (Adversarial Synthetic Queries for Protected Health Information de-identification) is constructed to supply this missing data: a benchmark of 1,051 fully synthetic clinical search queries with ground-truth PHI annotations for stress-testing HIPAA-compliant de-identification software. All queries were generated using Azure OpenAI GPT-4o. No real patient data were used. Research hypothesis: Current de-identification systems fail at the safe handoff from LLMs running inside HIPAA BAAs to external tools in two ways: 1) Leaking PHI 2) Over-redacting non-identifying clinical information reducing query utility. What the data shows: The dataset contains 832 PHI-positive queries (79.2 percent) and 219 hard negatives (20.8 percent), totaling 2,973 tagged PHI elements across 13 HIPAA Safe Harbor types. Most common: GEOGRAPHIC_LOCATION (27.8 percent), NAME (27.4 percent), DATE (27.1 percent). Hard negatives mimic PHI-containing text but contain no identifiers, enabling over-redaction measurement. Notable findings: Baseline validation using Amazon Comprehend Medical (DetectPHI) revealed severe recall-utility tradeoffs, as shown in validation_results. How the data was generated: Queries were generated using GPT-4o. A system prompt specified natural clinical questions containing 0 to 5 HIPAA identifiers. Output format: "===QUERY===" followed by "===PHI_TAGS===" with JSON {"identifier_type": "TYPE", "value": "..."}. Complete code in code/data_generation_pipeline.ipynb. The dataset serves developers building HIPAA-compliant LLM infrastructure, privacy researchers benchmarking algorithms, and compliance teams evaluating vendor claims.

title: Контекстно-орієнтована система організації даних для розподілених проєктних команд
abstract: Досліджено проблему фрагментованої організації даних у розподілених проєктних командах великих ІТ-компаній та сервісних організацій, що працюють у кількох часових поясах, юрисдикціях і доменах. Показано, що централізовані архітектури даних (Data Warehouse, Data Lake, Lakehouse), орієнтовані насамперед на звітність, погано відображають багатодоменну структуру таких організацій, створюють організаційні "вузькі місця" та не забезпечують контекстно-орієнтованої підтримки життєвого циклу проєктів. На підставі аналізу концепції мережі Data Mesh обґрунтовано релевантність доменно-орієнтованого підходу до організації даних із використанням дата-продуктів, контрактів на дані (data contracts), платформи самообслуговування та федеративного обчислювального управління, але виявлено розрив на рівні доступу стейкхолдерів до проєктного контексту. Проаналізовано сучасні практики інтеграції великих мовних моделей і розмовної аналітики в BI- та хмарні платформи. Показано, що такі рішення здебільшого залишаються платформно-специфічними та відтворюють схему інтеграцій M×N між агентами та сервісами. Протокол контексту моделі MCP (англ. Model Context Protocol) розглянуто як відкритий протокол прикладного рівня, що нормалізує взаємодію LLM-агентів із зовнішніми ресурсами через примітиви resources, tools, prompts і дає змогу зменшити інтеграційну складність до O(M+N). На цьому підґрунті запропоновано контекстно-орієнтовану архітектурну модель системи організації даних для розподілених проєктних команд у конфігурації "Data Mesh + MCP + LLM-агенти". Запропоновано архітектуру "Data Mesh + MCP + агенти на підставі великих мовних моделей (LLM)", у якій доменні дата-продукти (data products) та контракти на дані (data contracts) системи мережі Data Mesh формально зіставлено з MCP-ресурсами (resources) та інструментами (tools), а доступ до них здійснюється через платформу самообслуговування даними (self-service data platform) з інтегрованою підтримкою LLM-агентів. Аналітична модель інтеграційної складності демонструє перехід від квадратичного зростання витрат типу M×N у класичній схемі до лінійної залежності M+N в архітектурі "Data Mesh + MCP", що створює передумови для підвищення масштабованості інтеграційного шару, зниження інтеграційних витрат і прозорого, контекстно-орієнтованого доступу до проєктних артефактів у розподілених командах. Перспективою подальших досліджень є емпірична верифікація запропонованої архітектури в організаціях із багатодоменними портфелями проєктів та подальший розвиток моделей контекстно-орієнтованої взаємодії LLM-агентів із дата-продуктами та даними про проєктні ризики.

title: SbD MCP Server v0.9.0 — Software Bundle (npm package + GitHub source, ICSME 2026)
abstract: Offline-reproducible software bundle for the SbD MCP Server (v0.9.0), an ontology-grounded retrieval tool that exposes the Security-by-Design Theory-of-Everything (SbD-ToE) knowledge graph to GenAI coding assistants through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The server grounds model output in a curated, versioned ontology of AppSec Core-typed security requirements rather than relying on parametric memory alone. This item archives the tool itself in two complementary forms — the canonical npm package tarball (runnable) and the full GitHub source bundle (inspectable) — so that the v0.9.0 demonstration state remains reproducible independently of the upstream registries. title: Capsule: Atomic, File-First Long-Term Memory with Bounded Drift for Autonomous AI Agents
abstract: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents deployed on extended software engineering, research, and planning tasks require persistent long-term memory across sessions. Existing agent architectures predominantly rely on traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigms that partition documents into arbitrary, fixed-window character or token chunks stored in append-only vector databases. In long-running autonomous workflows, this approach exhibits three fatal pathologies:1. **Semantic Fragmentation**: Fixed-width token slicing arbitrarily splits interdependent entities, preconditions, and constraints across chunk boundaries, causing context omission and multi-hop reasoning failure.2. **Append-Only Memory Bloat**: Every agent turn indiscriminately writes redundant observations to the vector store, producing unbounded $O(N)$ index explosion, increased retrieval latency, and context poisoning.3. **Black-Box Opacity**: Embedding-only vector stores cannot be audited, inspected, diffed, or corrected by human engineers via standard version-control workflows. We introduce **Capsule**, an open-source, dual-plane memory architecture specifically designed for autonomous agents. Capsule enforces an *atomic fact representation* ("one self-contained fact per Markdown file") stored with structured YAML frontmatter directly on the filesystem (the *Storage Plane*), while maintaining high-speed derived indexes (SQLite FTS5 / PostgreSQL `tsvector` + vector embeddings) in an ephemeral, rebuildable database (the *Retrieval Plane*). Capsule introduces:- **Normalized SHA-256 Content-Hash Deduplication**: Intercepts redundant observations, merging updates into idempotent canonical nodes with tracked revision lineages.- **Token-Bounded Knapsack Context Composition**: Replaces blind top-$k$ chunk concatenation with a budget-constrained optimization problem that packs maximal information density into the prompt window. We rigorously evaluate Capsule against standard fixed-window RAG across four empirical benchmarks:- **Retrieval Efficiency**: Capsule achieves a **36.9% reduction in prompt token consumption** while improving multi-hop fact recall from **93.3% to 100.0%**, and more than doubling context information density from **34.1% to 71.4%**.- **Downstream Reasoning**: In an end-to-end evaluation using a frontier LLM (`Gemini 2.5 Flash`), Capsule increases multi-hop architectural question answering accuracy from **50.0% to 93.3% (+43.3% absolute improvement)** while slashing input token costs by **37.3%**.- **Multi-Turn Memory Bloat Simulation**: Over an extended 50-step iterative agent task, Capsule prunes **85.0% of redundant submissions**, bounding long-term memory growth and reducing token storage footprint by **51.8%** compared to traditional append-only vector stores.- **Component Ablations**: We isolate the contributions of hybrid retrieval, knapsack budget packing, and content deduplication, demonstrating that removing any single component causes steep degradation in token efficiency or context precision. Capsule is released as an open-source package (`pip install kapsule`) with native CLI utilities, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, and automated daemon harvesters.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Recognition-Gated Workspace Steering: Pratyabhijñā as an Engineering Specification for Language Model Control
abstract: Recent interpretability work established that a language model’s functional global workspace is defined by verbalizable representations, and released a linear instrument, the Jacobian lens, that reads any residual-stream state as a ranked token distribution. The field therefore possesses an actuator without a doctrine of use. This paper derives such a doctrine from Pratyabhijñā, a ninth-century recognition philosophy whose central identity, reflexive awareness as the supreme Word, anticipates the verbalizable-workspace finding. The doctrine is treated strictly as an engineering specification with five falsifiable clauses: what to write (verbalizable concept codes), where (the workspace band, in band coordinates), when (moments of uncommitted prediction, detected by step entropy), how to verify (readback through a band-targeted lens), and at what cost (a registered entropy budget). Each clause was tested on frozen decoder transformers through a preregistered, gate-audited experimental programme spanning loops L0 to L21, run autonomously by an expected-free-energy selector over registered experiment menus, with twenty-seven selector cycles, eighteen isolated adversarial reviews, and roughly eighteen GPU-hours of compute on a single shared node. Six clauses or mechanisms are confirmed: workspace-band structure and instructed loadability replicate across model families and scale with size (hit-rate@5 of 0.10 at 4B versus 0.55 at 27B, collapsing to 0.00 on a pruned and-distilled twin); band content is legible only to a lens targeted at the band; entropy-gated writes steer within a ±0.5-nat budget at six independent stream seeds (lift 0.30 to 0.35, sign-consistent alignment advantage, one-sided p = 0.016); a calibration recipe with amplitude inversely proportional to lens transport strength transfers steering to a second model family at four seeds with monotone dose response; and an untrained associative memory write path reproduces the analytic steering path on all three seeds tested. Registered negative results bound the doctrine’s scope: gated steering trades concept-surface throughput for legibility rather than maximising it (surface rate 0.16 versus 0.96 for continuous flooding at matched entropy cost), and contrastive refusal-direction steering leaves attack success on an already-aligned 4B model unchanged (0.25 to 0.25). A head-to-head benchmark against the Jacobian-lens final-target baseline shows the band-targeted instrument is roughly twice as sensitive at subtle write doses (detection 0.475 versus 0.24, p = 2.1 × 10−5) and 2.3 times more write-efficient than continuous flooding. The same activation signal that fails as a blanket steering direction, used instead as an input-conditioned recognition gate, yields a deployable jailbreak defence that matches brute force attack-success reduction at zero benign over refusal on models whose benign and attack projections separate cleanly, and this success is predictable before deployment from an offline clean gap test: across four model families the moat works on two and the predictor is correct on all four. All code, gates, lens checkpoints, an agent callable Model Context Protocol server, and interactive replay applications are released.

title: MH8-Acbeatz.com-MP3-GPT-PLaylist + All MH8 Acbeatz.com GPT driven Systems
abstract: MH8-Acbeatz.com-MP3-GPT-PLaylist + All MH8 Acbeatz.com GPT driven Systems> is the first decentralized protocol to embed SHA-256 cryptographic provenance into AI-assisted music at the moment of creation — not after. Each lyric, prompt, and generated audio file receives a deterministic 256-bit serial number (a "Music & Lyrical Birth Certificate") before it ever leaves the creator's pipeline, establishing immutable, verifiable authorship without reliance on any central registry or blockchain consensus mechanism. The system operates as a constellation of protocol-driven AI agents — ABE-GPT, Suno-GPT, Social-GPT, Support Office GPT, and MP3-GPT Playlist — orchestrated through a Cloudflare Worker acting as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, with R2 object storage and KV state management providing an append-only, tamper-evident storage layer. Economic primitives (Deal Board, Bounty Marketplace) and a multi-platform distribution model (acbeatz.com, GitHub, Ko-fi, Discord) complete the stack. This whitepaper presents the full protocol specification: system architecture, SHA-256 identity layer, streaming infrastructure, economic modules, novelty claims, IP positioning via defensive publication, a seven-vector threat model, current limitations, and a forward roadmap including IPFS integration, formal verification, and zero-knowledge provenance proofs. Author: Michael M. Hepler (acbeatz / allchemicalbeatz) License: CC BY 4.0 Version: 1.0 — April 2026 Abstract — Problem statement, MH8 solution, and system summary Introduction — AI music provenance gap, the "Birth Certificate" concept, and your contributions Scientific Framing & Related Work — Positioning against Audius, IPFS, C2PA, DIDs, and why SHA-256 at genesis is fundamentally different System Architecture — Agent ecosystem (ABE-GPT, Suno-GPT, Social-GPT, Support Office GPT, MP3-GPT Playlist), Cloudflare Worker pipeline as MCP server, and R2/KV storage layer SHA-256 Identity Layer — Full 6-step provenance pipeline from canonical payload to lineage chaining Streaming Layer — R2-backed delivery with embedded provenance Economic Modules — Deal Board, Bounty Marketplace, and LifeCoin concept Distribution Model — Multi-platform strategy across Zenodo, GitHub, Ko-fi, Discord, and social channels Novelty & Originality Claims — Five defensible firsts IP Positioning — Defensive publication via Zenodo DOI and CC BY 4.0 Threat Model — Seven attack vectors with mitigations Limitations — Honest constraints Future Work — Roadmap including IPFS, formal specs, ISMIR submission, ZK proofs References — Academic citations (FIPS 180-4, MCP, C2PA, W3C DIDs, etc.) Appendices — SHA-256 receipt example, agent identity schema, orchestrator API endpoints https://zenodo.org/records/18131984 (C T K L T) Core: https://acbeatz.com/n-eyes https://acbeatz.com https://github.com/acbeatz https://orcid.org/0009-0003-3846-9082

title: Arbitration Hacked: Toward a Unified Cybersecurity and Data Breach Framework for International Arbitral Proceedings
The Self-Hosted AI Agent Buyer's Guide
abstract: Episode summary: The world of self-hosted AI agents is a jungle of competing philosophies and acronyms. Are you building a slick UI for daily productivity, a robust backend for enterprise apps, or an automation engine for your smart home? We dissect the heavy hitters—including LobeHub, Dify, OpenClaw, n8n, and Anything LLM—to help you decide which platform actually owns your data. Whether you're a solo developer or managing a dev shop, this guide maps out the trade-offs between user-friendly interfaces and powerful, node-based workflows. Show Notes The landscape of self-hosted AI has exploded, moving far beyond simple chat interfaces into the realm of autonomous agents. As of April 2026, the market is divided by distinct philosophies on how an agent should work. For users seeking a polished, "SaaS-like" experience that runs locally, the conversation starts with LobeHub. It prioritizes the user interface, introducing "Agent Groups" and "White-Box Memory" that allow users to visually manage what an agent knows. It is the "prosumer" choice, designed for daily productivity rather than backend engineering. However, a different breed of platform exists for those building for others. Dify stands out as the enterprise-grade powerhouse. While LobeHub is a destination for chatting, Dify is a factory for building applications. It includes built-in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, deep observability, and visual workflow builders robust enough to handle complex, multi-step logic gates. It is the standard for production applications where reliability and token tracking are paramount. For the architect who wants an agent to permeate their entire digital life, OpenClaw offers an "Operating System" approach. Rather than a single chat window, OpenClaw aims to keep a persistent "brain" alive, piping it into Discord, Telegram, and terminals via "Channel Adapters." It treats the agent as a ubiquitous presence rather than a tool you visit. The distinction between "visual" and "code" tools also blurs with platforms like Flowise and n8n. Flowise remains the "LangChain visualizer," a sandbox for engineers to drag-and-drop nodes to see the plumbing of an LLM chain. It is excellent for prototyping but lacks the polished front-end of other options. n8n, conversely, is automation-first. It wasn't built for AI, but AI is now just another node in its massive library of integrations. This makes n8n the king of "triggered" agents—bots that wake up because an email arrived or a database row changed—though it comes with a steep learning curve. Finally, for the user who just wants to chat with their PDFs, Anything LLM and Open WebUI offer focused solutions. Anything LLM acts as the "easy button," packaging a vector store and chat interface into a workspace-centric tool. Open WebUI caters to the local LLM enthusiast, providing a sleek, ChatGPT-like wrapper for models running via Ollama. The unifying factor for all these platforms is the emerging Model Context Protocol (MCP). Described as the "USB-C" of AI, MCP allows any platform to connect to external tools—like a filesystem or database—without custom plugins. As the protocol matures, the competition may shift from who has the best built-in tools to who can best utilize the universal ecosystem of MCP servers. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/self-hosted-ai-agent-comparison
