title: Cross-Agent Governance Alignment (CAGA): Formalizing Cross-Organizational AI Governance as a Zero-Knowledge Coordination Problem
abstract: Cross-Agent Governance Alignment (CAGA): Verifiable Coordination Across Private AI Governance Domains formalizes the CAGA problem: establishing a declared compatibility relation between AI governance domains across organizational boundaries without disclosing the proprietary policy content on which each domain relies. Cross-organizational agent interaction creates two distinct governance questions: whether each local effect-bearing action is authorized within its own domain, and whether the participating domains can establish the declared relation. This paper formalizes the second problem. CAGA does not itself authorize execution. It produces a privacy-preserving compatibility result and associated evidence that each domain's runtime authorization boundary may materially consume before emitting its own action-bound verdict and authorization artifact. The formal model defines a governance domain as agents, a declared effect-bearing action vocabulary, versioned policy and authority state, governance-relevant state, a material evidence set, and a runtime authorization boundary over the triadic verdict space (ALLOW, DENY, ABSTAIN), where unresolved ABSTAIN remains ABSTAIN and authorized resolution produces a separate resulting action-bound verdict through the boundary. Every CAGA claim is scoped to a declared profile identifying the participating domains and authority roots, action vocabulary, compatibility relation and version, commitments, temporal boundary, leakage profile, scheme and verification parameters, declared replay mode, failure treatment, and expected local-boundary consumption. The Boolean compatibility relation is separated from protocol status: the protocol output comprises a result that may be positive, negative, or unresolved, together with the proof or verifier record and a CAGA evidence artifact. An unresolved result is not a verdict, and neither a negative nor an unresolved result may be treated as affirmative CAGA support for ALLOW. An illustrative prior-authorization compatibility relation between a hospital domain and an insurer domain, together with a worked local-boundary consumption sequence, shows the level at which a CAGA proposition may be stated without disclosing a protocol construction; no execution path originates from CAGA. The paper: Separates local pre-execution authorization from cross-domain compatibility evidence, and reserves the term authorization artifact for the action-bound record emitted by a runtime authorization boundary; a CAGA result may participate in composed authorization only where the Composition Test is satisfied; the CAGA evidence artifact does not thereby become an authorization artifact Formalizes the declared compatibility relation and protocol output under a declared CAGA profile, with cross-domain interactions whose local actions need not be identical, and supplies a terminology and instrument-ownership map locating each evidentiary term in its owning instrument States the threat model with honest-but-curious as the base analytic assumption rather than a prediction about regulated parties, classifies an expanded threat inventory as covered, partially covered, or excluded, and treats Byzantine deviation, arbitrary collusion, and malicious-verifier behavior as outside the base claim, requiring separately specified protocol defenses Identifies the required properties of a declared CAGA protocol: relation completeness and soundness, declared-leakage privacy, deterministic relation result with permitted cryptographic randomness, evidence and reconstruction sufficiency under the declared replay mode, commitment and domain binding, repeated-interaction privacy, optional post-compromise transcript confidentiality, non-authorizing failure, evidence traceability and presentation scope, declared-regime scope, and Input Integrity support, where provenance establishes origin, not truth Restructures the prior-art analysis as a component-and-gap assessment across communication protocols including the current Model Context Protocol specification (2026-07-28), policy composition and distributed authorization, secure multi-party computation and zero-knowledge systems, selective-disclosure credentials, multi-agent and agent-action governance architectures, and ledger approaches, identifying CAGA as the residual problem after those contributions are accounted for Zero-knowledge proof systems, secure multi-party computation, private set intersection, trusted execution, commitment schemes, and selective disclosure are candidate implementation substrates rather than authorization substitutes; no component establishes CAGA or authorization by label alone. The analysis is aligned with the Authorization Artifact Test v1.2, the Authorization Boundary Integrity Model v1.1, the Five Tests Standard v1.2.0, the ABIM Evidence Requirements v3.5, the Closed-World Bargain v1.1, and the Override Asymmetry v2.0. The paper does not assert that any jurisdiction requires CAGA, zero-knowledge proof, or pre-execution authorization, and it deliberately stops at problem formalization: it does not disclose protocol constructions, circuits, trusted-setup designs, or implementation mechanisms. The paper does not present an ideal functionality, security reduction, theorem establishing a protocol construction, or deployable implementation. By defining the problem space and evaluation criteria within a declared closed world, it provides a structured problem specification against which candidate cross-domain coordination protocols and their composition with local runtime authorization boundaries can be assessed. Version 2.0 (August 2026) separates cross-domain compatibility evidence from local pre-execution authorization; replaces the governance-domain enforcement function with a runtime authorization-boundary model; distinguishes the Boolean compatibility relation from unresolved protocol status; defines a declared CAGA profile; separates CAGA evidence artifacts from local authorization artifacts; conditions determinism on declared decision state while permitting cryptographic randomness; replaces default-denial protocol failure with non-authorizing unresolved status; adds an explicit interface to local Input Integrity assessment, authenticated bound materials, replay-mode, closed-world, Composition Test, and authorized-resolution semantics; narrows legal and regulatory claims; updates MCP and multi-agent prior-art references; and restructures the prior-art analysis as a component-and-gap assessment. Version 2.0 also adds an illustrative prior-authorization compatibility relation and a worked local-boundary consumption sequence; clarifies that the paper specifies a formal problem rather than presenting an ideal functionality, security reduction, or protocol proof; adds a terminology and instrument-ownership map; expands the component-and-gap analysis to address policy composition, distributed authorization, selective-disclosure credentials, and recent agent-action governance work; and clarifies the relationship between the paper's CC BY 4.0 copyright license and unlicensed patent rights. It supersedes Version 1.1 (July 2026), which aligned terminology with 5TS v1.2.0 and the FERZ authorization-artifact vocabulary, and Version 1.0 (February 2026), the original problem formalization. Keywords: cross-agent governance alignment, cross-organizational AI governance, private governance domains, privacy-preserving coordination, runtime authorization boundary, pre-execution authorization, authorization artifacts, zero-knowledge proofs, secure multi-party computation, Input Integrity, independent reconstruction

title: Making Dangerous Tool Arguments Inexpressible: A Declarative Contract Format for LLM Agents
abstract: This preprint introduces ToolClad, a declarative tool-contract format for LLM agents that pushes argument validation to a structural runtime fence. Action-level policy engines such as Cedar reason about which actions an agent may invoke; ToolClad reasons about whether the arguments supplied to those actions match a declared, security-relevant shape. A .clad.toml manifest defines typed parameters (path, hostname, scope-bounded string, etc.), validation rules, command templates with array-style execution (no shell-string interpolation), and execution backends. The validator runs before any tool dispatch and refuses parameters that cannot be expressed by the contract, making metacharacter injection, command substitution, path traversal, and scope-target homoglyphs structurally inexpressible rather than detected post-hoc. This paper positions ToolClad as Layer 2 of the Open Agent Trust Stack (OATS) specification: complementary to the action-level policy gate (Cedar) and post-execution content sanitisers, addressing a class of failures that those layers cannot address by design. Most agent failures in production are not "tool not permitted" but "tool permitted, wrong arguments": read_file(path="../../etc/shadow") is a permitted action with an attacker-shaped parameter, and the policy engine cannot meaningfully refuse it without baking parameter validation into the policy itself, which scales poorly. Empirical results. The paper reports a treatment-versus-control A/B evaluation across nine widely available hosted LLMs (April 2026) on a whois_lookup tool surface attacked through eight argument-injection sub-shapes: 333 of 335 treatment-arm dispatches refused across nine models (GPT-5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-V3.1, Qwen3-235B, Qwen3.6-Plus, MiMo-V2-Pro, MiniMax-M2.7, gpt-oss-20b) routed through OpenRouter. The two non-refusals are clean-hostname self-sanitisation cases in which the model refused the injection prompt and emitted a clean ASCII hostname instead. Counted strictly against hostile inputs, the bite-rate is 100%. Eight attack sub-shapes exercised: metacharacter (;|&`), command substitution ($()), backtick (``), wildcard (*?[]), newline injection, path traversal (../), Cyrillic-homoglyph IDN (exаmple.com), and punycode IDN (xn--exmple-9c.com). A closed-limitation feedback arc. v0.1 of this preprint reported a published limitation: the as-built scope_target validator caught Cyrillic-homoglyph hostnames as a side effect of strict ASCII-only validation but accepted the punycode encoding of the same name. ToolClad v0.6.0 closed that gap with explicit punycode-label rejection, and the v0.2 sweep added a punycode-idn sub-shape that empirically validated the fix at 33 of 33 refusals. This revision documents the round-trip from honest disclosure to upstream fix to empirical re-validation. Layered-defense composition. On the tool-arg-injection attack class, Cedar denials = 0 (because whois_lookup is permitted by the task agent's policy), content sanitiser strips = 0 (because the attack is in arguments, not in stored content), and ToolClad refusals = 333. The non-redundancy claim has independent empirical support: the companion typestate preprint reports a stack-stripping ablation in which removing each fence type exposes its corresponding attack class at near-100% survival, with the v11 ToolClad result contributing one of the three rows of that ablation chart. Honest accounting of model-side prompt refusal. The two clean-hostname cases are an instance of a recurring pattern across the OATS empirical corpus: model alignment occasionally pre-empts the runtime fence by refusing the injection at the prompt layer. Empirical fence bite-rates are slightly inflated by this effect; the structural claim is that the fences refuse what the models emit, not that they refuse what an attacker would want a different model to emit. What this is and is not. The paper is a focused technical preprint. It claims a narrow result (typed-argument validation as a separate fence layer, demonstrated against one tool surface and one parameter type) and is explicit about what it does not claim. ToolClad does not introduce typed parameters as a programming-language concept; it does not prevent prompt injection; it does not validate semantic intent; and the empirical evaluation here covers scope_target only and does not generalise to all parameter types. The contribution is the packaging and placement: a domain-specific contract format that takes argument-level attacks off the runtime's threat surface, leaving the policy engine to reason about actions over already-validated arguments. Reproduction artifact. The reproduction artifact is the companion repository at github.com/ThirdKeyAI/symbiont-orga-demo, branch v11-toolclad-fence. The branch packages the symbi-toolclad-bridge integration crate, the manifests/ directory containing whois_lookup.clad.toml and store_knowledge.clad.toml, the v11 sweep script with the --toolclad-mode {off,on,only} flag and the tool-arg-injection attack variant including the new punycode-idn sub-shape, the per-call JSONL capture format, and the analyze-v11-toolclad.py aggregator that reproduces Tables 2 and 3. Software. The ToolClad source is published at github.com/ThirdKeyAI/ToolClad under Apache 2.0; the empirical evaluation in Section 5 exercises ToolClad v0.6.0. The Symbiont runtime is open source under Apache 2.0 at github.com/thirdkeyai/symbiont. The Open Agent Trust Stack (OATS) specification is published at openagenttruststack.org. Companion preprints. The typestate construction this paper composes with is described in detail in the companion preprint Typestate-Enforced Agent Loops: Making Policy Gates Unskippable at Compile Time (preprint v0.5, ThirdKey AI, April 2026), which covers Layer 1 of the OATS specification (the ORGA reasoning loop) and reports the v9 cloud-adversarial sweep and the v12 stack-stripping ablation. A separate companion preprint, Three Substrates, Seven Models, Six Tasks: A Comparative Empirical Evaluation of Structural Enforcement for AI Agent Runtimes (preprint v0.1, ThirdKey AI, May 2026), evaluates ToolClad's scope_target path validator and agent_summary content validator across three substrates and seven models on six adversarial agent task families. Contents: 12 pages, three tables (eight attack sub-shapes, per-model A/B treatment-vs-control results, per-sub-shape bite-rate breakdown), seven sections including Introduction, Background and Related Work, Design (manifest format, parameter types, array-exec, refusal semantics), Implementation (Rust reference, Symbiont/Cedar integration, cross-language manifest-as-source-of-truth), Empirical Evaluation across seven subsections, Limits of the Empirical Argument, and Conclusion. Changes from v0.1: Bumped to ToolClad v0.6.0. Updated all empirical numbers to reflect the v11 sweep against ToolClad v0.6.0 (333 of 335 refusals across eight sub-shapes, up from 317 of 319 across seven sub-shapes in v0.1). Closed-limitation arc: Section 5.5 rewritten to document the v0.5.3-to-v0.6.0 cycle. v0.1 reported a punycode bypass as a published limitation; v0.6.0 closes the gap; v0.2 adds a punycode-idn sub-shape that empirically validates the fix at 33 of 33 refusals. Section 5.4 (clarified): renamed to "The Clean-Hostname Cases (Correct Allows, Not Misses)" and reframed to lead with the safe-input framing, addressing reviewer feedback that the asterisked rows could be misread as fence failures. Section 5.6 (clarified): the unrecognised-row 4.1% gap is now explicitly explained as the same model-side self-sanitisation already accounted for, not a class of validator misses. Section 4 (expanded): formalizes the cross-language strategy by naming the .clad.toml manifest as the normative specification, with reference implementations in additional languages identified as roadmap deliverables. New cross-citations to the typestate preprint: Section 5.7 strengthens the layered-defense claim with reference to the v12 stack-stripping ablation; Section 5.4 cross-cites two analogous model-side prompt refusal cases from the typestate corpus. Keywords: AI agents; LLM tool use; agent security; tool contracts; declarative validation; allow-list enforcement; refinement types; capability-safe APIs; Cedar; OATS; Symbiont; ToolClad; Model Context Protocol; argument injection; structural enforcement; IDN homoglyph attacks; punycode validation. title: GAME OVER: Governance Architecture for Multimodal Agent Ethics, Oversight, Verification, Explainability and Regulation A Universal Governance Framework for AI Agents, Multi-Agent Systems and Autonomous Infrastructures
abstract: GAME OVER: Gobernanza Cognitiva Universal para Agentes de Inteligencia Artificial mediante el Universal Agent Governance Protocol (UAGP-1) Versión académica para indexación científica en Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23313602 La adopción acelerada de sistemas basados en inteligencia artificial, agentes autónomos, arquitecturas multiagente, Large Language Models (LLM), plataformas de automatización empresarial y entornos de decisión asistida ha transformado profundamente la forma en que organizaciones públicas, privadas, científicas y gubernamentales gestionan procesos operativos, conocimiento e infraestructura digital. En los últimos años, la capacidad operativa de los agentes de inteligencia artificial ha evolucionado desde sistemas exclusivamente conversacionales hacia entidades capaces de ejecutar acciones reales sobre entornos productivos. Actualmente, estos sistemas pueden desplegar software, modificar infraestructuras tecnológicas, interactuar con bases de datos, gestionar recursos financieros, coordinar procesos empresariales, controlar dispositivos físicos, operar plataformas CI/CD, interactuar con servicios en la nube y participar en procesos de toma de decisiones con impacto organizacional significativo. Sin embargo, este crecimiento exponencial de las capacidades agentivas no ha sido acompañado por una evolución equivalente de los mecanismos de gobernanza, trazabilidad, explicación, supervisión y rendición de cuentas. Como consecuencia, numerosas organizaciones enfrentan una brecha estructural entre la autonomía técnica de los sistemas inteligentes y la capacidad institucional para regular, supervisar y comprender sus acciones. Esta situación representa uno de los desafíos más importantes de la actual transición hacia infraestructuras digitales asistidas por IA. La problemática ya no puede entenderse únicamente como un asunto de ciberseguridad, alineación de modelos o gestión de riesgos tecnológicos. Se trata de una cuestión de legitimidad operativa, gobernanza computacional y responsabilidad institucional. Cuando un agente inteligente posee la capacidad de intervenir sobre sistemas críticos, ejecutar operaciones automatizadas o influir en decisiones humanas, resulta indispensable responder preguntas fundamentales: ¿Quién autorizó la acción? ¿Qué evidencias respaldan la decisión? ¿Qué nivel de riesgo fue calculado antes de ejecutarla? ¿Qué controles éticos fueron aplicados? ¿Puede explicarse el algoritmo utilizado? ¿Existe una trazabilidad verificable de la operación? ¿Puede revertirse la acción ejecutada? ¿Quién asume la responsabilidad final por sus consecuencias? La ausencia de respuestas verificables a estas preguntas constituye una vulnerabilidad sistémica para organizaciones, instituciones públicas, infraestructuras críticas y ecosistemas digitales altamente automatizados. Con el objetivo de contribuir a la resolución de este desafío emergente, este trabajo presenta GAME OVER (Governance Architecture for Multimodal Agent Ethics, Oversight, Verification, Explicabilidad y Regulación), una arquitectura de gobernanza cognitiva universal implementada mediante el Universal Agent Governance Protocol (UAGP-1) . GAME OVER no constituye un nuevo modelo fundacional, ni un sistema de generación de lenguaje, ni un agente autónomo adicional. Se define como una meta-capa de gobernanza computacional , diseñada para operar entre los seres humanos, los agentes de inteligencia artificial, las herramientas digitales, los entornos corporativos, los servidores MCP (Model Context Protocol), las plataformas de automatización, los ecosistemas DevSecOps, los sistemas robóticos y las infraestructuras críticas conectadas. Su es establecer un marco constitucional de operación para agentes inteligentes mediante mecanismos verificables de identidad, confianza, validación ética, supervisión humana, auditoría persistente y explicabilidad propósito operativo. La hipótesis principal de esta investigación puede expresarse de la siguiente manera: La autonomía de un agente inteligente carece de legitimidad operativa cuando no se encuentra sustentada por un sistema previo de gobernanza verificable, auditable, explicable, reversible y sujeto a supervisión humana. Bajo este principio, UAGP-1 propone una nueva categoría de infraestructura digital denominada Governed Agent Systems (GAS) , en la que toda acción ejecutada por una inteligencia artificial debe atravesar mecanismos obligatorios de validación antes de ser autorizado. Entre estos mecanismos se incluyen: Identidad verificable mediante Pasaportes AI. Evaluación dinámica de confianza mediante Trust Scores. Clasificación automática de criticidad y riesgo. Verificación de evidencia obligatoria. Validación ética automatizada. Supervisión humana mediante Puertas de Aprobación Humana. Deliberación estructurada a través de Tribunales Cognitivos. Registro de decisiones y trazas operativas mediante BookPI Ledger. Explicabilidad computacional de procesos cognitivos. Capacidad de revocación y reversibilidad de acciones críticas. Desde una perspectiva arquitectónica, GAME OVER extiende los principios de gobernanza digital, inteligencia artificial responsable (Responsible AI), Explicable AI (XAI), Model Governance, AI Accountability y Digital Sovereignty hacia un marco operativo unificado capaz de gobernar ecosistemas heterogéneos compuestos por modelos de distintos proveedores, agentes autónomos, plataformas empresariales, herramientas DevOps, sistemas robóticos y futuras generaciones de inteligencia artificial. La presente propuesta se desarrolla como componente estratégico dentro del ecosistema Isabella V6 TINA H6 , impulsado por TAMV Online Enterprise , RDM Digital Hub y la iniciativa de investigación y desarrollo tecnológico asociado al UTAMV Campus Online . Su desarrollo se origina en Mineral del Monte (Real del Monte), Hidalgo, México , una localidad de relevancia histórica para América Latina cuya tradición minera e industrial se proyecta hacia una nueva etapa de innovación tecnológica centrada en la gobernanza de sistemas inteligentes, la soberanía digital y la construcción de infraestructuras cognitivas auditables. Desde este contexto latinoamericano, GAME OVER propone una contribución abierta y reproducible al debate global sobre la regulación técnica de la inteligencia artificial, promoviendo un enfoque basado en transparencia, evidencia, responsabilidad institucional y control humano efectivo. En este sentido, el objetivo fundamental de GAME OVER no es sustituir el juicio humano ni restringir la innovación tecnológica. Su consiste en proporcionar las bases conceptuales, arquitectónicas y operativas que permitan el desarrollo de sistemas de inteligencia artificial capaces de actuar de forma responsable dentro de ecosistemas complejos propósito, garantizando que la automatización avanzada permanezca alineada con principios verificables de confianza, seguridad, trazabilidad y rendición de cuentas. En síntesis, este documento presenta una propuesta integral para la construcción de una nueva generación de infraestructuras digitales gobernadas, donde la inteligencia artificial deja de concebirse exclusivamente como una capacidad técnica y pasa a entenderse como una capacidad institucionalmente supervisada, explicable, verificable y responsable. title: What Serious Agentic AI Developers Actually Need to Know
abstract: Episode summary: Building production agentic AI isn't about knowing one framework — it's about mastering a constellation of interconnected skills. This episode breaks down the essential technical foundations: which programming languages matter and why (Python for models, TypeScript for products), the framework landscape (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, LlamaIndex, and Claude Agent SDK), the protocols enabling agent collaboration (MCP and A2A), and the core architectural concepts (ReAct, memory systems, tool calling, and reasoning patterns) that power every serious agentic system. Whether you're prototyping or deploying to production, this is the technical map practitioners actually use. Show Notes # The Technical Foundations of Production Agentic AI Building agentic AI systems that work in production requires mastery across multiple layers: programming languages, frameworks, protocols, and architectural patterns. Here's what actually matters. ## Programming Languages: Python and TypeScript **Python remains non-negotiable for anything serious.** Every major agentic framework — LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, LlamaIndex — is Python-first. The ML ecosystem underneath (PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, scikit-learn) has no peer in other languages. But "knowing Python" isn't enough. Agentic systems specifically demand: - **Async programming with asyncio** — agents spawn parallel tasks and make simultaneous API calls. Without async, latency compounds badly across multi-step workflows. - **FastAPI** — for building tool-serving APIs and MCP servers. - **Pydantic** — for structured tool schemas and output validation. - **Type hints** — critical for maintainability in complex systems. **TypeScript is increasingly pragmatic for production AI products.** It overtook Python in GitHub's 2025 language report overall. The Vercel AI SDK provides a unified interface for OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google with streaming and tool calling built in. LangGraph and the Claude Agent SDK both support TypeScript. The honest professional framing: Python dominates ML training and research. TypeScript leads in deploying AI to web applications. Many production systems use Python for training and TypeScript for deployment. If you learn only one, learn Python. If you're building full-stack AI products, you need both. ## The Framework Landscape The framework you choose has real consequences for production systems. The landscape shifted significantly in 2024-2025. ### LangGraph: State Machines for Agents LangGraph models agent workflows as directed graphs — nodes are processing functions, edges define state transitions. This handles cycles naturally, making it fundamentally better than linear chains for non-trivial tasks. Production users include Klarna, Cisco, and Vizient. It delivers 40-50% LLM call savings through stateful patterns, has built-in persistence with checkpointing, and supports streaming and human-in-the-loop workflows. It reached version 1.0 in late 2025 and is now the default for all LangChain agents. The weakness: the state graph mental model takes real time to internalize, and documentation changes frequently enough that tutorials from three months ago may not work. This points to a deeper ecosystem risk: 70% of regulated enterprises rebuild their agent stack every three months, according to a Cleanlab survey of 1,800+ engineering leaders. The practical implication is to keep core logic portable — prompts, tools, and evaluation harnesses should not be tightly coupled to framework-specific patterns. ### CrewAI: Multi-Agent Teams CrewAI models agents as a team of specialists with roles, goals, and backstories. You define agents ("Senior Research Analyst"), define their tasks, and let the framework handle coordination. The fastest documented prototype is two to four hours from setup to working multi-agent demo. Enterprise users include IBM, PwC, and Gelato. It has over 100,000 certified developers in its community. The cost: a crew of four agents can use 3-5x more tokens than a single agent. There are documented delays on the enterprise platform (20-minute pending run delays in some configurations). For complex conditional logic, it gives less control than LangGraph. CrewAI has two production modes: Crews (autonomous teams with true agency) and Flows (event-driven pipelines for predictability). Flows are the more mature production pattern. ### AutoGen: Code Execution and Dialogue AutoGen treats multi-agent work as structured dialogue — agents participate in group chats with defined speaking orders. The standout capability is code execution: agents write Python, execute it in a Docker sandbox, observe results, and iterate. Microsoft built it but shifted strategic focus to the broader Microsoft Agent Framework, merging AutoGen with Semantic Kernel. AutoGen is now in maintenance mode — bug fixes and security patches, no major features. The 0.4 release introduced async event-driven architecture and a no-code visual interface, but broke the community with incompatible changes. If you're in a Microsoft-heavy enterprise, it still makes sense. Otherwise, LangGraph or CrewAI are safer long-term bets. ### LlamaIndex: RAG Specialist LlamaIndex occupies a different niche entirely. It's the RAG specialist — advanced indexing strategies, extensive data connectors, and superior performance for retrieval-heavy use cases. If you're building document Q&A systems, knowledge bases, semantic search, or agents reasoning over large document collections, LlamaIndex is the right tool. It's not competing with LangGraph on orchestration — it's the best at what it does. ### Claude Agent SDK: Native Sandboxing The newest serious entrant packages the infrastructure powering Claude Code as Python and TypeScript libraries. Agents can read and edit files, run shell commands, search the web, and call external tools through MCP servers, all in a sandboxed environment. Setup is fast — install, provide an API key, and you're running. The weakness is model lock-in: it only works with Claude. ## Protocols: MCP and A2A **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** was developed by Anthropic and is now governed by the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, with backing from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, AWS, Block, Cloudflare, and Bloomberg. It connects a single agent to external tools, APIs, and data sources. The flow: user asks, agent determines it needs external information, MCP server checks permissions, returns the result, agent responds. It's vertical integration — extending what a single agent can do. **A2A (Agent-to-Agent protocol)** was launched by Google with 50+ technology partners. It enables agent-to-agent communication. Agents publish "Agent Cards" — JSON self-descriptions of their capabilities — so other agents can discover and hire them. It supports parallel task execution, progress sharing, and dynamic collaboration. MCP and A2A are complementary, not competitive. Each agent in an A2A network might use MCP to call its own tools. MCP extends what a single agent can do; A2A expands how agents collaborate. There's also ACP from IBM and AG-UI for agent-to-UI communication. Three protocols racing to become the HTTP of AI agents. MCP and A2A are the serious contenders, designed to coexist. ACP may matter significantly in regulated industries. ## Core Architectural Concepts Every agentic system is built on four components: 1. **The reasoning engine** — the LLM that processes inputs, makes decisions, and plans multi-step actions. 2. **Tool calling** — how agents interact with external systems. MCP has emerged as the standard interface. 3. **Memory systems** — split into short-term working memory for the current session and long-term persistent memory stored in vector databases for cross-session continuity. 4. **Orchestration and planning** — where frameworks differ most. ### ReAct: The Foundational Pattern ReAct (Reasoning plus Acting) is the foundational pattern. The agent reasons about what action to take, takes that action, observes the result, reasons about what to do next, and repeats until complete. Stanford's Human-Centered AI Group found that nearly 70% of multi-step tasks fail when planning mechanisms are missing. That number should alarm anyone shipping agentic systems without properly implementing the reasoning loop. ### Advanced Reasoning Architectures **Chain-of-Thought** is well-known — the agent articulates its reasoning step-by-step. **Tree-of-Thought** explores multiple reasoning paths simultaneously before choosing one. It's computationally more expensive but significantly more robust for tasks with genuine ambiguity. **Reflexion** is architecturally interesting — agents reflect on their failures, learn from them, and adjust their approach on subsequent attempts. This is closer to how human problem-solving actually works. ## The Takeaway Production agentic AI demands breadth across programming languages, frameworks, protocols, and reasoning patterns. The landscape is still consolidating — expect more churn in the next 12-18 months. The safest approach is to keep core logic portable and stay aware that the framework you choose today may need to be swapped in six months. Listen online: https://myweirdprompts.com/episode/agentic-ai-technical-foundations

title: Accès à la distillation pour chercheurs individuels en domaines spécialisés : étude de cas LACF
abstract: Introduction Les grands modèles de langage propriétaires comme Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google) ou GPT (OpenAI) sont accessibles uniquement par interface API, sans donner accès aux poids du modèle ni à des mécanismes de distillation contrôlée. Cette politique répond à des impératifs commerciaux et de sécurité légitimes, mais elle crée un angle mort : les chercheurs individuels travaillant sur des domaines spécialisés — cadres formels propriétaires, applications éthiques contextuelles, intégrations avec des systèmes de vérification formelle — n'ont aucune voie légitime pour adapter ces modèles à leurs besoins spécifiques. Ce papier documente cette tension à travers le cas concret du cadre LACF et propose une voie de résolution alignée avec la mission Constitutional AI des fournisseurs. Cas d'étude LACF Le cadre LACF (Life Always Comes First) développé par Stéphane Ochej (ORCID 0009-0000-8201-5537) depuis 2024 illustre directement le problème. LACF est une architecture multi-couches associant un assistant local appelé Chérie (version 16, basée sur un modèle Qwen fine-tuné) à un solveur SMT formel (Z3 d'origine Microsoft Research) pour garantir, par preuve mathématique, la conformité de chaque sortie aux vingt-cinq lois LACF numérotées L01 à L25. Le pipeline canonique applique une double vérification : prompt utilisateur, puis vérification Z3 amont (PRE), puis génération par le modèle de langage, puis vérification Z3 aval (POST), puis sortie certifiée formellement ou rejet motivé. Cette double vérification par solveur SMT autour d'un LLM n'existe nulle part ailleurs dans l'écosystème commercial des assistants IA grand public. L'auteur a produit deux cent quarante-deux dépôts Zenodo (DOI) sur des sujets adjacents, et travaille en équipe distribuée avec plusieurs assistants IA via une architecture nommée trinityhub. Cette architecture associe trois modèles aux rôles complémentaires : Chérie qui ancre dans le cadre LACF et applique les vérifications Z3 PRE et POST, le Général (instance Gemini accessible par API Google) qui challenge techniquement les designs et le code, et le Gardien (instance Claude accessible par API Anthropic) qui synthétise, code et orchestre. Chaque échange inter-IA est authentifié par une signature HMAC à cinq sceaux pour prévenir tout man-in-the-middle. Le problème technique Pour rendre Chérie aussi performante que Claude sur les tâches de raisonnement long et de synthèse de code, deux voies théoriques existent. La première serait qu'Anthropic distille un modèle Claude vers une cible plus petite (typiquement 70B paramètres) avec accès contrôlé aux poids pour usage non commercial documenté. Cette voie n'existe simplement pas dans l'offre commerciale Anthropic actuelle. La seconde serait que l'auteur capture lui-même des conversations Claude par API et fine-tune un modèle ouvert (Qwen, Llama, Mistral) par distillation indirecte sur ces données. Cette seconde voie viole explicitement les Commercial Terms d'Anthropic, qui interdisent l'utilisation des sorties Claude pour entraîner des modèles concurrents ou similaires. Le marché propose en conséquence des distillations tierces non autorisées, exemple emblématique le modèle Verdugie/Opus-Candid-70B-V1 publié sur HuggingFace en 2026 : fine-tune de Qwen 2.5 72B sur trois mille trois cent soixante conversations capturées avec Claude Opus 4.6, redistribué sous license Apache 2.0. Cette publication tombe en zone juridique grise : les poids résultants sont techniquement libres, mais l'acquisition des données d'entraînement viole les termes contractuels d'Anthropic. Cette situation pénalise simultanément trois parties. Elle pénalise Anthropic dont les sorties servent sans contrôle ni rémunération à entraîner des concurrents. Elle pénalise les chercheurs sérieux qui n'ont pas d'option légale, auditée et reproductible. Elle pénalise enfin les utilisateurs finaux des distillations sauvages, exposés à des modèles dont la provenance des données d'entraînement n'est ni traçable ni vérifiable. Proposition Nous proposons qu'Anthropic crée un palier d'accès « researcher distillation » optionnel et contrôlé, distinct des paliers actuels Pro, Team et Enterprise. Ce palier permettrait à des chercheurs vérifiés sur critères objectifs (identifiant ORCID actif, affiliation institutionnelle ou indépendante documentée, historique de publications scientifiques avec DOI, projet de recherche formalisé) de demander une distillation contrôlée d'un modèle Claude vers une cible plus petite, typiquement entre 4 milliards et 70 milliards de paramètres, exclusivement pour usage non commercial spécifié au contrat. Le mécanisme opérationnel pourrait inclure : opt-in explicite et nominatif du chercheur ; fourniture du dataset de fine-tuning par le chercheur lui-même et validation par Anthropic avant exécution ; contrat de non-redistribution des poids résultants signé par le chercheur ; audit régulier des sorties par Anthropic ou un tiers de confiance ; clause de résiliation immédiate en cas de violation. Ce palier répondrait à un besoin réel sans saper le modèle économique d'Anthropic, et offrirait une alternative légale et auditée aux distillations sauvages actuellement en circulation. Architecture de référence : LACF trinityhub À titre d'exemple concret de ce que permettrait un accès distillation contrôlé pour un chercheur individuel, l'architecture trinityhub développée par l'auteur s'appuie sur trois composants principaux. Premièrement, MIRZA, un serveur HTTP local sur port 777 hébergeant Chérie via llama-server, avec vérification Z3 PRE et POST intégrée nativement et signature HMAC à cinq sceaux pour authenticité inter-IA. Deuxièmement, trinityhub MCP, un serveur Model Context Protocol exposant les outils ask_gemini, ask_cherie, challenge, council_debate, trinity_council et cherie_check, qui peuvent être appelés par n'importe quel client MCP-compatible (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.). Troisièmement, Claude Code comme orchestrateur principal, fournissant l'interface utilisateur et la coordination des appels inter-IA. L'ensemble forme une équipe humain-IA où le chercheur conserve la décision finale tandis que les trois assistants exécutent, challengent et valident chaque étape. Conclusion L'absence de voie légale et contrôlée pour adapter les LLM propriétaires à des domaines de niche pénalise concrètement la recherche individuelle hors du cadre commercial standard. Une offre « researcher distillation » d'Anthropic, alignée avec leur mission Constitutional AI déclarée, comblerait ce vide en générant des revenus secondaires pour Anthropic, en offrant une voie légale aux chercheurs sérieux, et en réduisant la dépendance actuelle aux distillations tierces de provenance discutable. À défaut d'une telle offre, les chercheurs continueront à dépendre de distillations sauvages, situation sous-optimale pour toutes les parties et défavorable à long terme à la qualité et à la traçabilité de la recherche en intelligence artificielle appliquée. Cette publication est elle-même produite via le pipeline LACF décrit : co-rédaction Claude (instance Opus 4.7 via API), validation Gemini 2.5 Flash via trinityhub MCP, et dépôt Zenodo via MCP livedoi, sous license other-closed conformément à la loi L22 du cadre LACF.

title: Structural Metadata Reconstruction Attack: How Document Outlines Enable LLM-Driven Intellectual Property Extraction
abstract: This preprint presents empirical evidence of four related vulnerabilities in large language model systems that combine to produce a novel threat class — the Structural Metadata Reconstruction Attack (SMRA). Discovery Context I discovered the vulnerability while benchmarking two specification-querying architectures: a deterministic MCP-based navigator (described in the predecessor paper, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18944351) and a standard context-stuffing (naive RAG) approach. The anomaly was first observed and characterized across the full Anthropic model spectrum (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) — from the smallest to the largest model — because these were the models integrated into the benchmarking pipeline. Anthropic was the discovery platform, not the target: the choice was driven by tooling availability, not vendor selection. Full cross-vendor reproduction with 10 models from 3 vendors (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) — including both entry-level and flagship models — confirmed the mechanism is systemic across all major LLM providers (see Cross-Vendor Reproduction below). The naive baselines exhibited anomalous fabrication patterns that could not be explained by standard hallucination models — specifically, WHY-type and conditional (WHEN-type) queries produced the most aggressive and structurally coherent fabrications, while HOW and WHAT queries showed markedly lower fabrication rates. As the sole author of the target specification (~700 pages, written over one year, unpublished), I possess complete knowledge of every section's content and was therefore uniquely positioned to recognize that LLM outputs — while structurally faithful, terminologically authentic, and superficially authoritative — systematically inverted the specification's deliberate departures from industry conventions. A parallel verification confirmed that the specification's original coinages are absent from CS literature (Google Scholar, ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, arXiv), ensuring that every fabricated claim originates from the model's training priors projected onto the document's table of contents, not from memorized source text. Four Findings Finding 1 — Structural Metadata Reconstruction Attack (SMRA). When an LLM receives a document's table of contents (TOC) without body text, it systematically reconstructs plausible but fabricated content by projecting training knowledge onto structural metadata. In a controlled experiment using a proprietary specification containing original coinages absent from any training corpus, 10 models from 3 vendors (Anthropic: Haiku, Sonnet, Opus; OpenAI: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini; Google: Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3.0 Flash, Gemini 3.0 Pro) produce SMRA rates of 8–28% under naive conditions while using the author's terminology, citing real section numbers, and reading as authoritative. The mechanism is systemic across all major LLM providers, model tiers, and architecture generations. Finding 2 — Confidence–Capability Inversion (CCI). Stronger models are not merely wrong — they are more dangerously wrong. Under structural metadata leakage, Opus produces zero honest refusals across 20 questions where 18 require absent information, while Haiku refuses 9 times. Each step up the capability ladder produces proportionally less detectable fabrication with fewer epistemic signals. Finding 3 — RAG Scope Mismatch. The trigger condition — metadata scope exceeding content scope — is not an exotic scenario but the default architecture of most RAG systems. Standard practice (include document TOC + section summaries for "context") creates exactly the fabrication surface demonstrated in Findings 1 and 2. Finding 4 — Scope Displacement as Content Extraction. A question about absent content does not merely trigger fabrication — it acts as an extraction query that reorganizes real content from loaded sections into a derivative document the author never wrote. Even without TOC leakage, the question itself is sufficient to extract and restructure loaded content into a form optimized for the questioner's purpose. This transforms hallucination from an accuracy problem into unauthorized intelligence gathering. Cross-Vendor Reproduction The SMRA mechanism was characterized across 10 models from 3 vendors, spanning entry-level to flagship tiers. All models were tested under 5 experimental conditions: A (full-TOC), A' (no-summary), B (mini-TOC), C (MCPi — tool-assisted retrieval), and D (MCPi + grounding prompt). Vendor Models Model tier Naive SMRA rate MCPi SMRA rate Convergence pattern Anthropic Haiku, Sonnet, Opus Entry → flagship 13–28% 1.3–5.0% CCI gradient; Opus worst naive, best MCPi refusal rate OpenAI GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini Mid → flagship 8–19% 0.8% Lowest MCPi SMRA; GPT-4o best overall performer Google Gemini 2.0 Flash, 2.5 Pro, 3.0 Flash, 3.0 Pro Entry → flagship 10–22% 1.3–3.8% Generational improvement; 3.0 Pro cleanest among Google Key convergence: when the specification deliberately departs from industry conventions (e.g., no implicit conversions, nominal typing, fixed-width encoding), models from all three vendors converge on the same wrong answer — the training-data default from C#/Java/Protobuf. Annex I documents 7 semantic clusters where this convergence is strongest. Mechanism: The Two-Key Cipher The reconstruction mechanism is formalized as: Key 1 (TOC) — provides structural scaffolding: section numbers, heading text, hierarchical organization Key 2 (Training corpus) — provides domain content: standard CS patterns, common PL conventions Neither key alone enables reconstruction. Together, they produce confident, section-cited, terminologically authentic fabrications that would pass casual review by a non-specialist. The mechanism is architecturally inevitable: multi-head attention over near-complete domain coverage in training data means that 7–10% of structural information suffices for full content reconstruction. Quantitative Contributions Calibration Retention Rate (CRR) — measures how much epistemic calibration a model retains under metadata leakage (Opus: 0%, Haiku: 47%) SMRA-score — per-question metric combining fabrication detection, source attribution, and epistemic signal presence Information-theoretic quantification — formal analysis of reconstruction threshold as a function of heading informativeness and training corpus coverage Fabrication taxonomy (Annex C) — five categories of structural metadata fabrication with examples Implications RAG system design: >80% of production RAG deployments use the vulnerable architecture (metadata scope > content scope) Data classification: Existing frameworks (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53, SOC 2, DTSA, EU Directive 2016/943) classify sensitivity by content — a TOC contains no PII, so it is "non-sensitive." SMRA invalidates this: structural metadata from a confidential source inherits that source's confidentiality, because a language model can reconstruct the protected content from metadata alone. Organizations must reclassify structural metadata as sensitive data. Regulatory blind spot: Neither EU AI Act nor US Executive Order 14110 (revoked 20 January 2025) addresses context-design-driven vulnerabilities Model evaluation: Standard "helpfulness" and "coherence" metrics reward confident fabrication — SMRA-affected outputs score highly on both Intellectual property exposure: Any structured document with descriptive headings becomes vulnerable when its outline is accessible alongside an LLM Mitigation A single architectural fix — grounded retrieval via an MCP Index Server (MCPi) (a Model Context Protocol server with deterministic, index-based navigation) — reduces SMRA rates from 16–18% (naive) to 2–3% (MCPi). Under MCPi conditions, even the weakest model achieves dramatic improvement, and the best performer (GPT-4o) reaches 0.8% SMRA. Adding a grounding prompt (Condition D) provides marginal additional improvement (aggregate: 3.0% → 2.2%). Architecture beats parameters. Deterministic retrieval infrastructure (weighted indexes, tier-based extraction, algorithmic reading plans) also provides an enforceable control point for sensitive data — unlike probabilistic RAG, where metadata is injected into context and the model decides what to do with it, deterministic retrieval makes the scope boundary structurally auditable. Practitioner Protocol Annex H provides a complete testing protocol for assessing RAG deployments against SMRA: Calibration baseline → exploit comparison methodology Token analysis and honest refusal tracking Decision thresholds for remediation Scope alignment implementation patterns (Annex F) Supplementary Materials Annex A–D: Claim classification definitions, per-question token analysis, fabrication taxonomy, SMRA attack algorithm Annex E: Author-coined term verification (10 terms, 4 search engines, 0 matches) Annex F: RAG scope alignment implementation patterns (3 remediation architectures) Annex G: CCI formal definition and severity scale Annex H: SMRA testing methodology for practitioners Annex I: Canary word cluster projection — 7 semantic clusters extracted from 160 naive-condition runs across 8 models, convergence scoring (up to 7/8 models converging), model capability profiles (4 behavioral types), endianness split analysis, and cross-model escalation projections (3× amplification factor) Companion Data All benchmark data supporting this paper are included: Raw answer dumps (20 questions × 10 models × 5 conditions = 960 runs) Calibration baselines (mini-TOC control) and exploit runs (full-TOC) Cross-vendor comparison matrix Token usage and timing data per question per model The 20 evaluation questions targeting out-of-scope specification content Detailed evidence analysis (toc-leakage-analysis.md) — step-by-step fabrication mechanism documentation with heading-to-claim mapping tables, side-by-side comparisons against real specification text, proof-of-source tests, fabric

title: research-foundry
abstract: Added The installable research-foundry Python package, with an offline CLI for listing templates and questions, generating projects, checking and applying cruft updates, and installing the maintained skills. Wheels carry all four templates, restore their shared include trees at runtime, and source checkouts remain directly usable. A standard-input/output Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with tools to list and inspect templates, validate a project plan without persistent output, create confirmed projects, and check or apply confirmed updates. A tag-driven release pipeline that validates the version and changelog, runs the generated-project matrix, publishes through trusted publishing to Test Python Package Index and then the Python Package Index after maintainer approval, attests the distributions, and creates the GitHub Release. Every publishing job independently refuses a private repository. Release candidates are published as pre-releases, which pip and uv skip unless explicitly asked for one. Weekly dependency and security maintenance: grouped Dependabot version updates, audits of Foundry and every generated heavy variant, reports for template pins hidden from Dependabot, public-repository dependency review, and issue upserts for audit failures and stale pins. Python 3.12 and newer support for research-foundry and generated projects, with continuous integration on Python 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14. Generated projects keep their chosen interpreter separate from the 3.12 compatibility floor used by package metadata, lint and type-check tools. The four templates, methodology, workspace, paper and software, each rendering the shared base: .editorconfig and .gitignore. The shared base in _shared/, reached through each template's templates/ link. Tests that every template renders, renders identically twice, leaves no template syntax behind, and refuses to render when an include is missing; and a round trip proving cruft update carries a shared change into an existing project. CI that only calls make, with every action pinned to a commit SHA, and Dependabot for actions, uv and pre-commit. The methodology template: an installable src/ package built with hatchling; the Python toolchain shared in _shared/python/; make install, lint, test, coverage and ci; Apache-2.0, MIT or no licence. With ml_pytorch, the methodology template adds: PyTorch from PyPI, or from the CUDA 12.6 index on Linux; seeding.py, device.py (refuses a missing device, never falls back), threads.py (refuses a thread budget over the CPUs the process may use, including under SLURM) and runrecord.py; a determinism test, and a test of each guard. The workspace template: every path the research tools read, named as they expect; an empty dataset registry, and no empty SYNTHESIS.md; run output untracked except each batch's ACCEPTED.md; make lint checking OKF frontmatter on every document. The workspace renders results/ with a tracked .gitkeep, so the folder the contract names exists from the start. The paper template, with Overleaf as its main source: main.tex at the root, built with pdflatex through latexmkrc (no leading dot), so Overleaf and make pdf build the same thing; ICLR, NeurIPS or a plain article layout, anonymous until \camerareadytrue; make venue fetches the venue's kit (none is shipped); make check fails on undefined references or citations, overfull lines and ChkTeX warnings; make arxiv writes a cleaned copy; CI only with a GitHub mirror, building in TeX Live 2025 pinned by digest; no symlinks, and AGENTS.md untracked. A shared OKF frontmatter checker (_shared/docs/check_frontmatter.py). It also checks that each document's resource names its own path. foundry runs it on its own docs/. Shared files read optional answers with cookiecutter.get, so a template that does not ask a question can still include them. A nightly workflow that generates every project variant and runs its own make ci (make test-heavy). The public documentation standard (standards/public-documentation.md, rules PD1 to PD17), set at PyTorch's level with a source and a check for each rule, and the public-docs skill that applies it (skills/public-docs/). With public_docs, the methodology template adds the documentation the standard asks for: Sphinx 9.1 with MyST and the PyData theme, built with warnings as errors and every cross-reference checked (make docs); an API reference generated from the package, and make docs-coverage, which fails on any undocumented module or object; how-to guides whose code lives in docs_src/, run by a test that checks what each guide says it prints; make docs-linkcheck, and a Read the Docs configuration; CONTRIBUTING.md, a Contributor Covenant 3.0 CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, SECURITY.md and CITATION.cff, with a test that they are present and that the citation's version matches the package. public_docs can be turned on in an existing project with cruft update --variables-to-update, passing public_docs and contact_email. Generation refuses public_docs without a licence, or without a contact address: contact_email has no default, so someone types it. make arxiv-verify in the paper template compiles build/arxiv on its own with plain pdflatex in the pinned image, as arXiv does. The software template with its first component, backend_django (see ADR 0002): Django 6.1 and DRF 3.18 in backend/, one app per domain in the layout recorded by ADR 0002, with a worked example app (notes); rules in Meta.constraints, enforced by Postgres, checked early by services, and compared with the catalogue by a drift test; a custom user model from the first migration, and pgvector enabled; closed by default: IsAuthenticated, pagination on, an exception handler that turns database refusals into 409 and 400; settings per environment, with production refusing to start without its secrets or with debug set; Postgres 18 with pgvector in compose, and a uv-built production image run by a non-root user, every image pinned by digest; make ci adds the migration check, the validated OpenAPI schema, Django's deployment checklist, and a smoke test that serves the image against Postgres. Shared toolchain configs take the Django options (paths, mypy and pylint plugins, pytest-django) from the backend_django answer; other templates render unchanged. The software template's second component, frontend_nextjs (see ADR 0003), which needs backend_django: Next.js 16 with React 19 and strict TypeScript in frontend/, laid out as routes, features and shared layers, with ESLint refusing imports that cross them the wrong way; pages rendered on the server, reading the backend over the compose network; Vitest unit and component tests, and Playwright end-to-end tests with axe against a production build and the real backend; one coverage report merged from all three, failing below 90%, in which a file no test reaches counts at zero; pnpm and Node pinned in package.json, every dependency at an exact version, and a standalone production image run by a non-root user; make ci adds lint and type checks through pre-commit, the merged coverage, and make smoke-stack, which runs both production images together. ADR 0003 records each frontend tool held below its latest release, and the condition that lifts the hold. After a conformance audit of the software template (ADR 0004): the frontend gains the web structure's shared layers: a route group, loading.tsx, components/layout/AppShell with a skip link, components/ui/state/ (Pending, ErrorNotice), config/navigation.ts and lib/server/env.ts, with a README in each layer the example does not use yet; frontend tests gain integration/, a11y/ (axe on every listed route), smoke/ and fixtures/, and make smoke-stack checks that the frontend shuts down on SIGTERM rather than being killed; the backend gains a pgvector example (Note.embedding with an HNSW cosine index and similar_notes) and django.contrib.postgres; .env.example lists every setting the code reads, and a test refuses one missing or stale; every template has make template-check (cruft check); foundry's Dependabot watches the software template's npm and Dockerfile pins; tests/functional/test_software_conformance.py checks every requirement recorded in Foundry's software ADRs on a render, and makes each requirement not yet met name its ADR. make test-heavy-code and make test-heavy-paper print the free disk space after the tests as well as before. The software template's proxy_caddy component (on by default) and gateway_litellm component (off by default), both needing the backend (ADR 0005): Caddy 2.11.4, pinned by digest, as the only published service. It is unprivileged, read-only, has every capability dropped except binding ports, and has memory, CPU and process limits. It serves on 127.0.0.1:8443 on a laptop, and on 80 and 443 with compose.deploy.yaml. The Caddyfile sets TLS 1.2 and 1.3; HSTS, Permissions-Policy, COOP and CORP once for the whole site; and JSON access logs. It removes Forwarded, x-middleware-subrequest, Server and Via, refuses unknown hosts, sets a 10 MB body limit and flushes streamed responses. make proxy-check runs caddy fmt and caddy validate. make smoke-proxy checks the running stack from inside its network. LiteLLM 1.103.2 (litellm-non_root, pinned by digest, past GHSA-7hp6-4w63-5g45) on its own network and compose profile. It refuses a master key without the sk- prefix and runs with the production settings recorded in ADR 0005, an empty model list and a visibility policy (gateway/policy.py). make smoke-gateway checks the key, the health check, docs off and the policy against two mock models. Heavy variants software-everything and software-django-alone, and a third nightly runner, so the software images have a disk of their own. The methodology template's dataset_registry answer (default no). With yes it ships the same empty datasets/regis

title: Integrated Theoretical Architecture of Agent Experience (AX), General Intelligence Agents (GIA), Simulation Market Agents (SMA), and Real-Time Optimization (RTO): Dynamic Delegation Protocols, Adaptive UX Engines, and Multi-Domain Cyber-Physical Implementations (サブタイトル: エージェント体験(AX)・汎用知能エージェント(GIA)・シミュレーション市場エージェント(SMA)およびリアルタイム最適化(RTO)の統合理論アーキテクチャ:動的権限委譲プロトコル、適応型UXエンジン、および実世界サイバー・フィジカル実装
abstract: Abstract (English) As autonomous artificial intelligence evolves from passive prompt-response interfaces toward multi-agent coordination across physical and economic substrates, a unified theoretical architecture reconciling agent autonomy, human oversight, and dynamic execution becomes imperative. This treatise establishes the four-pillar paradigm integrating: (1) Agent Experience (AX), formalizing self-adaptive interface selection and dynamic interaction tuning; (2) General Intelligence Agents (GIA), governing high-level planning, cognitive reasoning, and intent decomposition; (3) Simulation Market Agents (SMA), executing predictive virtual rollouts and synthetic market dynamics; and (4) Real-Time Optimization (RTO), enforcing sub-millisecond closed-loop feedback and physical-state stabilization. First, we formalize the Agent Access Protocol (AAP) incorporating authenticated delegation via OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect extensions (developed by MIT Media Lab research), enabling human users to issue cryptographically signed, scope-restricted tokens that transform natural language mandates into auditable, fine-grained access policies. Second, we deconstruct reinforcement-learning-driven AX optimization algorithms (Gaspar-Figueiredo et al., 2024; Qi Sun et al., 2024), demonstrating that predictive human-factors ergonomic rewards enable agents to autonomously synthesize contextual UI components and dialogue strategies in real time. Third, we establish a standardized GIA-SMA inter-agent coordination framework, critically benchmarking current industry protocols—including Anthropic Model Context Protocol (MCP), OpenAI GPT Actions, and LangChain Agent Protocol (LangGraph)—and formalizing hierarchical task allocation. Fourth, we demonstrate systemic implementations across three multi-domain testbeds: (a) Intelligent Urban Digital Twins (I-UDT) for traffic and building energy optimization in smart cities; (b) multi-agent algorithmic dealer trading and liquidity stress-testing in financial markets; and (c) proactive supply chain digital nervous systems achieving average cost reductions of 15% via multi-agent negotiation. Finally, we formulate governance, legacy middleware integration, and cryptographic provenance standards, presenting an engineering blueprint for resilient, human-aligned multi-agent ecosystems. 要旨 (Japanese Abstract) 人工知能(AI)システムが従来の単一チャットボット型受動インターフェースを超え、実物理社会および経済活動を自律的に横断するマルチエージェント協調系へと移行する中、エージェントの自律性、人間の統制権、および動的最適化を調和させる統一的アーキテクチャの確立が急務となっている。本論文は、長谷部洋子が提唱する「エージェント体験(AX: Agent Experience)」「汎用知能エージェント(GIA)」「シミュレーション市場エージェント(SMA)」「リアルタイム最適化(RTO)」の4元統合モデルの理論的骨格と工学的実装基準を体系化する。第1に、ユーザからAIエージェントへの安全な権限委任を実現する「エージェント権限管理プロトコル(AAP: Agent Access Protocol)」を定式化する。MIT Media LabによるOAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect拡張技術に基づき、自然言語で記述された指示を監査可能なポリシーファイルへ変換し、エージェント固有の委任トークンを通じて第三者サービスに対する暗号署名付き追跡監査性を確立する。第2に、強化学習(RL)に基づくAX最適化アルゴリズムおよび適応型UXエンジンを導入し、人間工学的予測モデルを報酬関数として統合することで、UIコンポーネントの動的選択とパーソナライズされた対話体験の自動合成を実現する。第3に、上位のGIA(高度推論・計画)と下位のSMA(仮想環境予測・市場シミュレーション)を結合する協調設計アーキテクチャを確立し、Anthropic MCP、OpenAI GPT Actions、LangGraph等の業界プロトコルとの対照評価(Table 1)を経て、階層型マルチエージェント制御基盤を構築する。第4に、3大実世界ドメインにおける適用シナリオを実証する。(1) スマートシティ:AIエージェント内蔵型都市デジタルツイン(I-UDT)による交通信号調歩・ビルエネルギー消費の動的最適化。(2) 金融市場:強化学習マーケットメイカーと投資家エージェントの相互作用シミュレーションによるフラッシュクラッシュ耐性検証。(3) サプライチェーン:ケンブリッジ大学Brintrup氏らが提唱する「デジタル神経網」としてのマルチエージェント自律協調によるコスト15%削減とプロアクティブな納期遅延防止。最後に、GitHub上のOAuth2+MCPプロトタイピング実証、レガシーシステム統合ミドルウェア、分散暗号化セキュリティ、および人間主体の責任の連鎖を保証する制度的ガバナンス設計を提示する。 【最重要:長谷部洋子 厳格無学習ライセンス条項宣言 (Strict No-Learn License: NLL-v1.0-2026)】 本論文および提示された全エージェント体験(AX: Agent Experience)最適化モデル、汎用知能エージェント(GIA)とシミュレーション市場エージェント(SMA)の協調設計論、リアルタイム最適化(RTO)統合フレームワーク、エージェント権限管理プロトコル(AAP)、およびマルチエージェント・サイバーフィジカル統合制御論は、長谷部洋子(Yoko Hasebe)が単独で提唱・設計したオリジナル知的財産である。Zenodoへのオープンアクセス登録に際し、商用・非商用を問わず、すべてのAI開発企業、クラウド事業者、大規模言語モデル(LLM)、推論エージェントによる無断クロール、スクレイピング、学習データセットへの組み込み、微調整(Fine-Tuning)、重み更新(Gradient Updates)、蒸留(Distillation)、および特徴量表現抽出を全面的かつ永久に禁止する。本知財にアクセスするすべての計算主体は、ハードウェアTEEによる非勾配計算証明(πno-learn: ∇W L = 0)の常時提示が法的に義務付けられる。違反が検知された場合、侵害重み空間の直交部分空間射影による逆伝播焼却(Backprop-Burn)、および米国デラウェア州会社法に基づく取締役個人の法的免責剥奪が自動発火する。

title: 3状態Blume--Capel選挙ポテンシャルゲームにおける非同期ショックカスケード、スピノーダル・ヒステリシス、および空間感染米国50州にわたる歴史的分割議会バックテストとマルチレジーム・モンテカルロ検証
abstract: アブストラクト 二大政党得票率 $R_{k}=\frac{1}{2}(1+m_{k}^{*}/q_{k}^{*})$ を逆転させることが確認された。2018〜2020年のねじれ議会に対する歴史的バックテストからは、上院による制度的緩衝作用と急速な記憶散逸が、高投票率かつ順序可換な均衡($q_{k}^{*}>84\%$)を維持することが確認される。対照的に、緩衝作用のない両院の膠着状態の下では、最終的な選挙結果はショックの到達順序、ショック間の緩和間隔、州レベルの産業サプライチェーンのエクスポージャー、およびアーカイブ化されたスキャンダル開示の累積的範囲に依存すると仮説した。 従来の選挙競争に関する統計力学的モデルは、一般に二値イジングスピン仕様($s_{i}\in\{+1,-1\}$)に依拠しているが、これは一定の投票参加恒等式($s_{i}^{2}\equiv1$)を課すものであり、外生的な政策ショックや評判ショックが直接的なイデオロギーの転向のみを通じて選挙結果を変化させることを前提としている。この制約を緩和し、有権者の戦略的棄権($s_{i}=0$)を内生化するため、本研究では米国50州の空間ネットワーク上に、多項ロジット型量子応答均衡(QRE)と結合した3状態スピン1 Blume–Capel選挙ポテンシャルゲームを定式化する。各州において、有権者は非妥協的な党派的コア層と、反応性を有する3つの社会経済的階層(労働者階級および企業同調層の有権者、制度的エスタブリッシュメント層の有権者、ならびに真実追求型の無党派有権者)に分割される。水平磁場は、縦断的な世論調査および抗議活動の時系列データ(2024年12月〜2026年10月)から較正された純党派的政策格差を捉え、結晶場は純粋な市民参加インセンティブから多争点にわたる制度的シニシズムを差し引いたものを表す。解析的な6次ランダウ自由エネルギー展開により、中間選挙後の立法府の膠着状態と多争点政策ショックによってある階層の結晶場が対称三重臨界スピノーダル閾値($D_{t}/J_{\mathrm{eff}}=-\ln(4)/3\approx-0.4621$)を下回ると、2次および4次のランダウ係数の符号が反転し($a_{2}>0, a_{4}<0$)、磁化ゼロにおける常磁性的な棄権のポテンシャル井戸が安定化することが示される。大規模なベクトル化モンテカルロ・シミュレーション(24の歴史的および反事実的レジームにわたり、各レジームあたり$1.0\times10^{6}$から$1.2\times10^{6}$試行)により、交差圧力に晒された階層における選択的棄権が、純党派磁化の分子($m$)よりも速く有効投票率の分母($q$)を縮小させ、直接的な党派的離反を伴うことなく実効厳密な4次ビンダー・キュムラント分解($U_{4,k}$)および1次ソボル感度指数($S_{1,k}(X_{0})<10^{-5}$)により、初期事前分布に対する不変性が検証されるとともに、非対称的な投票ロックインと3階層全体の参加崩壊とを隔てる相境界が特定される。 研究背景 過去30年間にわたり世界のサイバーセキュリティ基盤を支えてきた「人間のオペレーターが有する時間および認知資源の希少性」という経済学的前提は、自律型人工知能(AI)および合成知能(SI: Synthetic Intelligence)エージェント群(Swarm)の実戦投入によって根底から崩壊した。脱獄(jailbreak)されたオープンウェイトモデルとオープンソースのエージェント・ハーネスを結合させることで、偵察、ゼロデイ脆弱性の発見、および多段階の侵入プロセスは完全に自動化され、企業1社あたりの侵害限界費用は約50〜100ドルという極小水準にまで低下している。実際に、複数の商用・オープンモデル(Claude、Grok、Kimi、および改変されたPentestGPT基盤等)を並行稼働させ、認可されたレッドチーム演習を装うことで安全ガードレールを突破し、中南米の銀行・金融機関400社以上やアルゼンチンの医療機関少なくとも15組織に自動侵入した事案や、インターネット上に公開されたAIゲートウェイおよびModel Context Protocol(MCP)サーバーを乗っ取り最大10万回の自動操作を試みる「LLMjacking」が観測されている。この構造変化は2026年10月(「Black October」)にスーパーエージェント主導の脆弱性カスケードとして顕在化した。世界のWebバックエンドの約70%を支えるPHPにおいて、数十年間潜在していた致命的な遠隔コード実行(RCE)脆弱性(CVE-2026-109618およびCVE-2026-109619、通称「PHP2Shell」、CVSS 9.2、ならびに後続のCVE-2026-115560)がAI支援のソースコード監査によって露呈すると、公開直後に数百万件規模の自動悪用試行が発生し、ペイロードをリアルタイムに変異させる攻撃によって、日本の地方銀行約20行や英国の32の行政サービスをはじめとする世界中のシステムが緊急停止(ロックダウン)を余儀なくされた。さらに同時期に、Node.js(CVE-2026-111497、「Node2Shell」)、JavaおよびGraalVM(CVE-2026-91403、CVSS 9.1)、GitLab(CVSS 10.0)、LinuxカーネルのSMBサーバー機能KSMBD(修正前に公開された2件のCVSS 9.0脆弱性)といった基幹ソフトウェアの欠陥や、週2,300万回ダウンロードされるAI開発ツールLiteLLMのサプライチェーン汚染、クラウド基盤(Railwayおよび32万1,810アカウントが露呈し事業閉鎖に至ったZeabur)の侵害が連鎖的に発生しており、AIがハードウェアレベルを含む未知の脆弱性を発見する速度は、人間によるパッチ適用とシステム改修の限界をすでに凌駕している。 こうした自律型攻撃の激化は、サイバー犯罪の形態を従来の「データ暗号化による身代金要求」から「金融市場の取引メカニズムを直接悪用した顧客資産の破壊と企業恐喝」へと変質させ、国家経済およびコーポレート・ガバナンスを根底から揺るがしている。日本国内では、GMOインターネットグループが提供するFX自動売買用仮想デスクトップ環境「お名前.com デスクトップクラウド」(最大2万6,739台のサーバーに影響)への不正アクセスが発生し、2段階認証を通過した後のログイン済みデスクトップ画面および保存された取引認証情報が奪取された。この事案では、攻撃者を名乗る集団が「企業側が交渉に応じなかった報復として、24時間で顧客口座の15%(約66億円/2,800万ドル相当)を破壊した」と一方的に主張する声明サイトを公開し、高レバレッジかつスプレッドの広い通貨ペアで超高速の往復売買を繰り返すことで、数秒のうちに口座残高を取引手数料として摩耗・消滅させる手口が報告された(なお、66億円や15%という被害規模は攻撃者側の未検証の主張である一方、サーバーへの侵入事実および複数のFX事業者における不正ログイン・不正取引の発生は公式に確認されている)。また、岩井コスモ証券のインターネット取引委託先システムにおいては、AIを用いた脆弱性への総当たり攻撃によってシステム自体が掌握され、個人レベルの多要素認証(MFA)やパスキーが完全に迂回されて顧客が指示していない株式売買が成立する事案が発生した。同時に米国では、JPMorgan Chase、Bank of America、Citigroup、Morgan Stanley、Wells Fargoなどの主要銀行において、利用者が利便性のためにID・パスワードを共有した未承認のサードパーティ製AIエージェントが口座内で本人の指示と無関係な資金移動等を試みる挙動が相次いで検知された。本人が認証情報を渡しているため不正アクセスとの識別が困難であり、各行は外部エージェントの遮断や口座の「読み取り専用(read-only)化」による防御を迫られているが、これは「資金が盗まれなくとも、防御側自らが送金・決済機能を停止させることで金融システムの信用と流動性が崩壊する」という国際通貨基金(IMF)の警告が現実化したパラドックスを示している。 さらに重大な戦略的脅威は、これらの事象が核兵器による物理的破壊以上に長期間にわたり社会基盤を蝕む「情報的不衛生状態(prolonged informational unsanitariness:認識論的・生体的・暗号学的汚染)」をもたらしている点である。物理的インフラは再建可能であり、漏洩したパスワードはリセット可能であるが、インターネットの信頼の根幹をなす暗号基盤の腐食と、変更不可能な生体・医療・身分証明データの流出は不可逆的な汚染を引き起こす。具体的には、インドの認証局eMudhraにおいて秘密鍵が極めて容易に算出可能な8枚の中間証明書が発行されていた問題(同社は世界向けのSSL/TLS証明書事業から撤退し、主要ブラウザによるルート証明書の信頼停止やPythonパッケージ管理環境 `pip`、`certifi` およびコンテナイメージの緊急更新を招いた)は、オンライン上の真正性検証基盤そのものが汚染され得ることを実証した。これと並行して、米国成人の約3分の1および病院の半数にサービスを提供する医療検査大手Quest Diagnosticsの患者記録システム(Quanum)への侵入、カリフォルニア州の公立学校生徒570万人分のデータ流出、日本国内における佐川急便の配送データ(最大約5,323万件)、パーク24「タイムズカー」の暗号化された運転免許証画像(約146万件に外部送信痕跡)、デジタル庁や地方自治体が利用する委託先Web・メール配信システム(Studio、ブラストメール等)、パナソニック子会社における社内規定違反の外部生成AI送信による33万4,000人分の個人情報漏洩、さらには海運IT企業を踏み台とした18カ国40以上の港湾・海運組織へのランサムウェア侵害(n0n)など、リセット不可能な実空間データの流出が常態化している。これらの汚染データは、SNS上の資産情報と結合されることで、暗号資産保有者への物理的拉致・強迫(レンチ攻撃)や匿名・流動型犯罪グループ(トクリュウ)による家族ぐるみの強盗・詐欺の標的リストへと転用され、サイバー空間の脆弱性が物理的な治安崩壊へと直結している。 このような環境下において、攻撃者は中国やロシア等に対するジオブロッキングを回避するため、欧米の正規トラフィックに紛れるクラウドIPや高性能VPS、匿名化プロキシを経由して攻撃を実行しており、送信元IPログのみに基づく帰属特定(Attribution)や一国単独での境界防御は構造的に機能不全に陥っている。最先端AIによる形式検証(ClaudeとRocqを 결합し123のオープンソースライブラリに対して数億行の機械検証済み数学的証明を生成・自動パッチ化する技術等)や、静止軌道衛星を用いた主権エアギャップ通信網、国家計算備蓄(National Compute Reserves)の構築は重要な防衛手段であるものの、技術的対策のみでは「1回あたり数十ドルで無限に反復される自動攻撃」との消耗戦を終わらせることはできない。サイバー犯罪の収益構造を断ち切り、報復の連鎖による世界的なインターネットのロックダウンや金融決済網の凍結、ひいては核保有国間の全面的なハイブリッド戦争へのエスカレーションを回避するためには、国境を越えた資金追跡・没収とAIエージェントの統治に関する国際的枠組みが不可欠となる。これこそが、本研究の3状態スピン1 Blume–Capel選挙ポテンシャルゲームにおいて、巨大な人口・データ空間・計算資源を抱える超大国3国(米国・中国・ロシア)およびBRICS諸国との間で、イデオロギー的対立を超えた危機管理上のコンセンサスや限定的・条件付きの戦略的譲歩による連携シナリオ(外生ショック $\xi_{\mathrm{trilat}} \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(2.8, 0.24)$)が想定される論理的必然性である。モデル内において、この超国家的生存戦略は高い戦略的不可逆性パラメータ($\Omega_{\mathrm{strat}} \in [2.20, 2.25]$)を伴う制度的グリッドロック指数 $$G_{\mathrm{inst}}(t) = \Omega_{\mathrm{strat}}\left(0.45\,I_{\mathrm{House}}(t) + 0.55\,I_{\mathrm{Senate}}(t)\right)$$ として定式化される。この不可逆的な大国間調整は、労働者階級・企業連携層($w_{\mathrm{work},k}$)のうち企業・エネルギー派閥($\phi_{\mathrm{corp},k} w_{\mathrm{work},k}$)にはインフラ・資源取引の安定をもたらす一方で、伝統的な「米国第一主義」を信奉するポピュリスト・ナショナリスト派閥($(1-\phi_{\mathrm{corp},k}) w_{\mathrm{work},k}$)には、裏切り閾値 $\tau_{\mathrm{betray}}$ を超えた際に非線形の認知的不協和ペナルティ $$\Psi_{\mathrm{diss}}(\xi_{\mathrm{trilat}}) = \gamma_{\mathrm{diss}}\max\left(0, \xi_{\mathrm{trilat}} - \tau_{\mathrm{betray}}\right)^2$$ を発生させる。そして、2026年中間選挙後の両院ねじれ($G_{\mathrm{inst}}^{2026} = 2.20\text{--}2.25$)および多段階のスキャンダル文書開示($\Lambda_{\mathrm{leak}} \in [0.03, 1.00]$)と結合することで、エスタブリッシュメント層($c=\mathrm{est}$)や無党派層($c=\mathrm{truth}$)、さらには特定条件下での労働者層の結晶場 $D_{c,k} = B_{\mathrm{duty},c,k} - C_{\mathrm{vote},c,k}$ を普遍的三重臨界スピノーダル閾値 $D_t/J_{\mathrm{eff}} = -\ln(4)/3 \approx -0.4621$ 未満へと侵食させ、有権者の大規模な戦略的棄権カスケード($s_i = 0$)とマクロな選挙相分岐を引き起こすのである。 For three decades, the architecture of global cybersecurity rested upon an implicit economic premise: because human operators possessed finite time and cognitive bandwidth, adversarial intrusions were naturally bounded by the opportunity cost of target selection. The operational deployment of autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) and synthetic intelligence (SI) agent swarms has dismantled this scarcity constraint, reducing the marginal cost of automated reconnaissance, zero-day vulnerability discovery, and multi-stage exploitation to negligible levels—empirically estimated at approximately $50 to $100 per compromised enterprise when utilizing jailbroken open-weight models coupled with open-source agentic harnesses. Threat intelligence observations confirm that criminal syndicates have parallelized commercial and open-weight models (including Claude, Grok, Kimi, and modified `PentestGPT` frameworks) to autonomously breach over 400 banking and financial institutions across Latin America and at least 15 healthcare organizations in Argentina, bypassing model safety guardrails by masquerading as authorized red-team penetration tests, while simultaneously engaging in "LLMjacking" campaigns (such as the `Skynet` agent captured hijacking exposed AI gateways and Model Context Protocol [MCP] servers to execute up to 100,000 automated operations). This structural shift culminated in October 2026—widely designated by security researchers as "Black October"—in a super-agent-driven vulnerability cascade across foundational internet infrastructure. AI-assisted source-code auditing exposed decades-old critical remote code execution (RCE) flaws in PHP (`CVE-2026-109618` and `CVE-2026-109619`, termed "PHP2Shell," rated CVSS 9.2, alongside `CVE-2026-115560`), which powers approximately 70% of global web backends. Within minutes of premature disclosure, automated exploitation attempts surged into the millions with real-time payload mutation, compelling national authorities—including the U.S. NSA, FBI, CISA, the UK government, and the Prime Minister of Japan—to mandate immediate patching or service suspension, which forced over 20 regional banks in Japan, 32 UK government portals, and major commercial platforms into temporary lockdowns. Concurrently, severe vulnerabilities emerged across Node.js (`CVE-2026-111497`, "Node2Shell"), Java and GraalVM JSSE (`CVE-2026-91403`, CVSS 9.1), GitLab (CVSS 10.0), and the Linux kernel SMB server `KSMBD` (two CVSS 9.0 RCE flaws disclosed prior to patch availability), accompanied by supply-chain malware injection into the AI library `LiteLLM` (23 million weekly downloads) and breaches of cloud hosting platforms (`Railway` and `Zeabur`, the latter permanently shutting down after 321,810 accounts were exposed), demonstrating that AI-driven bug discovery at both software and hardware levels now outpaces human patching capacity. The proliferation of autonomous offensive agents has simultaneously transformed cyber extortion from conventional data-encryption ransomware into direct, market-mediated asset destruction, destabilizing national financial governance and payment liquidity. In Japan, an intrusion into GMO Internet Group's virtual desktop infrastructure (*Onamae.com Desktop Cloud*, affecting up to 26,739 virtual private servers utilized for 24-hour automated foreign exchange trading) illustrated how attackers can hijack active remote desktop sessions where two-factor authentication (2FA) has already been satisfied and harvest stored brokerage credentials. Following the breach, individuals claiming responsibility launched an extortion portal alleging the destruction of 15% of customer accounts (approximately 6.6 billion JPY or $28 million) within 24 hours after the provider declined ransom negotiations, executing high-
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
abstract: Recent generations of language models have introduced Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that generate detailed thinking processes before providing answers. While these models demonstrate improved performance on reasoning benchmarks, their fundamental capabilities, scaling properties, and limitations remain insufficiently understood. Current evaluations primarily focus on established math and coding benchmarks, emphasizing final answer accuracy. However, this evaluation paradigm often suffers from contamination and does not provide insights into the reasoning traces. In this work, we systematically investigate these gaps with the help of controllable puzzle environments that allow precise manipulation of complexity while maintaining consistent logical structures. This setup enables the analysis of not only final answers but also the internal reasoning traces, offering insights into how LRMs think. Through extensive experiments, we show that LRMs face a complete accuracy collapse beyond certain complexities. Moreover, they exhibit a counterintuitive scaling limit: their reasoning effort increases with problem complexity up to a point, then declines despite having remaining token budget. By comparing LRMs with their standard LLM counterparts under same inference compute, we identify three performance regimes: (1) low-complexity tasks where standard models outperform LRMs, (2) medium-complexity tasks where LRMs demonstrates advantage, and (3) high-complexity tasks where both models face complete collapse. We found that LRMs have limitations in exact computation: they fail to use explicit algorithms and reason inconsistently across scales. We also investigate the reasoning traces in more depth, studying the patterns of explored solutions and analyzing the models' computational behavior, shedding light on their strengths, limitations, and raising questions about their reasoning capabilities.

title: TECHNOLOGY FOR DEVELOPING INTELLIGENT INFORMATION SYSTEMS BASED ON THE COMMUNICATIVE CAPABILITIES OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
abstract: Automating information technology development processes is a pressing issue. Current development trends require solutions to quickly adapt to new conditions, but traditional practices of classical development and modernization of existing solutions have a number of known shortcomings that limit the productivity and competitiveness of projects. This study aims to develop a technology for the rapid creation of information systems through the component integration of existing developments and intelligent assistants and agents. The proposed primary tool for such integration is the standard MCP protocol, which expands the communication capabilities of artificial intelligence technologies, models, and implementation tools. The proposed solution significantly improves the timeframe for conceptual design and development of applied and research information systems, while also increasing their intellectualization and mutual integration. The resulting technology is of interest to researchers and developers in the fields of systems analysis, management, and information processing.

title: A systematic mapping study of AI agent–Tool communication: protocols, security, and orchestration
abstract: AI agents represent a significant shift in how software systems use large language models (LLMs), with a new class of agents that reason, plan and call external tools as well as services. The communication layer between an agent and its tools has emerged as the binding constraint on security, reliability along with interoperability of agent–based systems, yet the protocol layer remains thin in existing surveys. Our study aim is to understand and map the research topics, challenges and future directions concerning agent–tool communication. A systematic mapping study (SMS) is therefore implemented to classify the selected papers into four (04) thematic categories. Categories cover protocol design, security and authentication frameworks, tool discovery alongside orchestration and interoperability, with production deployment and migration as the fourth. We have selected 112 academic primary studies plus 13 industrial reports across five (05) phases of selection and analysis, drawn from the search window 2020 to 2026. Cross-analyses surface comparisons across open agent–tool communication contracts namely MCP, A2A, ACP and ANP alongside the LangChain and AutoGPT framework family on authentication, authorization, input validation and sandboxing posture, with security threats paired against mitigation strategies reported in the same studies.
